title: CA Final Direct Tax Laws & International Taxation - Non Resident Taxation (Chapter 21)
description: Exhaustive, rigorous, and application-oriented CA Final MCQ practice bank for Chapter 21 (Non Resident Taxation) covering Sections 5, 6, 9, 9A, 10(4)-(23FE), 44B, 44BB, 44BBA, 44BBB, 44C, 44DA, 112/112A, Chapter XII-A (115C-115-I), Chapter XII (115A-115BBA), Chapter XII-BB (115JG), Chapter XVII-B TDS (192, 194E, 194LB-LD, 195, 196A-D, 197, 206AA/Rule 37BC), and Miscellaneous provisions (163, 173, 228A, 285).

questions.question:
Consider the following statements regarding the fundamental international taxation concepts of 'Residence-based taxation' and 'Source-based taxation' and their adoption under the Indian Income-tax Act, 1961:
I. Residence-based taxation asserts that an individual is taxable in the jurisdiction where they establish residence or domicile, irrespective of the geographic source of the income, whereas in the case of companies, the place of incorporation or place of effective management is generally considered the place of residence.
II. Source-based taxation asserts that a state exercises jurisdiction to tax income arising within its territory, irrespective of the residence of the taxpayer.
III. Under the Indian Income-tax Act, 1961, an Indian resident is taxed solely on residence-based principles, completely superseding source-based rules for foreign-sourced income.
IV. Double taxation typically arises in cross-border transactions because the country of residence and the country of source both assert concurrent taxing rights over the same income stream.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
options: I, II and IV only
I, II and III only
II and IV only
I, II, III and IV
questions.explanation: Statements I, II and IV are correct, whereas Statement III is incorrect. Statement I accurately reflects international tax principles where natural persons are taxed on worldwide income based on residence/domicile, and corporate residence is determined by place of incorporation or POEM. Statement II correctly defines source-based taxation as taxing income that originates or arises within the state's jurisdiction regardless of taxpayer residence. Statement IV correctly explains that juridical double taxation arises when the source state exercises source jurisdiction and the residence state exercises residence/worldwide jurisdiction over the same income. Statement III is incorrect because resident taxation in India does not 'supersede' source rules; rather, India taxes residents on their global income while providing foreign tax credit mechanisms under Sections 90 and 91 to relieve double taxation.

questions.question:
Mr. John, a foreign citizen of Australia, was engaged as a technical consultant by an Indian engineering conglomerate. His travel itinerary for P.Y. 2025-26 was as follows:
- Arrived at Mumbai airport on 2nd October, 2025 at 11:30 PM.
- On 20th November, 2025, he boarded an offshore survey vessel within Indian territorial waters (8 nautical miles off the coast of Gujarat) and remained on board until 15th January, 2026, when the vessel returned to port.
- He departed from India on 1st February, 2026 at 4:00 AM.
- He had never visited India prior to 1st April, 2021. His physical stay in India during the preceding four previous years was: P.Y. 2024-25: 140 days; P.Y. 2023-24: 120 days; P.Y. 2022-23: 115 days; P.Y. 2021-22: Nil.
Determine the residential status of Mr. John for A.Y. 2026-27 under the Income-tax Act, 1961.
options: Non-resident, because his stay in India in P.Y. 2025-26 is only 59 days if the offshore survey period is excluded.
Resident and Ordinarily Resident, because he satisfied the 182-day stay condition during previous year 2025-26.
Non-resident, because as a foreign citizen visiting India on a temporary contract, the basic condition of 60 days is extended to 182 days.
Resident, because his stay in India in P.Y. 2025-26 is 123 days (which is at least 60 days) and his stay during the 4 preceding previous years is 375 days (which is at least 365 days).
questions.explanation: Under Section 6(1)(c), an individual is resident if he is in India for 60 days or more in the relevant previous year and 365 days or more in the 4 preceding previous years. Both the date of arrival (2nd October 2025) and departure (1st February 2026) are counted as days in India. Furthermore, stay in India includes stay in the territorial waters of India (up to 12 nautical miles from the coastline) under Section 2(25A); hence, the 8 nautical miles offshore vessel period is fully included. Total stay in P.Y. 2025-26 is 30 days in October (31-2+1), 30 in November, 31 in December, 31 in January, and 1 day in February = 123 days. His stay in the 4 preceding years is 140 + 120 + 115 + 0 = 375 days (>= 365 days). Since he is an Australian citizen, the relaxation of 60 days to 182 days under Explanation 1 does not apply to him. Thus, he is a Resident (specifically RNOR, as his stay in the 7 preceding years is only 375 days, which is less than 730 days).

questions.question:
Mr. Vikram, an Indian citizen, was employed as a Senior Systems Architect with an IT company in Bengaluru. On 10th August, 2025, he was deputed to Frankfurt, Germany to manage a 3-year core-banking transformation project for a German banking client. He departed from India on 10th August, 2025 and did not return to India during the remainder of P.Y. 2025-26. Prior to his departure, he had lived in India continuously his entire life. The Assessing Officer contends that since Mr. Vikram stayed in India for 132 days during P.Y. 2025-26 and more than 365 days in the 4 preceding years, he satisfies Section 6(1)(c) and must be assessed as a Resident.
Evaluate the validity of the Assessing Officer's contention.
options: The AO's contention is valid, because leaving India on a 3-year deputation assignment does not constitute leaving India permanently for employment abroad.
The AO's contention is valid, because the relaxation from 60 days to 182 days is available only if the individual takes up employment with a foreign government or multinational institution.

The AO's contention is invalid, because for an Indian citizen who leaves India during the previous year for the purposes of employment outside India, the 60-day threshold in Section 6(1)(c) is substituted by 182 days; since his stay is only 132 days, he is a Non-resident.
The AO's contention is invalid, because an Indian citizen leaving India is completely exempt from income-tax in the year of relocation under Section 10(4).
questions.explanation: The contention of the Assessing Officer is invalid. Under Explanation 1(a) to Section 6(1), in the case of an individual who is a citizen of India and who leaves India in any previous year as a member of the crew of an Indian ship or for the purposes of employment outside India, the requirement of '60 days' in Section 6(1)(c) is substituted by '182 days'. As established in CBDT Circular No. 346 and judicial rulings (British Gas India, Nishant Kohli), 'employment outside India' includes deputation, secondment, or taking up employment abroad, and does not require permanent emigration or employment with a foreign entity. From 1st April 2025 to 10th August 2025, Mr. Vikram's stay in India was 132 days (April: 30, May: 31, June: 30, July: 31, August: 10). Since 132 days is less than 182 days, he does not satisfy Section 6(1) and is a Non-Resident for A.Y. 2026-27.

questions.question:
Mr. Rajesh, an Indian citizen, is a marine engineer employed as a crew member on an Indian merchant ship engaged in the carriage of freight in international traffic. The vessel departed from Chennai port on 5th June, 2025 bound for Rotterdam (Netherlands). The relevant entries in his Continuous Discharge Certificate (CDC) are:
- Date of joining the ship entered in CDC: 5th June, 2025
- Date of signing off from the ship entered in CDC: 9th December, 2025
Mr. Rajesh stayed in India for 400 days during the 4 preceding previous years and 800 days in the 7 preceding previous years.
Determine the number of days of stay of Mr. Rajesh in India during P.Y. 2025-26 and his residential status for A.Y. 2026-27 under the Income-tax Act, 1961.
options: Stay in India is 177 days; Residential status is Non-resident.
Stay in India is 178 days; Residential status is Resident and Ordinarily Resident.
Stay in India is 188 days; Residential status is Non-resident.
Stay in India is 188 days; Residential status is Resident and Ordinarily Resident.
questions.explanation: Under Explanation 2 to Section 6(1) read with Rule 126 of the Income-tax Rules, 1962, for an Indian citizen who is a crew member of an Indian ship on an eligible voyage, the period to be excluded from his stay in India commences from the date entered into the CDC in respect of joining the ship and ends on the date entered in the CDC in respect of signing off from the ship. The excluded period is from 5th June 2025 to 9th December 2025: June (30-5+1 = 26 days), July (31 days), August (31 days), September (30 days), October (31 days), November (30 days), December (9 days) = 188 days. Financial Year 2025-26 has 365 days. Hence, his stay in India is 365 - 188 = 177 days. Since he is an Indian citizen leaving as a crew member of an Indian ship, the 60-day condition is substituted by 182 days under Explanation 1(a). Because his stay is 177 days (< 182 days), he is a Non-Resident for A.Y. 2026-27, making his past stay irrelevant.

questions.question:
Mr. Kabir is a Person of Indian Origin (PIO) settled in London. During P.Y. 2025-26, he visited India for 135 days. He has been in India for 420 days during the 4 preceding previous years. His income profile for P.Y. 2025-26 is as follows:
- Income accrued and received in the UK from a local retail business: ₹32,00,000
- Income accrued and received in Germany from a consultancy profession set up in India: ₹6,00,000
- Dividend income received from Indian companies: ₹4,50,000
- Interest on fixed deposits with Indian banks: ₹5,50,000
- Rental income from commercial property in Bengaluru (net of 30% deduction): ₹2,10,000
Determine whether Mr. Kabir is a resident in India for A.Y. 2026-27 under Section 6(1).
options: Non-resident, because he is a PIO visiting India whose stay is less than 182 days, and his Indian-sourced income (excluding foreign income) is only ₹12,10,000, which is below ₹15 lakhs.
Non-resident, because the 120-day rule under Explanation 1(c) to Section 6(1) applies strictly to Indian citizens and does not extend to Persons of Indian Origin.

Resident, because his 'total income other than income from foreign sources' is ₹18,10,000 (exceeding ₹15 lakhs), his stay in P.Y. 2025-26 is 135 days (>= 120 days), and his stay in the 4 preceding years is 420 days (>= 365 days).
Resident and Ordinarily Resident, because anyone visiting India whose stay exceeds 120 days is automatically an ordinary resident.
questions.explanation: Under Explanation 1(c) to Section 6(1), for an Indian citizen or Person of Indian Origin (PIO) who resides outside India and comes on a visit to India, having 'total income, other than income from foreign sources' exceeding ₹15 lakhs, the condition of stay in India is 120 days (plus 365 days in 4 preceding years). 'Income from foreign sources' means income accruing or arising outside India, EXCEPT income derived from a business controlled in or profession set up in India. Here, Kabir's income other than foreign sources includes: (i) Profession set up in India (accrued in Germany): ₹6,00,000; (ii) Dividend from Indian companies: ₹4,50,000; (iii) Interest on Indian bank deposits: ₹5,50,000; (iv) Rental income from Bengaluru property: ₹2,10,000. Total = ₹18,10,000. The UK retail business of ₹32,00,000 is foreign source income and excluded. Since ₹18,10,000 > ₹15,00,000, his stay of 135 days (>= 120 days) and 4-year stay of 420 days (>= 365 days) makes him a Resident (specifically RNOR u/s 6(6)(c)). Option C is correct.

questions.question:
Mr. Sameer, an Indian citizen, has been residing in Dubai (UAE) for the past 12 years. During P.Y. 2025-26, he did not visit India at all (0 days of stay). He is not liable to income-tax in the UAE, as the UAE levies no personal income-tax on individuals. His income details for P.Y. 2025-26 are:
- Salary earned and received in Dubai from a UAE employer: ₹50,00,000
- Income from a trading business in Dubai controlled wholly from Mumbai: ₹11,00,000
- Rental income from a residential house in Pune (computed under house property): ₹3,50,000
- Interest on savings bank account and fixed deposits with State Bank of India: ₹2,00,000
Evaluate whether Mr. Sameer is a Deemed Resident of India for A.Y. 2026-27 under Section 6(1A), and determine his residential category under Section 6(6).
options: Non-resident, because physical presence of at least 60 days in India is a mandatory requirement for invoking residency provisions under the Income-tax Act.
Non-resident, because his Indian-sourced income is only ₹5,50,000, which does not exceed the statutory threshold of ₹15 lakhs.
Resident and Ordinarily Resident (ROR), because he has paid zero tax globally and is deemed resident under Section 6(1A).

Deemed Resident under Section 6(1A) and classified as Resident but Not Ordinarily Resident (RNOR), because his total income other than foreign sources is ₹16,50,000 (exceeding ₹15 lakhs) and he is not liable to tax in any other country.
questions.explanation: Under Section 6(1A), an individual, being an Indian citizen, having total income, other than the income from foreign sources, exceeding ₹15 lakhs during the previous year shall be deemed to be resident in India, if he is not liable to tax in any other country by reason of his domicile or residence. Total income other than foreign sources includes: (i) Dubai business controlled from Mumbai: ₹11,00,000 (included because it is a business controlled in India); (ii) Rental income from Pune: ₹3,50,000; (iii) Indian bank interest: ₹2,00,000. Total = ₹16,50,000 (exceeds ₹15 lakhs). Salary of ₹50,00,000 earned and received in UAE is foreign source income and excluded. Since Mr. Sameer is an Indian citizen, not liable to tax in UAE, and not resident u/s 6(1), he is a Deemed Resident u/s 6(1A). Under Section 6(6)(d), a deemed resident is ALWAYS an RNOR. Physical presence in India is NOT required for Section 6(1A). Thus, Option D is correct.

questions.question:
Examine the following statements regarding the application of Section 6(1A) (Deemed Residency) read with Section 2(29A) of the Income-tax Act, 1961:
I. A foreign citizen who is a Person of Indian Origin (PIO) holding a Canadian passport can be classified as a Deemed Resident under Section 6(1A) if his Indian-sourced income exceeds ₹15 lakhs and he is resident in a zero-tax jurisdiction.
II. Section 2(29A) defines 'liable to tax' to mean that there is an income-tax liability on such person under the law of that country for the time being in force, and includes a person who has subsequently been exempted from such liability under the law of that country.
III. If an individual is subject to the tax laws of a foreign country on his income, but pays zero tax due to basic personal tax exemptions or tax rebates under foreign law, he cannot be treated as 'not liable to tax' for triggering Section 6(1A).
IV. An individual who is already determined to be a resident under the basic stay conditions of Section 6(1) can simultaneously be assessed as a deemed resident under Section 6(1A).
Which of the statements given above are correct?
options: I and IV only
II and III only
I, II and III only
II, III and IV only
questions.explanation: Statements II and III are correct, while Statements I and IV are incorrect. Statement I is incorrect because Section 6(1A) applies strictly and exclusively to an individual who is a 'citizen of India'; a Person of Indian Origin (PIO) who is a foreign citizen cannot be a deemed resident. Statement II is correct because Section 2(29A) defines 'liable to tax' in relation to a person and with reference to any country to mean that there is an income-tax liability on such person under the law of that country for the time being in force and includes a person who has subsequently been exempted from such liability under the law of that country. Statement III is correct because being liable to tax refers to fiscal jurisdiction; if an individual is within the tax framework of a foreign country but pays nil tax due to basic thresholds or statutory deductions, they are still 'liable to tax', preventing Section 6(1A) from applying. Statement IV is incorrect because Section 6(1A) expressly states that it shall not apply to an individual who is a resident of India in the previous year under Section 6(1). Option B is correct.

questions.question:
Mr. Alok, an Indian citizen, is a digital entrepreneur who frequently travels across non-tax-paying jurisdictions and claims he is not liable to tax in any country. During P.Y. 2025-26, he visited India and his physical presence in India was recorded as 186 days. His total income computed under the Indian Income-tax Act (excluding foreign sources) for P.Y. 2025-26 is ₹45,00,000. He contends that he should be treated as a 'Deemed Resident' under Section 6(1A) and consequently be conferred the status of Resident but Not Ordinarily Resident (RNOR) under Section 6(6)(d), which would shield his foreign income from Indian taxation.
Evaluate Mr. Alok's contention under the provisions of the Income-tax Act, 1961.
options: His contention is valid, because Section 6(1A) contains an overriding non-obstante clause that applies whenever an Indian citizen is not liable to tax anywhere in the world.
His contention is valid, because any Indian citizen with Indian income exceeding ₹15 lakhs who is not liable to tax abroad is mandatorily classified as RNOR regardless of physical stay.
His contention is invalid, because an individual who stays in India for more than 182 days is automatically a Resident and Ordinarily Resident (ROR) without any further conditions.

His contention is invalid, because Section 6(1A) applies only if an individual is NOT a resident under Section 6(1); since Mr. Alok stayed in India for 186 days (>= 182 days), he is a resident under Section 6(1)(a) and his status (ROR vs RNOR) must be determined under Section 6(6)(a)/(b).
questions.explanation: Mr. Alok's contention is invalid. Section 6(1A) contains an explicit statutory exclusion: 'However, this provision will not apply in case of an individual who is a resident of India in the previous year as per section 6(1).' Since Mr. Alok's physical presence in India during P.Y. 2025-26 was 186 days, he satisfies the primary basic condition of stay of 182 days or more under Section 6(1)(a). Therefore, he is an ordinary resident under Section 6(1). Because he is resident under Section 6(1), Section 6(1A) cannot be invoked by him. His classification as ROR or RNOR will depend strictly on whether he satisfies the additional conditions of Section 6(6)(a) or (b) (being non-resident in 9 out of 10 preceding previous years or stay of 729 days or less in 7 preceding previous years). He cannot circumvent ROR status by claiming deemed residency under Section 6(1A). Thus, Option D is correct.

questions.question:
Mr. David, a foreign citizen and international sports coach, was resident in India for the first time during P.Y. 2025-26 by staying in India for 185 days. His physical presence in India during the previous years preceding P.Y. 2025-26 was as follows:
- P.Y. 2024-25: 190 days (Resident)
- P.Y. 2023-24: 185 days (Resident)
- P.Y. 2022-23: 180 days (Non-resident, stay in 4 preceding years was 0)
- P.Y. 2021-22 to P.Y. 2015-16: 0 days in each year (Non-resident)
Determine Mr. David's residential status for A.Y. 2026-27.
options: Resident and Ordinarily Resident (ROR), because he was resident in 2 out of 10 preceding previous years.

Resident but Not Ordinarily Resident (RNOR), because although he was resident in 2 out of 10 preceding previous years, his stay in India during the 7 preceding previous years was only 555 days (less than 730 days).
Non-resident, because he has not been resident in India for at least 5 out of the 10 preceding previous years.
Resident and Ordinarily Resident (ROR), because stay in 7 preceding years is only an alternative condition and not mandatory.
questions.explanation: Mr. David is a resident in P.Y. 2025-26 under Section 6(1)(a) since his stay is 185 days (>= 182 days). Under Section 6(6), for an individual to be 'Resident and Ordinarily Resident' (ROR), he must satisfy BOTH additional conditions: (1) He must be resident in India in at least 2 out of the 10 previous years immediately preceding the relevant previous year; AND (2) He must have stayed in India for a total period of 730 days or more during the 7 previous years immediately preceding the relevant previous year. If he satisfies either condition of Section 6(6) (being non-resident in 9 out of 10 years OR stay of 729 days or less in 7 years), he is RNOR. Here, Mr. David was resident in 2 out of 10 years (P.Y. 2024-25 and 2023-24). However, his aggregate stay in the 7 preceding previous years is 190 + 185 + 180 + 0 + 0 + 0 + 0 = 555 days, which is less than 730 days. Failing this condition renders him a Resident but Not Ordinarily Resident (RNOR) for A.Y. 2026-27. Option B is correct.

questions.question:
Ms. Ananya, an Indian citizen residing in the USA, visits India every year. During P.Y. 2025-26, she stayed in India for 150 days. Her stay in India during the 4 preceding previous years was 400 days, and during the 7 preceding previous years was 760 days. She was a resident in India in 4 out of the 10 preceding previous years. Her total income (other than income from foreign sources) for P.Y. 2025-26 is ₹28,00,000.
What is the residential status of Ms. Ananya for A.Y. 2026-27 under the Income-tax Act, 1961?
options: Resident and Ordinarily Resident (ROR), because she meets both conditions of Section 6(6)(a) and (b) by being resident in 4 out of 10 years and staying 760 days in 7 years.
Non-resident, because she is an Indian citizen visiting India whose stay does not exceed 181 days.

Resident but Not Ordinarily Resident (RNOR), because an Indian citizen visiting India whose stay is 120 days or more but less than 182 days and whose Indian income exceeds ₹15 lakhs is statutorily classified as RNOR under Section 6(6)(c), irrespective of past stay.
Deemed Resident under Section 6(1A), because her income exceeds ₹15 lakhs.
questions.explanation: Ms. Ananya is an Indian citizen visiting India. Under Explanation 1(c) to Section 6(1), since her total income other than foreign sources exceeds ₹15 lakhs (₹28,00,000) and her stay in India is 120 days or more (150 days) and in 4 preceding years is 365 days or more (400 days), she is a Resident. Crucially, under Section 6(6)(c), an individual who is an Indian citizen or PIO having total income (other than foreign sources) exceeding ₹15 lakhs who has been in India for 120 days or more but less than 182 days during that previous year is MANDATORILY classified as 'not ordinarily resident'. The statute creates a separate categorical RNOR classification for such 120-day visitors. Even though Ms. Ananya was resident in 4 out of 10 preceding years and stayed for 760 days in 7 preceding years, Section 6(6)(c) statutorily classifies her as an RNOR. Option C is correct.

questions.question:
The 'Ramakant HUF' has its ancestral family home in Varanasi, where two elderly family members reside. The Karta of the HUF, Mr. Ramakant, has been permanently based in Singapore for the last 15 years running an international trading business. All strategic financial decisions, investment choices, bank account operations, and asset allocation decisions concerning the HUF are taken exclusively by Mr. Ramakant from Singapore. During P.Y. 2025-26, Mr. Ramakant visited Varanasi for 14 days solely for a family wedding, during which no family business or commercial matters were transacted. The Assessing Officer claims that because the HUF has an ancestral house in India and the Karta stayed in India for 14 days, the control and management of the HUF is partly in India, making the HUF a Resident.
Evaluate the Assessing Officer's claim in light of Section 6(2) and established principles.
options: The AO's claim is invalid, because 'control and management' refers to de facto central control and management—the 'head and brain'—where key decisions are made; merely owning a home or visiting India for social events without taking business decisions does not situate control and management in India, making the HUF a Non-resident.
The AO's claim is valid, because ownership of immovable property in India where members reside is conclusive proof of control and management.
The AO's claim is valid, because physical presence of the Karta in India for even a single day during the previous year automatically shifts control and management partly to India.
The AO's claim is invalid, because an HUF can only be resident if 100% of its coparceners reside in India throughout the previous year.
questions.explanation: Under Section 6(2), an HUF is resident in India if the control and management of its affairs is situated wholly or partly in India. If control and management is situated wholly outside India, it is a non-resident. Landmark judicial decisions (San Paulo Brazilian Rly. Co., V.V.R. Firm) and CBDT guidelines establish that 'control and management' refers to the central control and management—the 'head and brain'—where key strategic and management decisions are de facto made. Merely owning an ancestral house in India where family members reside does not locate control and management in India unless important business decisions are taken there. Furthermore, a brief personal visit by the Karta without transacting any business does not shift control. Since all strategic decisions were taken by Mr. Ramakant exclusively from Singapore, control and management was situated wholly outside India, rendering the HUF a Non-Resident. The AO's claim is invalid. Option A is correct.

questions.question:
The 'Mehta & Sons HUF' is engaged in manufacturing textiles. During P.Y. 2025-26, its management and affairs were partly controlled from Surat, India, and partly from Dubai, UAE. Hence, the HUF is Resident in India for A.Y. 2026-27. The Karta of the HUF, Mr. Harsh Mehta, has the following stay record in India:
- P.Y. 2025-26: 125 days
- Preceding 7 previous years (P.Y. 2018-19 to P.Y. 2024-25): Total stay in India was 710 days.
- In the 10 previous years preceding P.Y. 2025-26, Mr. Harsh Mehta was resident in India in 6 previous years.
Determine the residential status of the 'Mehta & Sons HUF' for A.Y. 2026-27.
options: Resident and Ordinarily Resident (ROR), because the HUF's business is partly controlled in India and the Karta was resident in 6 out of 10 preceding previous years.
Non-resident, because the Karta did not stay in India for 182 days in P.Y. 2025-26.
Resident and Ordinarily Resident (ROR), because physical presence of the Karta is evaluated only during the relevant previous year and not in preceding years for an HUF.

Resident but Not Ordinarily Resident (RNOR), because the Karta satisfies the condition of being resident in at least 2 out of 10 preceding years, but fails the condition of staying 730 days or more in the 7 preceding previous years (stay was only 710 days).
questions.explanation: Under Section 6(2), since the control and management of the HUF's affairs is situated partly in India, the Mehta & Sons HUF is a Resident. To determine whether a resident HUF is 'Resident and Ordinarily Resident' (ROR) or 'Resident but Not Ordinarily Resident' (RNOR), Section 6(6) requires that the Karta must satisfy BOTH additional conditions applicable to individuals: (1) The Karta must be resident in India in at least 2 out of the 10 previous years immediately preceding the relevant previous year; AND (2) The Karta must have stayed in India for a total period of 730 days or more during the 7 previous years immediately preceding the relevant previous year. If the Karta fails EITHER condition, the HUF is RNOR. Here, Karta was resident in 6 out of 10 preceding years (Satisfied), but his stay in the 7 preceding years was 710 days, which is less than 730 days (Failed). Therefore, the HUF is Resident but Not Ordinarily Resident (RNOR). Option D is correct.

questions.question:
'Apex Global Partners' is a partnership firm constituted under the Indian Partnership Act, 1932, consisting of 4 partners: Partner A (resident in the UK), Partner B (resident in the USA), Partner C (resident in Germany), and Partner D (resident in India). The partnership deed provides that all business decisions must be approved by a simple majority of partners. During P.Y. 2025-26, all key strategic business decisions, signing of export contracts, and financial disbursements were conducted via virtual meetings chaired by Partner D from Mumbai, and bank accounts were operated from Mumbai. The three non-resident partners argue that since 75% of the partners are non-residents and physical meetings took place outside India, the firm must be assessed as a Non-resident.
Evaluate the residential status of 'Apex Global Partners' for A.Y. 2026-27 under Section 6(4).
options: Non-resident, because the residential status of a partnership firm is determined by the residential status of the majority of its partners holding greater than 50% profit share.

Resident, because under Section 6(4), a firm is resident in India if the control and management of its affairs is situated wholly or partly in India; the residential status of individual partners is wholly immaterial.
Resident but Not Ordinarily Resident (RNOR), because the majority of partners are non-residents.
Non-resident, because a firm cannot be resident in India unless 100% of its partners are Indian residents.
questions.explanation: Under Section 6(4), a firm, Association of Persons (AOP), or Body of Individuals (BOI) is resident in India if the control and management of its affairs is situated wholly or partly in India. Where control and management is situated wholly outside India, it is a non-resident. Key statutory principles: (1) The residential status of individual partners/members is completely immaterial when determining the residential status of a Firm/AOP/BOI; (2) If even a part of the control and management is situated in India (such as strategic decisions taken by Partner D and banking operations handled from Mumbai), the firm is Resident in India; (3) A firm can only be Resident or Non-Resident; the status of RNOR does not exist for firms. Therefore, Apex Global Partners is a Resident in India for A.Y. 2026-27. Option B is correct.

questions.question:
Consider the following statements regarding the residential status of companies under Section 6(3) of the Income-tax Act, 1961:
I. An Indian company is always treated as resident in India, even if its entire business operations are located abroad and all meetings of its Board of Directors are held outside India.
II. A foreign company is treated as resident in India in any previous year only if its Place of Effective Management (POEM), in that year, is in India.
III. 'Place of Effective Management' (POEM) is statutorily defined in Explanation to Section 6(3) as the place where key management and commercial decisions that are necessary for the conduct of the business of an entity as a whole are, in substance made.
IV. A company incorporated outside India that is held to be resident in India by virtue of its POEM being in India is classified as a 'Resident but Not Ordinarily Resident' (RNOR).
Which of the statements given above are correct?
options: I, II and III only
II, III and IV only
I, III and IV only
I, II, III and IV
questions.explanation: Statements I, II and III are correct, while Statement IV is incorrect. Statement I is correct because under Section 6(3)(i), an Indian company is resident in India in every previous year by virtue of its incorporation; POEM is completely irrelevant for an Indian company. Statement II is correct because under Section 6(3)(ii), a foreign company is resident in India only if its POEM in that year is in India. Statement III is correct because Explanation to Section 6(3) defines POEM as 'a place where key management and commercial decisions that are necessary for the conduct of the business of an entity as a whole are, in substance made'. Statement IV is incorrect because companies can only be Resident or Non-Resident; the category of RNOR applies exclusively to Individuals and HUFs under Section 6(6). Thus, Statements I, II and III are correct. Option A is correct.

questions.question:
Zeta Holdings Inc., a company incorporated under the laws of Mauritius, is an investment holding company. During P.Y. 2025-26, all key strategic decisions regarding acquisition and divestment of group investments are made by its Board of Directors in meetings held in New Delhi, India. The company's total gross receipts and turnover for the financial year 2025-26 amounted to ₹38 crore (comprising dividend and capital gains). The Assessing Officer seeks to invoke the CBDT POEM Guidelines (Circular No. 6/2017) to determine the company's POEM as being in India.
Evaluate the applicability of the POEM Guidelines to Zeta Holdings Inc. for A.Y. 2026-27.
options: The POEM Guidelines apply fully, because any company earning passive income is mandatorily subject to the Active Business Outside India (ABOI) test regardless of turnover.
The company is automatically deemed to be an Indian company because its turnover is below ₹50 crore and its meetings were in Delhi.
The POEM Guidelines do not apply, but the Assessing Officer can unilaterally treat the company as resident without seeking any approvals.

The POEM Guidelines (Circular No. 6/2017) shall not apply to Zeta Holdings Inc., because CBDT Circular No. 8/2017 explicitly clarifies that POEM guidelines shall not apply to a company having turnover or gross receipts of ₹50 crores or less in a financial year.
questions.explanation: The CBDT, vide Circular No. 8/2017 dated 23.02.2017, explicitly clarified that the guidelines for determination of Place of Effective Management (POEM) of a company shall not apply to a company having turnover or gross receipts of ₹50 crores or less in a financial year. Since Zeta Holdings Inc.'s turnover/gross receipts for the financial year 2025-26 was ₹38 crore, which does not exceed ₹50 crore, the POEM guidelines issued under Circular No. 6/2017 do not apply to it. This statutory circular creates a safe harbour to shield small foreign entities and shell companies with low gross turnover from complex POEM assessments. Therefore, Option D is correct.

questions.question: Under the CBDT Guiding Principles for determination of Place of Effective Management (POEM) of a foreign company (Circular No. 6/2017), a company shall be said to be engaged in 'Active Business Outside India' (ABOI) if which of the following cumulative conditions are satisfied?
options: Passive income <= 50% of total income; Assets in India < 50% of total assets; Employees in India/resident in India < 50% of total employees; and Payroll expenses on Indian employees < 50% of total payroll expenditure.

Active income >= 50% of total income; Assets in India <= 50% of total assets; Employees in India <= 50% of total employees; and Payroll expenses on Indian employees <= 50% of total payroll expenditure.
Passive income < 50% of total income; Assets in India < 50% of total assets; Employees in India < 50% of total employees; and Board meetings in India < 50% of total board meetings.
Domestic sales < 50% of global turnover; Assets in India < 50% of total assets; Directors resident in India < 50% of total directors; and Payroll in India < 50% of total payroll.
questions.explanation: As per CBDT Circular No. 6/2017, a company shall be said to be engaged in 'active business outside India' (ABOI) if: (1) its passive income is not more than 50% of its total income (<= 50%); (2) less than 50% of its total assets are situated in India (< 50%); (3) less than 50% of the total number of employees are situated in India or are resident in India (< 50%); and (4) the payroll expenses incurred on such employees is less than 50% of its total payroll expenditure (< 50%). All four conditions must be cumulatively satisfied based on the average data of the previous year and two years prior to that. Note the specific distinction: passive income is 'not more than 50%', whereas assets, employees, and payroll must be strictly 'less than 50%'. Option A correctly states these four cumulative tests.

questions.question:
Global Trade Ltd, a company incorporated in the United Kingdom, has the following income breakup (3-year average):
1. Profit from purchase of goods from non-associated enterprises and sale to Associated Enterprises (AEs): ₹40 lakhs
2. Profit from purchase of goods from AEs and sale to independent third parties: ₹30 lakhs
3. Profit from purchase of goods from AEs and sale to other AEs: ₹50 lakhs
4. Royalty income received from third parties: ₹20 lakhs
5. Dividend income from foreign subsidiaries: ₹10 lakhs
6. Interest income from loans advanced to third parties: ₹10 lakhs
(Global Trade Ltd is a trading company and not a bank or public financial institution). Total Income of Global Trade Ltd is ₹160 lakhs.
Calculate the quantum of 'Passive Income' and determine whether Global Trade Ltd satisfies the passive income test for ABOI under Circular No. 6/2017.
options: Passive income is ₹50 lakhs (31.25% of total income); satisfies the passive income test.
Passive income is ₹120 lakhs (75% of total income); fails the passive income test.
Passive income is ₹90 lakhs (56.25% of total income); fails the passive income test because passive income exceeds 50% of total income.
Passive income is ₹40 lakhs (25% of total income); satisfies the passive income test.
questions.explanation: Under Circular No. 6/2017, 'Passive income' of a company is defined as the aggregate of: (i) Income from transactions where BOTH the purchase and sale of goods is from/to its associated enterprises (AEs); and (ii) Income by way of royalty, dividend, capital gains, interest (except for banking cos and PFIs), or rental income. Here: (1) Purchases from non-AEs and sales to AEs: NOT passive income; (2) Purchases from AEs and sales to non-AEs: NOT passive income; (3) Purchases from AEs and sales to AEs: Included = ₹50 lakhs; (4) Royalty income: Included = ₹20 lakhs; (5) Dividend income: Included = ₹10 lakhs; (6) Interest income (non-banking co): Included = ₹10 lakhs. Total Passive Income = ₹50L + ₹20L + ₹10L + ₹10L = ₹90 lakhs. Percentage of passive income to total income = (₹90 lakhs / ₹160 lakhs) * 100 = 56.25%. Since passive income is more than 50% of total income, Global Trade Ltd fails the passive income test. Option C is correct.

questions.question:
Orion Corp. is incorporated in Delaware, USA. To determine whether Orion Corp. is engaged in 'Active Business Outside India' (ABOI) for P.Y. 2025-26, the 3-year average data (for P.Y. 2025-26, 2024-25, and 2023-24) was compiled:
- Total Income: ₹100 crore (Passive Income: ₹42 crore)
- Total Assets: ₹250 crore (Assets situated in India: ₹110 crore)
- Total Employees: 400 (Employees situated or resident in India: 180)
- Total Payroll Expenditure: ₹40 crore (Payroll expenditure on Indian employees: ₹22 crore)
Determine whether Orion Corp. satisfies the test of 'Active Business Outside India' (ABOI) for P.Y. 2025-26 under CBDT Circular No. 6/2017.
options: Yes, Orion Corp. is engaged in ABOI because passive income is <= 50%, assets in India are < 50%, and employees in India are < 50%.
No, Orion Corp. is not engaged in ABOI because payroll expenditure on Indian employees is 55% of total payroll (exceeding the 50% limit), even though the other three conditions are satisfied.
No, Orion Corp. is not engaged in ABOI because assets situated in India exceed 40%, which violates the threshold.
Yes, Orion Corp. is engaged in ABOI because satisfying any 3 out of the 4 conditions is sufficient under CBDT Circular No. 6/2017.
questions.explanation: For a company to be engaged in 'Active Business Outside India' (ABOI), all four conditions must be CUMULATIVELY satisfied based on the 3-year average data: (1) Passive income: ₹42 cr / ₹100 cr = 42% (<= 50% -> Satisfied); (2) Assets in India: ₹110 cr / ₹250 cr = 44% (< 50% -> Satisfied); (3) Employees in India: 180 / 400 = 45% (< 50% -> Satisfied); (4) Payroll expenditure on Indian employees: ₹22 cr / ₹40 cr = 55%. Condition (4) strictly requires that payroll expenses incurred on employees situated or resident in India must be LESS than 50% of total payroll expenditure. Here it is 55%, which fails the requirement. Since the 4 conditions are cumulative, failure of even a single condition means Orion Corp. is not engaged in active business outside India. Option B is correct.

questions.question:
Zenith Ltd, a company incorporated in Singapore, is a 100% subsidiary of an Indian parent, Bharat Ltd. Zenith Ltd satisfies all conditions of 'Active Business Outside India' (ABOI). During P.Y. 2025-26, Zenith Ltd held 6 meetings of its Board of Directors: 4 meetings in Singapore and 2 meetings in New Delhi. However, an enquiry by the Revenue revealed that under an internal governance framework, for all commercial contracts exceeding SGD 500,000 (which constituted 98% of the total contract value of Zenith Ltd), the Board of Zenith Ltd had no decision-making power and was mandated to obtain prior approval and follow the binding directions of the Managing Director of Bharat Ltd in Mumbai.
Determine the POEM and residential status of Zenith Ltd for A.Y. 2026-27.
options: POEM is presumed to be outside India because Zenith Ltd is engaged in ABOI and the majority of board meetings (4 out of 6) were held outside India; the internal approval process cannot override board meetings.
Zenith Ltd is deemed to be an Indian company because it is a 100% subsidiary of an Indian parent.
POEM is outside India because Singapore has a double taxation avoidance agreement (DTAA) with India that automatically bars India from examining POEM.

POEM shall be considered to be in India because, although the company is engaged in ABOI, the Board has de facto stood aside and the key management and commercial decisions are being exercised by the Indian holding company.
questions.explanation: Under Circular No. 6/2017 (specifically Example 4): For a company engaged in active business outside India, POEM shall be presumed to be outside India if the majority of board meetings are held outside India. However, this presumption is rebutted if the Board of Directors is NOT exercising its powers of management and such powers are being exercised by the holding company or any other person resident in India (i.e. the Board of Directors has stood aside or its powers have been usurped). Here, 98% of Zenith Ltd's contracts require mandatory prior approval and binding directions from Bharat Ltd's MD in Mumbai. This demonstrates that the Board has de facto abdicated its decision-making authority to the Indian parent. Therefore, POEM is considered to be in India, and Zenith Ltd is a Resident in India for A.Y. 2026-27. Option D is correct.

questions.question:
TechGlobal Inc., a multinational enterprise based in the US, established a Regional Headquarter (RHQ) in Bengaluru, India. The Indian RHQ provides centralized support services to subsidiaries located across the Asia-Pacific (APAC) region within the general and objective principles of global policies laid down by the parent entity. These support services cover:
- Global payroll software integration
- Standardized human resource (HR) performance appraisal frameworks
- Enterprise IT infrastructure and network platform support
- Routine banking operational procedures
The Assessing Officer contends that because the Indian RHQ supervises these functions, the Boards of the APAC subsidiaries have 'stood aside' and therefore the POEM of all APAC subsidiaries is located in India.
Evaluate the validity of the Assessing Officer's contention in light of CBDT Circular No. 25/2017.
options: The contention is valid, because any operational or HR supervision conducted from India automatically establishes POEM of foreign subsidiaries in India.
The contention is valid, because the Indian RHQ is an Association of Persons (AOP) which makes all subsidiaries Indian residents.

The contention is invalid, because CBDT Circular No. 25/2017 clarifies that operating within general and objective global policies in routine fields like payroll, HR, IT, and routine banking operational procedures does not constitute a case of the Board standing aside and alone will not be a basis for establishing POEM in India.
The contention is invalid, but only if the Indian RHQ pays a flat 40% equalization levy to the Indian Government.
questions.explanation: CBDT Circular No. 25/2017 dated 23.10.2017 explicitly clarifies that so long as the Regional Headquarter operates for subsidiaries/group companies in a region within the general and objective principles of global policy of the group laid down by the parent entity in the field of Payroll functions, Accounting, HR functions, IT infrastructure and network platforms, Supply chain functions, and Routine banking operational procedures, and not being specific to any entity or group of entities per se, it would, in itself, NOT constitute a case of the Board of Directors standing aside. Such activities of the Regional Headquarter in India alone will not be a basis for establishment of POEM for such subsidiaries/group companies. (GAAR may only be invoked if there is abusive tax avoidance). Thus, the AO's contention is invalid. Option C is correct.

questions.question:
BlueOcean Ltd, a company incorporated in Cyprus, is not engaged in active business outside India (fails ABOI). Its senior management is decentralized:
- The Chief Operating Officer (COO) and Sales Director operate from Athens, Greece.
- The Chief Technology Officer (CTO) operates from London, UK.
- The Managing Director (MD) and the Chief Financial Officer (CFO), together with their executive support staff, are permanently based in and operate from an office in Gurugram, India, where they formulate and approve key commercial strategies, raise corporate finance, and direct global business acquisitions via video conferencing.
- The majority of the company's factory employees work in Cyprus.
Where is the 'Head Office' and Place of Effective Management (POEM) of BlueOcean Ltd located under Circular No. 6/2017?
options: Gurugram, India, because where senior management is decentralized, the Head Office is the location where the highest level of management (MD and CFO) and their direct support staff are located and where key strategies are formulated.
Cyprus, because the majority of factory employees work there and the company is incorporated in Cyprus.
Athens, because the Chief Operating Officer directs daily production from Greece.
London, because the technology infrastructure is managed from the UK.
questions.explanation: Under Circular No. 6/2017, for a company not engaged in ABOI, POEM is determined via a two-stage process: identifying who makes key management/commercial decisions and where they are made. The location of the Head Office is a vital factor. 'Head Office' of a company is the place where senior management and their direct support staff are located. In cases where senior management is decentralized and operates from different locations on a permanent basis participating via video conferencing, the Head Office would normally be the location where the highest level of management (for example, the Managing Director and Financial Director/CFO) and their direct support staff are located. Head office is not necessarily where the majority of employees work or where the board meets. Since the MD and CFO and their direct support staff are permanently based in Gurugram formulating key policies, the Head Office and POEM are in India. Option A is correct.

questions.question:
Under CBDT Circular No. 6/2017, the determination of Place of Effective Management (POEM) is based on all relevant facts and substance over form, rather than isolated facts.
Which of the following isolated facts, by themselves, do NOT constitute conclusive evidence that the POEM of a foreign company is in India?
I. The fact that a foreign company is completely owned by an Indian company.
II. The existence of a Permanent Establishment (PE) of the foreign entity in India.
III. The fact that one or some of the Directors of the foreign company reside in India.
IV. The presence of local management in India in respect of activities carried out by the foreign company in India.
V. The existence in India of support functions that are preparatory and auxiliary in character.
options: I, II and III only
I, III and V only
II, IV and V only
I, II, III, IV and V
questions.explanation: CBDT Circular No. 6/2017 specifically lists five isolated facts that do NOT by themselves establish effective management or POEM in India: (i) The fact that a foreign company is completely owned by an Indian company; (ii) The fact that there exists a Permanent Establishment (PE) of a foreign entity in India; (iii) The fact that one or some of the Directors of a foreign company reside in India; (iv) The fact of local management being situated in India in respect of activities carried out by a foreign company in India; and (v) The existence in India of support functions that are preparatory and auxiliary in character. POEM is determined by examining whether key management and commercial decisions for the business as a whole are made in India, adopting a holistic approach over a period of time rather than relying on isolated facts. All five statements are correct negative factors. Option D is correct.

questions.question:
To prevent arbitrary application of POEM provisions by field officers, the CBDT has prescribed strict administrative safeguards under Circular No. 6/2017.
Which of the following procedural steps is/are MANDATORY before an Assessing Officer (AO) can hold a foreign company as resident in India on the basis of POEM?
I. The AO must obtain prior approval from the Principal Commissioner or Commissioner (PCIT/CIT) before initiating any proceedings to hold a foreign company resident on the basis of POEM.
II. Before issuing any final finding holding the foreign company resident on the basis of POEM, the AO must seek prior approval of a Collegium of three members consisting of Principal Commissioners or Commissioners constituted by the Principal Chief Commissioner of Income-tax.
III. The Collegium of Commissioners is statutorily required to provide an opportunity of being heard to the foreign company before issuing any directions in the matter.
IV. The Dispute Resolution Panel (DRP) must confirm the POEM order within 30 days before any notice under Section 148 is issued.
options: I and II only
I, II and III only
II and III only
I, II, III and IV
questions.explanation: Under CBDT Circular No. 6/2017, the administrative safeguards are twofold: (1) Stage 1 (Initiation): The Assessing Officer (AO) shall, BEFORE initiating any proceedings for holding a company incorporated outside India, on the basis of its POEM, as being resident in India, seek prior approval of the Principal Commissioner or the Commissioner (PCIT/CIT). (Statement I is correct). (2) Stage 2 (Final Finding): In case the AO proposes to hold the foreign company as resident on the basis of POEM, any such finding shall be given by the AO ONLY after seeking prior approval of a collegium of three members consisting of Principal Commissioners or Commissioners constituted by the Principal Chief Commissioner of the region. (Statement II is correct). (3) The collegium so constituted SHALL provide an opportunity of being heard to the company before issuing any directions. (Statement III is correct). Statement IV is incorrect as DRP is not part of the POEM circular's approval mechanism. Hence, Statements I, II, and III are correct. Option B is correct.

questions.question:
Gamma Inc., a company incorporated in Ireland, is held to be resident in India for the first time during P.Y. 2025-26 on account of its POEM being in India. Gamma Inc. had never been assessed to tax in India in earlier years. Gamma Inc. is regularly assessed to tax in Ireland, where tax depreciation is allowed on an individual asset basis under Irish tax laws.
As on 1st April, 2025 (the 1st day of P.Y. 2025-26), the details of a specialized machine owned by Gamma Inc. are:
- Original Cost in 2022: €1,000,000
- Written Down Value (WDV) as per Irish Tax Records: €620,000
- Written Down Value (WDV) as per Financial Books of Account: €700,000
- Fair Market Value: €850,000
In terms of Notification No. 29/2018 issued under Section 115JH of the Income-tax Act, 1961, what value shall be adopted as the opening WDV of the machine for Indian tax computation for P.Y. 2025-26?
options: €700,000, being the book value appearing in the financial accounts maintained under Irish corporate law.
€1,000,000, being the historical cost of acquisition.
€620,000, being the WDV of the depreciable asset as per the tax records in the foreign country on the 1st day of the previous year.
€850,000, being the fair market value as on the date the company became resident in India.
questions.explanation: Notification No. 29/2018 dated 22.06.2018 issued under Section 115JH provides specific transition rules for determining opening WDV for a foreign company that becomes resident in India for the first time due to POEM: (1) If the foreign company is assessed to tax in the foreign jurisdiction: Where depreciation is required to be taken into account for the purpose of computation of its taxable income, the Written Down Value (WDV) of the depreciable asset as per the tax records in the foreign country on the 1st day of the previous year shall be adopted as the opening WDV for the said previous year. (2) If the foreign company is not assessed to tax in the foreign jurisdiction, the WDV appearing in its books of account on the 1st day of the previous year is adopted. Since Gamma Inc. is assessed to tax in Ireland and tax records show a WDV of €620,000 on 1st April, 2025, that exact figure (€620,000 converted into INR as per Rule 115) must be adopted as the opening WDV. Option C is correct.

questions.question:
Delta Corp., a company incorporated in Japan whose accounting year runs from 1st January to 31st December (calendar year), is held to be resident in India for the first time during P.Y. 2025-26 (1st April 2025 to 31st March 2026) due to POEM. Delta Corp. has brought forward business losses from calendar year 2023 under Japanese tax records.
Consider the following statements regarding the transition provisions under Notification No. 29/2018 (Section 115JH):
I. Delta Corp. is required to prepare a single profit and loss account and balance sheet for the 15-month period from 1st January, 2025 to 31st March, 2026 because the period from 1st January, 2025 to 31st March, 2025 is less than 6 months.
II. The brought forward loss from foreign tax records shall be allowed to be set off against ANY income of Delta Corp., including its existing Indian income that was otherwise chargeable to tax in India even without POEM.
III. The brought forward loss shall be allowed to be carried forward and set off only for the remaining period out of the 8-year limit calculated from the year in which the loss occurred for the first time in the foreign jurisdiction.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
options: I and III only
I and II only
II and III only
I, II and III
questions.explanation: Statements I and III are correct, while Statement II is incorrect. Statement I is correct: Under Notification No. 29/2018, where the foreign company's accounting year is a calendar year and it becomes resident during P.Y. 2025-26, the period from 1st January 2025 to 31st March 2025 is less than 6 months. Hence, it is included in the accounting year immediately preceding the accounting year in which it is held resident, resulting in a single 15-month period from 1st January 2025 to 31st March 2026. (Example 1 of the Notification). Statement II is incorrect: The notification expressly provides that brought forward loss and unabsorbed depreciation shall be allowed to be set off ONLY against such income of the foreign company which has become chargeable to tax in India on account of it becoming resident in India due to application of POEM, and NOT against income which otherwise would have been chargeable to tax in India. Statement III is correct: Loss and unabsorbed depreciation are allowed to be set off and carried forward for the remaining period calculated from the year in which they occurred for the first time. Option A is correct.

questions.question:
A foreign company, Omega Inc., becomes resident in India for the first time during P.Y. 2025-26 on account of its Place of Effective Management (POEM) being in India.
Which of the following propositions correctly reflect the tax consequences prescribed under Notification No. 29/2018 issued under Section 115JH of the Income-tax Act, 1961?
I. Omega Inc. shall be assessed at the corporate tax rate applicable to domestic companies (e.g., 22% or 25%) since it has attained the status of an Indian resident.
II. Omega Inc. shall continue to be taxed at the rate applicable to a foreign company (i.e. 35% plus applicable surcharge and cess), because in case of conflict between provisions applicable to the foreign company as a resident and as a foreign company, the latter shall prevail.
III. Where more than one provision of Chapter XVII-B (TDS) applies to Omega Inc. as a resident as well as a foreign company, the provision applicable to the foreign company alone shall apply.
IV. Omega Inc. is entitled to claim foreign tax credit under Section 90 or Section 91 in respect of taxes paid in foreign jurisdictions on doubly taxed income.
options: I, III and IV only
II, III and IV only
II and III only
I, II, III and IV
questions.explanation: Notification No. 29/2018 dated 22.06.2018 under Section 115JH explicitly provides: (1) Rate of Tax: Subject to specific exceptions, the foreign company shall continue to be treated as a foreign company even if resident in India. In case of conflict between the provisions applicable to the foreign company as resident and as foreign company, the latter shall prevail. Therefore, the rate of income-tax applicable to a foreign company (35% plus surcharge and cess) remains applicable. Statement I is incorrect and Statement II is correct. (2) TDS Provisions: Where more than one provision of Chapter XVII-B applies to the foreign company as resident as well as foreign company, the provision applicable to the foreign company alone shall apply. Compliance with provisions applicable prior to becoming resident is considered sufficient. (Statement III is correct). (3) Foreign Tax Credit: The foreign company is entitled to relief or deduction under Section 90 or Section 91 in accordance with Rule 128. (Statement IV is correct). Thus, Statements II, III, and IV are correct. Option B is correct.

questions.question:
Mr. Keith, a foreign citizen and Resident but Not Ordinarily Resident (RNOR) in India for Previous Year 2025-26, has the following income receipts and accruals during the year:
1. Profit from a retail garment business in London, which is controlled entirely from a head office situated in Jaipur: ₹12,00,000 (out of which ₹5,00,000 was remitted to India).
2. Profit from an architectural consultancy profession in Dubai, set up in India, but managed independently from Dubai during the year: ₹8,00,000 (received in Dubai).
3. Rental income from a commercial property located in New York, credited directly to his bank account in London: ₹6,00,000 (later remitted to India).
4. Interest on UK Government Treasury Bonds credited to his London bank account: ₹3,00,000.
5. Fees for technical services rendered in New Delhi to an Indian corporate client, received in his London bank account: ₹4,50,000.
What is the total income of Mr. Keith chargeable to tax in India for Assessment Year 2026-27?
questions.explanation: Under Section 5(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961, the total income of an RNOR includes: (i) income received or deemed to be received in India, (ii) income accruing or arising or deemed to accrue or arise in India, and (iii) income accruing or arising outside India derived from a business controlled in or profession set up in India. Here: (1) London business profit of ₹12,00,000 is taxable because the business is controlled from Jaipur, India; remittance of ₹5,00,000 is not relevant since the full profit is taxed on accrual. (2) Dubai consultancy profession profit of ₹8,00,000 is taxable because the profession was set up in India. (3) Rental income from NY property (₹6,00,000) and UK bond interest (₹3,00,000) accrued and were received outside India; mere subsequent remittance to India does not constitute receipt under Section 5. (5) Fees for technical services of ₹4,50,000 rendered in India are deemed to accrue or arise in India under Section 9(1). Thus, Total Income = ₹12,00,000 + ₹8,00,000 + ₹4,50,000 = ₹24,50,000.

questions.question: Captain Rajesh, an Indian citizen, is a qualified master mariner and qualifies as a Non-Resident for PY 2025-26 under Section 6. During the previous year, he was employed on a foreign-going crude oil tanker flying the flag of the Marshall Islands, operating in international waters outside the territorial waters of India for 240 days. His contractual remuneration of USD 60,000 (INR 50,00,000) for services rendered outside India was directly credited by his foreign employer into his Non-Resident External (NRE) savings bank account maintained with State Bank of India, Kochi Branch. The Assessing Officer issued a reassessment notice proposing to tax the entire ₹50,00,000 under Section 5(2)(a) on the premise that the income was first received in India into an Indian bank account. Evaluate the validity of the Assessing Officer's action.
options: The AO's action is valid because Section 5(2)(a) treats all income first received in an Indian bank account as taxable in India, overriding any CBDT administrative circulars.
The AO's action is valid, but Captain Rajesh is entitled to a 50% ad-hoc deduction towards maritime offshore living allowances under Section 10(14).

The AO's action is invalid; as per CBDT Circular No. 13/2017 and 17/2017, salary accrued to a non-resident seafarer for services rendered outside India on a foreign-going ship is not taxable merely because it is credited directly to an NRE bank account in India.
The AO's action is invalid only if the ship flies the Indian flag; since the ship flies a foreign flag (Marshall Islands), the circular does not apply and the salary is fully taxable.
questions.explanation: Under Section 5(2) of the Income-tax Act, 1961, a non-resident is taxable in India only in respect of income received or deemed to be received in India, or income accruing or arising or deemed to accrue or arise in India. In response to representations regarding maritime personnel, the CBDT issued Circular No. 13/2017 (dated 11.04.2017) and Circular No. 17/2017 (dated 26.04.2017), clarifying that salary accrued to a non-resident seafarer for services rendered outside India on a foreign-going ship (whether bearing an Indian flag or a foreign flag) shall not be included in total income merely because the said salary has been credited directly into an NRE account maintained with an Indian bank. Because Captain Rajesh rendered services outside India and is a non-resident, the accrual took place outside India, and the credit to the NRE account is not treated as receipt of taxable income in India. Therefore, the AO's action is contrary to binding CBDT circulars and invalid.

questions.question:
With reference to the principles governing the scope of total income under Section 5 of the Income-tax Act, 1961, consider the following statements:
I. 'Accrual' refers to the vesting of the right to receive income, whereas 'due' refers to the right to enforce payment of that income.
II. Explanation 1 to Section 5 provides that an item of income accruing or arising outside India shall be deemed to be received in India if it is taken into account in a balance sheet prepared in India.
III. Explanation 2 to Section 5 prohibits double taxation by enacting that income once taxed on the basis of accrual or deemed accrual cannot again be subjected to tax on the ground of its actual or deemed receipt.
IV. The receipt of income refers exclusively to the first occasion when the recipient gets the money under their control; subsequent transmission or remittance of that money does not constitute 'receipt' in India.
Which of the above statements are correct?
options: I, II and IV only
II and III only
I, II, III and IV
I, III and IV only
questions.explanation: Statements I, III, and IV are correct, while Statement II is incorrect. Explanation 1 to Section 5 specifically clarifies the exact opposite: an item of income accruing or arising outside India shall NOT be deemed to be received in India merely because it is taken into account in a balance sheet prepared in India. Statement I accurately reflects the distinction established in landmark rulings (such as ED Sassoon & Co. Ltd.): income accrues when the right to receive it vests, whereas it becomes due when the right to enforce immediate payment arises. Statement III correctly states Explanation 2 to Section 5, which bars double assessment of the same income once on accrual and again on receipt. Statement IV correctly states the fundamental principle that 'receipt' refers to the initial acquisition of control over the funds; subsequent transfer or remittance does not constitute receipt.

questions.question: Global Retail Inc., a company incorporated in the United States, has no permanent establishment, office, or branch in India. It appointed Mr. Arvind, an Indian resident, as its buying agent in India. Arvind's activities are strictly confined to purchasing organic cotton fabrics from local textile mills in Tamil Nadu solely for the purpose of exporting them to Global Retail Inc.'s fulfillment centers in the US. In PY 2025-26, Arvind procured fabrics worth ₹40 crore and packed them in rented warehouse space in Chennai for 20 days prior to shipping. Global Retail Inc. realized a global operating profit of ₹8 crore on the retail sale of these fabrics in North America. The Assessing Officer contends that maintaining warehouse operations and purchasing goods through an agent creates a business connection in India, and seeks to attribute and tax 25% of the global profits (₹2 crore) in India under Section 9(1)(i). Determine the correctness of the Assessing Officer's contention.
options: The AO's contention is incorrect; under Explanation 1(b) to Section 9(1)(i), no income shall be deemed to accrue or arise in India to a non-resident through or from operations which are confined to the purchase of goods in India for the purpose of export.
The AO's contention is correct because holding inventory in a rented warehouse in Chennai exceeds the threshold of mere purchasing and constitutes a dependent agent PE.
The AO's contention is incorrect only if Global Retail Inc. has an advance ruling from the Board for Advance Rulings confirming the tax exemption.
The AO's contention is correct because procurement exceeding ₹2 crore automatically triggers Significant Economic Presence under Explanation 2A to Section 9(1)(i).
questions.explanation: Explanation 1(b) to Section 9(1)(i) provides an explicit statutory carve-out: in the case of a non-resident, no income shall be deemed to accrue or arise in India through or from operations which are confined to the purchase of goods in India for the purpose of export. Incidental warehousing and packaging prior to shipment do not breach this statutory exception because they are inextricably linked and directly subordinate to the export purchase operations. Furthermore, the proviso to Explanation 2A specifically clarifies that activities confined to the purchase of goods in India for export shall not constitute a Significant Economic Presence (SEP). Therefore, no part of the global profit of ₹8 crore is deemed to accrue or arise in India, and the Assessing Officer's contention is completely erroneous.

questions.question: Global News Network Ltd. (GNN), a non-resident corporate entity incorporated in the United Kingdom, is engaged in running an international news agency and publishing financial newspapers and digital magazines globally. GNN maintains a bureau office in New Delhi staffed by accredited foreign correspondents and analysts. During Previous Year 2025-26, the bureau's sole activity was gathering political and economic news, ground reports, and video footage in India and transmitting them electronically to GNN's editorial headquarters in London. GNN broadcasts and publishes this content worldwide. GNN does not solicit advertising or carry out any commercial publishing within India, although 8,000 Indian subscribers read GNN's international edition online. The Assessing Officer seeks to bring to tax in India an estimated 20% of GNN's global revenue as attributable to its Indian news-gathering bureau under Section 9(1)(i). Examine the legal validity of the proposed assessment.
options: The assessment is valid because maintaining a physical bureau office with 10 correspondents in New Delhi creates a fixed place business connection in India.
The assessment is valid to the extent of subscription fees received from the 8,000 Indian subscribers who access GNN's content online.

The assessment is invalid because under Explanation 1(c) to Section 9(1)(i), no income shall be deemed to accrue or arise in India to a non-resident engaged in running a news agency or publishing newspapers/magazines from operations confined to collecting news and views in India for transmission outside India.
The assessment is invalid only if the United Kingdom reciprocal tax treaty provides a zero withholding tax rate on journalistic activities.
questions.explanation: Under Explanation 1(c) to Section 9(1)(i) of the Income-tax Act, 1961, in the case of a non-resident engaged in the business of running a news agency or of publishing newspapers, magazines or journals, no income shall be deemed to accrue or arise in India to him through or from activities which are confined to the collection of news and views in India for transmission out of India. The maintenance of an office and employment of correspondents in India for this restricted objective does not forfeit the statutory immunity, provided the operations remain confined to collecting news and transmitting it abroad. Consequently, no portion of GNN's income from news collection is deemed to accrue or arise in India, making the AO's proposed assessment invalid.

questions.question:
Examine the availability of exemption under Explanation 1(d) to Section 9(1)(i) of the Income-tax Act, 1961, in respect of income derived through or from operations confined to the shooting of cinematograph films in India in the following three independent scenarios:
Scenario 1: 'Alps Cinema LLC', a foreign partnership firm based in Switzerland, has four partners: three are Swiss citizens residing in Zurich, and one partner is an Indian citizen residing in Geneva.
Scenario 2: 'Paramount Cine Inc.', a company incorporated in Delaware, USA, has 100 equity shareholders, all of whom are US citizens residing in California; none of the shareholders are citizens or residents of India.
Scenario 3: 'Tokyo Films Ltd.', a Japanese company, where 97% shares are held by Japanese citizens residing in Tokyo, and 3% shares are held by Mr. Rohan, who is a foreign citizen of Indian origin who has acquired permanent resident status in India.
In which of the above scenario(s) will the income from shooting cinematograph films in India be NOT deemed to accrue or arise in India?
options: Scenarios 1 and 2 only
Scenario 2 only
Scenarios 2 and 3 only
Scenarios 1, 2 and 3
questions.explanation: Explanation 1(d) to Section 9(1)(i) provides that in the case of a non-resident, no income shall be deemed to accrue or arise in India through or from operations which are confined to the shooting of any cinematograph film in India, if such non-resident is: (i) an individual who is not a citizen of India; or (ii) a firm which does not have ANY partner who is a citizen of India OR who is resident in India; or (iii) a company which does not have ANY shareholder who is a citizen of India OR who is resident in India. In Scenario 1, Alps Cinema LLC has an Indian citizen partner (even though non-resident); hence it fails the condition and exemption is not available. In Scenario 2, Paramount Cine Inc. has no shareholder who is an Indian citizen or resident in India; hence exemption is available. In Scenario 3, Tokyo Films Ltd. has a shareholder (Mr. Rohan) who is resident in India; hence it fails the negative condition. Therefore, exemption applies in Scenario 2 only.

questions.question: Kalahari Diamonds Ltd., a foreign corporate entity incorporated in Botswana, is primarily engaged in diamond mining operations. To facilitate viewing by global and Indian traders, the company displayed parcels of uncut and unassorted rough diamonds at the Bharat Diamond Bourse, which is a Special Zone notified by the Central Government in the Official Gazette. Representatives of Indian diamond cutting and polishing houses visited the display pavilion, inspected the rough stones, and noted lot numbers. Kalahari Diamonds Ltd. did not effect any sales, did not enter into contracts, and accepted no money inside the Special Notified Zone (SNZ); all subsequent bids, commercial negotiations, invoices, and bank settlements occurred in Gaborone, Botswana, and Antwerp, Belgium. The Assessing Officer alleges that showcasing merchandise in India created a business connection under Section 9(1)(i). Which of the following statements represents the correct legal position?
options: A business connection is established because physical display in an Indian zone constitutes an open invitation to offer, and 10% of global profit is taxable.
The company is exempt only if at least 50% of the displayed uncut diamonds are eventually processed by micro, small, and medium enterprises in India.
The display constitutes a Significant Economic Presence under Explanation 2A because the fair market value of the displayed rough diamonds exceeds ₹2 crore.

No income shall be deemed to accrue or arise in India under Explanation 1(e) to Section 9(1)(i) because activities of a foreign diamond mining company confined to the display of uncut and unassorted diamonds in a notified Special Zone are statutorily exempt.
questions.explanation: Under Explanation 1(e) to Section 9(1)(i) of the Income-tax Act, 1961, in the case of a foreign company engaged in the business of mining of diamonds, no income shall be deemed to accrue or arise in India to it through or from activities which are confined to the display of uncut and unassorted diamonds in any special zone notified by the Central Government in the Official Gazette in this behalf. This provision was specifically inserted to encourage foreign mining companies to display rough diamonds in India (such as at the Bharat Diamond Bourse SNZ in Mumbai) without fearing tax exposure or the imputation of a business connection. Since Kalahari Diamonds Ltd. is a foreign mining company and confined its activities in the notified zone strictly to display, Explanation 1(e) applies squarely and no income is deemed to accrue or arise in India.

questions.question:
Under Explanation 2 to Section 9(1)(i) of the Income-tax Act, 1961, a business connection of a non-resident in India includes business activities carried out through a person acting on behalf of the non-resident. Which of the following conditions correctly establishes a business connection through an agent under this Explanation?
Condition I: The agent habitually exercises in India an authority to conclude contracts on behalf of the non-resident, or habitually concludes contracts, or habitually plays the principal role leading to the conclusion of contracts by that non-resident.
Condition II: The contracts are for the provision of services by the non-resident, or for the transfer of ownership of/granting the right to use property owned by the non-resident or which the non-resident has the right to use.
Condition III: The agent has no authority to conclude contracts, but habitually maintains in India a stock of goods or merchandise from which he regularly delivers goods or merchandise on behalf of the non-resident.
Condition IV: The agent habitually secures orders in India, mainly or wholly for the non-resident or for other non-residents controlling, controlled by, or subject to the same common control as that non-resident.
options: Conditions I, II, III and IV all correctly establish a business connection.
Conditions I, II and III only; securing orders creates a business connection only if the agent also collects sale consideration.
Conditions I and II only; maintaining stock without authority to fix prices cannot constitute a business connection.
Conditions III and IV only; authority to conclude contracts is regulated solely under Double Taxation Avoidance Agreements and not the domestic Act.
questions.explanation: Explanation 2 to Section 9(1)(i) defines the scope of business connection through an agent. It encompasses: Clause (a): Habitual exercise of authority to conclude contracts, or habitually concluding contracts, or habitually playing the principal role leading to the conclusion of contracts by the non-resident (aligned with the BEPS Action 7 Multilateral Instrument standard), where contracts are in the name of the NR, for transfer/use of NR's property, or for provision of services by the NR. Clause (b): Habitually maintaining in India a stock of goods or merchandise from which he regularly delivers goods or merchandise on behalf of the non-resident. Clause (c): Habitually securing orders in India, mainly or wholly for the non-resident, or for other non-residents in a control relationship (controlling, controlled by, or under common control with the non-resident). All four conditions are integral statutory components of Explanation 2.

questions.question: M/s Sagarika Maritime Services LLP is a renowned ship brokerage and general shipping agency firm operating in Mumbai. During Previous Year 2025-26, it provided chartering brokerage and cargo booking services in the ordinary course of its business to nine unrelated foreign shipping lines. One of these lines was Poseidon Tankers Ltd., a company incorporated in Greece. Out of Sagarika's total gross commission earnings of ₹10 crore during the year, ₹1.80 crore (18%) was earned from Poseidon Tankers Ltd., while the remaining 82% came from the other eight foreign principals. Poseidon Tankers Ltd. does not hold any equity or management rights in Sagarika. The Assessing Officer seeks to treat Sagarika as a dependent agent permanent establishment / business connection of Poseidon Tankers Ltd. under Section 9(1)(i), arguing that Sagarika regularly negotiated and concluded charter fixtures on behalf of Poseidon. Determine whether Sagarika constitutes a business connection of Poseidon Tankers Ltd.
