options: Yes, because concluding contracts on behalf of a non-resident principal always constitutes a business connection irrespective of independent status.
Yes, because any commission exceeding ₹1 crore from a single non-resident principal automatically strips an agent of independent status.

No, because business connection does not include a broker, general commission agent, or any other agent having an independent status acting in the ordinary course of business, provided he does not work mainly or wholly for the non-resident.
No, but only if Poseidon Tankers Ltd. files an annual declaration under Rule 11UB certifying that Sagarika is an independent broker.
questions.explanation: Explanation 2 to Section 9(1)(i) explicitly provides that a business connection shall NOT be established where the non-resident carries on business through a broker, general commission agent, or any other agent having an independent status, provided such person is acting in the ordinary course of his business. The Explanation further clarifies that a broker, general commission agent, or other agent shall be deemed to have an independent status where he does not work mainly or wholly for the non-resident. Here, Sagarika acted in the ordinary course of its brokerage business for nine unrelated clients, and transactions with Poseidon Tankers Ltd. constituted only 18% of its total turnover. Therefore, Sagarika does not work mainly or wholly for Poseidon, retains its independent status, and cannot be treated as a business connection of Poseidon Tankers Ltd.

questions.question:
Mr. Dhanush acts as an exclusive commercial representative in Bengaluru. During PY 2025-26, he secured purchase orders in India for three non-resident companies:
1. Alpha Ltd. (incorporated in Singapore): 40% of Dhanush's total orders secured.
2. Beta Inc. (incorporated in the USA): 35% of Dhanush's total orders secured.
3. Gamma BV (incorporated in the Netherlands): 25% of Dhanush's total orders secured.
Alpha Ltd. owns 70% of the voting power in Beta Inc., and both Alpha Ltd. and Gamma BV are 100% subsidiaries of Zenith Global Holding Corp (Jersey). Dhanush did not secure orders for any other enterprise. The non-resident entities argue that Dhanush does not constitute a business connection for Beta Inc. or Gamma BV individually because he does not work 'wholly or mainly' (i.e. > 50%) for either of them taken in isolation.
Evaluate the validity of this argument under Explanation 2 to Section 9(1)(i).
options: The argument is valid; each non-resident entity is an independent corporate taxpayer, and since Dhanush secured less than 50% orders for Beta Inc. and Gamma BV, no business connection exists for them.

The argument is invalid; under Explanation 2, if an agent habitually secures orders mainly or wholly for a non-resident or for other non-residents who control, are controlled by, or are subject to the same common control as that non-resident, a business connection is established for all such non-residents.
The argument is invalid only for Beta Inc. because Alpha Ltd. controls Beta Inc., but valid for Gamma BV because Dhanush secured only 25% orders for Gamma BV.
The argument is valid because the corporate veil between parent and subsidiary entities cannot be pierced under Section 9(1)(i) without invoking General Anti-Avoidance Rules (GAAR).
questions.explanation: Explanation 2 to Section 9(1)(i) explicitly addresses situations where a person acts on behalf of multiple non-residents belonging to the same group. Where a person habitually secures orders in India mainly or wholly for a non-resident, or for that non-resident and other non-residents who: (i) control the non-resident, (ii) are controlled by the non-resident, or (iii) are subject to the same common control as the non-resident, a business connection is established for all such non-residents. Here, 100% of the orders secured by Dhanush are for entities under common control (Zenith Global Holding Corp owns Alpha Ltd. and Gamma BV, and Alpha controls Beta Inc.). Because Dhanush acts exclusively for this closely related group, he does not have independent status, and his order-securing activities establish a business connection for Alpha Ltd., Beta Inc., and Gamma BV alike.

questions.question:
Nippon Heavy Industries Ltd. (NHI), a company incorporated in Japan, manufactures automated heavy machinery in Osaka. It maintains an assembly workshop and technical liaison office in Pune, India, which constitutes a business connection under Section 9(1)(i). In Previous Year 2025-26, NHI executed contracts for supplying and installing robotic assembly lines to Indian car manufacturers, realizing a total revenue of ₹60 crore. The total net global profit from these contracts was ₹9 crore. An exhaustive functional, asset, and risk (FAR) analysis established that:
- 40% of the total economic activities (R&D, core fabrication, engineering design) were performed in Japan.
- 35% of the activities (customization, on-site assembly, testing, installation) were carried out at the Pune workshop in India.
- 25% of the activities (procurement of specialized electronic chips) were performed in Taiwan.
NHI has no other activities in India. In accordance with Section 9(1)(i) read with Explanation 1(a) and Explanation 3, what amount of income is deemed to accrue or arise in India?
options: ₹9.00 crore (the entire global profit under the force of attraction doctrine)
₹6.00 crore (attributable to both assembly and global procurement)
₹2.25 crore (attributable to Indian operations after 30% standard expense deduction)
₹3.15 crore (being 35% of the net profit of ₹9 crore reasonably attributable to Indian operations)
questions.explanation: Under Explanation 1(a) to Section 9(1)(i) of the Income-tax Act, 1961, in the case of a business of which all the operations are not carried out in India, the income of the business deemed to accrue or arise in India shall be only such part of the income as is reasonably attributable to the operations carried out in India. Explanation 3 reinforces this principle where business is carried on through an agent or establishment: only so much of income as is attributable to the operations carried out in India shall be deemed to accrue or arise in India. Here, the total net profit earned from the contracts is ₹9 crore. The functional analysis demonstrates that 35% of the total operations were carried out in India through the Pune establishment. Therefore, income deemed to accrue or arise in India = 35% of ₹9,00,00,000 = ₹3,15,00,000 (₹3.15 crore). The remaining 65% of the profit arose from operations performed outside India (Japan and Taiwan) and cannot be deemed to accrue or arise in India.

questions.question:
StreamByte SaaS Corp., an enterprise incorporated in Ireland without any branch, office, server, or employees in India, provides cloud-based digital workflow tools. During Previous Year 2025-26, it recorded the following transactions with persons in India:
1. Subscription fees collected from Indian SME enterprises for online data analytics and software downloads: ₹1.65 crore.
2. Revenue from individual Indian retail customers for downloading mobile utility applications: ₹45 lakh.
3. Payments made by StreamByte SaaS Corp. to an Indian software development firm for outsourced coding services: ₹50 lakh.
4. Web hosting fees collected from a Singapore company for hosting data accessed primarily by Southeast Asian users: ₹80 lakh.
Determine whether StreamByte SaaS Corp. has a Significant Economic Presence (SEP) in India for PY 2025-26 under Explanation 2A to Section 9(1)(i).
options: Yes, because the aggregate payments arising from transactions in goods, services, or property, including provision of download of data or software in India, amounted to ₹2.10 crore, which exceeds the statutory threshold of ₹2 crore.
No, because payments from individual retail users (₹45 lakh) must be excluded, leaving commercial revenue at ₹1.65 crore, which is below the ₹2 crore threshold.
No, because the net inflow after subtracting payments made to the Indian software vendor (₹50 lakh) is ₹1.60 crore (₹2.10 crore - ₹0.50 crore), which is below ₹2 crore.
Yes, because the total business turnover including payments made to the Indian software vendor and fees from Singapore equals ₹3.40 crore.
questions.explanation: Explanation 2A(a) to Section 9(1)(i) provides that Significant Economic Presence (SEP) is constituted by any transaction in respect of any goods, services or property carried out by a non-resident with any person in India, including provision of download of data or software in India, if the aggregate of payments arising from such transaction or transactions during the previous year exceeds ₹2 crore. In this case: enterprise subscription fees from Indian persons = ₹1.65 crore; retail customer app download fees from Indian persons = ₹0.45 crore. Both transactions represent payments arising from transactions carried out with persons in India. Aggregate payments = ₹1.65 crore + ₹0.45 crore = ₹2.10 crore. Since ₹2.10 crore exceeds the prescribed threshold of ₹2 crore, Clause (a) of Explanation 2A is triggered and StreamByte SaaS Corp. has an SEP in India for PY 2025-26. (Payments made by the non-resident to Indian vendors are outflows and cannot be netted off; Singapore receipts have no nexus with persons in India).

questions.question: BuzzMedia Inc., a digital media and networking corporation registered in California, USA, offers a free microblogging and messaging platform accessible worldwide. During Previous Year 2025-26, BuzzMedia Inc. had 3,80,000 active registered users residing in India. BuzzMedia Inc. did not charge any subscription, registration, or service fees from these Indian users. However, BuzzMedia Inc. systematically and continuously engaged in interaction with these users, gathered behavioral data, and solicited user engagement through personalized content algorithms. Its total direct billing to Indian users was nil. The company contends that in the absence of any monetary revenue or payment from India, no Significant Economic Presence (SEP) can arise under Section 9(1)(i). Examine the legal correctness of BuzzMedia Inc.'s contention.
options: The contention is correct; monetary consideration is an essential sine qua non for establishing any business connection or SEP under the Income-tax Act, 1961.

The contention is incorrect; under Explanation 2A(b) to Section 9(1)(i), systematic and continuous soliciting of business activities or engaging in interaction with at least 3,00,000 users in India constitutes SEP, irrespective of whether any revenue is directly charged from users.
The contention is incorrect, but the user threshold prescribed under the Income-tax Rules is 5,00,000 users, so BuzzMedia Inc. is still outside the SEP net.
The contention is correct because digital interactions without physical servers in India are protected by international customary law against unilateral taxation.
questions.explanation: Under Explanation 2A(b) to Section 9(1)(i) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 read with Rule 11UD, Significant Economic Presence (SEP) is established if a non-resident engages in systematic and continuous soliciting of business activities or engages in interaction with users in India, provided the number of users is at least 3,00,000 (3 lakhs). Clause (b) is an independent, non-monetary threshold designed specifically for digital business models where monetization occurs indirectly (e.g., through advertising or data analytics) while services are offered free of charge to users. Because BuzzMedia Inc. engaged in systematic interaction with 3,80,000 Indian users, it comfortably exceeded the 3,00,000 user threshold. Therefore, BuzzMedia Inc.'s contention is incorrect, and an SEP constitutes a business connection in India.

questions.question:
Which of the following statements correctly describe the statutory attributes of Significant Economic Presence (SEP) under Explanation 2A to Section 9(1)(i) of the Income-tax Act, 1961?
Statement 1: The transactions or activities shall constitute SEP in India whether or not the agreement for such transactions or activities is entered into in India.
Statement 2: The transactions or activities shall constitute SEP in India whether or not the non-resident has a residence or place of business in India.
Statement 3: The transactions or activities shall constitute SEP in India whether or not the non-resident renders services in India.
Statement 4: Once an SEP is established, the entire global business profits of the non-resident, including profits from unconnected off-line transactions with Indian residents, are deemed to accrue or arise in India.
Statement 5: Only so much of income as is attributable to the transactions or activities referred to in clause (a) or clause (b) of Explanation 2A shall be deemed to accrue or arise in India.
options: Statements 1, 2, 3 and 4 only
Statements 1, 2 and 5 only
Statements 1, 2, 3 and 5 only
Statements 2, 3, 4 and 5 only
questions.explanation: Statements 1, 2, 3, and 5 are correct, while Statement 4 is incorrect. Explanation 2A expressly enacts three overriding non-nexus conditions: transactions or activities constitute an SEP whether or not: (i) the agreement is entered in India, (ii) the non-resident has a residence or place of business in India, or (iii) the non-resident renders services in India. Crucially, the fourth proviso/sub-clause of Explanation 2A mandates that where a business connection is established by reason of SEP, only so much of income as is ATTRIBUTABLE to the transactions or activities referred to in clause (a) or clause (b) shall be deemed to accrue or arise in India. The Indian Income-tax Act rejects the unconstrained 'force of attraction' doctrine; unconnected global or offline business profits of the non-resident cannot be swept into the Indian tax net merely because an SEP exists in respect of specific digital activities.

questions.question: Nordic Crafts AB, a company incorporated in Stockholm, Sweden, operates an advanced digital B2B procurement portal. Through this platform, it interacts with 4,20,000 Indian registered artisans, craftsmen, and small weavers across various states in India. Nordic Crafts AB uses the platform systematically to solicit bids, inspect handicraft samples digitally, place purchase orders, and arrange payments totaling ₹15 crore during Previous Year 2025-26. All goods purchased through this portal are solely and exclusively exported to Sweden and other EU countries for retail sale; none of the goods are sold or distributed in India. The Assessing Officer claims that because Nordic Crafts AB interacts with over 3,00,000 users in India and transactions exceed ₹2 crore, an SEP is formed under Explanation 2A, making a portion of procurement savings taxable in India. Evaluate the Assessing Officer's stance.
options: The AO is correct because the user threshold of 3,00,000 and monetary threshold of ₹2 crore are both breached, superseding all general exemptions.
The AO is correct, but only 10% presumptive profit under Section 44BB can be attributed to the Indian procurement operations.
The AO is incorrect only because the bilateral Double Taxation Avoidance Agreement between India and Sweden overrides Explanation 2A automatically.

The AO is incorrect; the proviso to Explanation 2A explicitly provides that transactions or activities of a non-resident in India which are confined to the purchase of goods in India for the purpose of export shall not constitute a significant economic presence.
questions.explanation: The proviso to Explanation 2A to Section 9(1)(i) expressly enacts: 'Provided that transactions or activities of a non-resident in India which are confined to the purchase of goods in India for the purpose of export shall not constitute significant economic presence of such non-resident in India.' This statutory carve-out harmonizes Explanation 2A with the long-standing principle in Explanation 1(b) that purchasing goods in India solely for export does not generate taxable income in India. Even though Nordic Crafts AB interacted with more than 3,00,000 Indian artisans and purchased goods exceeding ₹2 crore via its digital platform, all such activities were confined strictly to the purchase of goods for export. Therefore, by virtue of the explicit statutory proviso, no SEP is constituted, and the AO's stance is completely untenable.

questions.question:
In the context of Explanation 1(a) and Explanation 2A to Section 9(1)(i) of the Income-tax Act, 1961, which of the following streams of revenue earned by a non-resident digital enterprise are specifically defined as 'income attributable to the operations carried out in India'?
(i) Income from advertisements targeting customers who reside in India or who access the advertisement through an Internet Protocol (IP) address located in India.
(ii) Income from the sale of data collected from persons who reside in India or from persons who use an IP address located in India.
(iii) Income from the sale of goods or services using data collected from persons who reside in India or who use an IP address located in India.
(iv) Income from hosting advertisements targeting foreign residents located abroad on servers physically situated in Germany.
options: (i), (ii) and (iii) only
(i) and (ii) only
(ii) and (iii) only
(i), (ii), (iii) and (iv)
questions.explanation: Explanation 1(a) to Section 9(1)(i), read with Explanation 3A / digital nexus provisions, explicitly specifies that income attributable to the operations carried out in India includes: (1) Income from advertisement which targets a customer who resides in India or a customer who accesses the advertisement through an Internet Protocol address located in India; (2) Income from the sale of data collected from a person who resides in India or from a person who uses an Internet Protocol address located in India; and (3) Income from the sale of goods and services using data collected from a person who resides in India or from a person who uses an Internet Protocol address located in India. These provisions also extend to the transactions/activities creating a Significant Economic Presence under Explanation 2A. Item (iv) has no nexus with Indian users, Indian IP addresses, or Indian data, and is not deemed to accrue or arise in India. Hence, items (i), (ii), and (iii) only are covered.

questions.question:
Vertex Investments Ltd., a company incorporated in the British Virgin Islands (BVI), held 1,00,000 equity shares in Bharat Petro-Chem Ltd., an Indian listed company. On 10th October 2025, Vertex entered into a Share Purchase Agreement in London with Caspian Ventures Ltd. (a company incorporated in Jersey) to sell its entire shareholding in Bharat Petro-Chem Ltd. for a total consideration of USD 10 million (equivalent to ₹84 crore). The share certificates and transfer forms were delivered in London, and the entire sale consideration was remitted from Caspian's bank account in Zurich to Vertex's bank account in London. Vertex contends that since the contract was executed outside India, both transferor and transferee are non-residents, and the consideration was paid outside India, no capital gains accrued or arose in India.
Analyze Vertex's contention in light of Section 9(1)(i) and Explanation 4.
options: Vertex's contention is valid because the situs of contract and situs of payment were both outside India.
Vertex's contention is valid, but the transferee Caspian Ventures Ltd. must pay equalization levy on the transaction.

Vertex's contention is invalid; under Section 9(1)(i) read with Explanation 4, capital gains arising from the transfer of a capital asset situated in India are deemed to accrue or arise in India in all cases, irrespective of whether the transfer document was executed outside India or payment was made outside India.
Vertex's contention is invalid only if Bharat Petro-Chem Ltd. approves the transfer in a board meeting held in India within 30 days.
questions.explanation: Under Section 9(1)(i) of the Income-tax Act, 1961, all income arising through or from the transfer of a capital asset situated in India is deemed to accrue or arise in India. Shares of an Indian company are legally situated in India. Furthermore, Explanation 4 clarifies that the expression 'through' shall mean and include 'by means of', 'in consequence of', or 'by reason of'. It is well settled that capital gains arising from the transfer of a capital asset situated in India are deemed to accrue or arise in India irrespective of: (i) whether the asset is movable or immovable, tangible or intangible; (ii) whether the place of registration or execution of the transfer document is in India or outside; and (iii) whether the place of payment of consideration is within India or outside India. Because the underlying shares transferred were shares of an Indian company, the capital asset was situated in India, and the capital gains are deemed to accrue or arise in India. Vertex's contention is completely invalid.

questions.question:
Orchid Global Holdings Ltd. (incorporated in Mauritius) holds assets across several Asian jurisdictions. On 20th January 2026, Mr. Henry, a non-resident individual holding 20% equity shares in Orchid Global Holdings Ltd., sold his entire holding to Bluebell Inc. (USA) for ₹25 crore, realizing a capital gain of ₹10 crore.
The accounting period of Orchid Global Holdings Ltd. ends on 31st March each year.
- As on 31st March 2025 (the preceding accounting year end), the book value of total global assets was ₹100 crore.
- On the date of transfer (20th January 2026), the book value of total assets was ₹110 crore (an increase of 10% over the last balance sheet date).
- The Fair Market Value (FMV) of assets as on 31st March 2025 was:
  * Assets located in India: ₹14 crore
  * Total assets located globally (including Indian assets): ₹25 crore
- The FMV of assets as on 20th January 2026 was:
  * Assets located in India: ₹18 crore
  * Total assets located globally: ₹38 crore
Determine whether the shares of Orchid Global Holdings Ltd. derive their value substantially from assets located in India under Explanation 6 to Section 9(1)(i).
options: Yes, because the specified date of valuation is 31st March 2025 (book value increase on date of transfer being < 15%), on which date the FMV of Indian assets (₹14 crore) exceeds ₹10 crore AND represents at least 50% (56%) of the total global assets (₹25 crore).
No, because the specified date is 20th January 2026, on which date the FMV of Indian assets (₹18 crore) represents only 47.37% of total global assets (₹38 crore), which is less than 50%.
No, because Mr. Henry is an individual non-resident shareholder and indirect transfer provisions apply exclusively to corporate transferors.
Yes, because the FMV of Indian assets exceeded ₹10 crore on both dates, regardless of whether the 50% ratio test is satisfied.
questions.explanation: Under Explanation 6 to Section 9(1)(i), a foreign company's shares derive their value substantially from Indian assets if, on the 'specified date', the value of Indian assets: (i) exceeds ₹10 crore, AND (ii) represents at least 50% of the value of all assets owned by the foreign company. The 'specified date' is the date on which the accounting period preceding the date of transfer ends (here, 31st March 2025). The date of transfer becomes the specified date ONLY if the book value of assets on the date of transfer exceeds by AT LEAST 15% the book value as on the last balance sheet date. Here, book value increased from ₹100 crore to ₹110 crore—an increase of only 10% (< 15%). Hence, the specified date remains 31st March 2025. As on 31st March 2025: Value of Indian assets = ₹14 crore (exceeds ₹10 crore threshold); Proportion of Indian assets = ₹14 crore / ₹25 crore = 56% (represents at least 50% of all assets). Both conditions are satisfied on the specified date. Therefore, the shares of Orchid Global Holdings Ltd. derive their value substantially from assets located in India.

questions.question:
Under Explanation 6 to Section 9(1)(i) of the Income-tax Act, 1961, what is the 'specified date' for determining whether a share or interest in a foreign company derives its value substantially from assets located in India in the following two independent cases?
Case X: Jupiter Corp (a foreign company whose accounting period ends on 31st December) transfers shares on 15th September 2025. The book value of its total assets on 31st December 2024 was USD 50 million. On 15th September 2025, the book value of its total assets is USD 56 million (an increase of 12%).
Case Y: Saturn Corp (a foreign company whose accounting period ends on 31st March) transfers shares on 20th November 2025. The book value of its total assets on 31st March 2025 was USD 80 million. On 20th November 2025, the book value of its total assets is USD 94 million (an increase of 17.5%).
options: Case X: 15th September 2025; Case Y: 31st March 2025
Case X: 31st March 2025; Case Y: 31st March 2025
Case X: 15th September 2025; Case Y: 20th November 2025
Case X: 31st December 2024; Case Y: 20th November 2025
questions.explanation: Explanation 6 to Section 9(1)(i) defines 'specified date' as the date on which the accounting period of the company or entity ends preceding the date of transfer of a share or an interest. However, the date of transfer shall be the specified date of valuation in a case where the book value of the assets of the company or entity on the date of transfer exceeds by AT LEAST 15% the book value of the assets as on the last balance sheet date preceding the date of transfer. In Case X: The increase in book value is from USD 50m to USD 56m, which is 12%. Since 12% is less than 15%, the specified date is the end of the preceding accounting period, i.e., 31st December 2024. In Case Y: The increase in book value is from USD 80m to USD 94m, which is 17.5%. Since 17.5% exceeds 15%, the exception applies and the specified date is the date of transfer, i.e., 20th November 2025. Thus, Case X is 31st December 2024 and Case Y is 20th November 2025.

questions.question:
Solaris Holdings Ltd., a company incorporated in the United Kingdom, transferred 10,000 equity shares in Neptune Enterprises NV (incorporated in the Netherlands) to an unrelated foreign company on 1st December 2025 for a total net capital gain of ₹20 crore.
The shares of Neptune Enterprises NV derive their value substantially from assets located in India within the meaning of Explanation 6:
- Fair market value of assets located in India on the specified date: ₹48 crore.
- Fair market value of all global assets owned by Neptune Enterprises NV on the specified date: ₹80 crore.
- Solaris Holdings Ltd. held a 12% voting power and share capital in Neptune Enterprises NV throughout the preceding 12 months (small shareholder exemption does not apply).
Under Explanation 7 to Section 9(1)(i), what is the amount of capital gains deemed to accrue or arise in India in the hands of Solaris Holdings Ltd.?
options: ₹20.00 crore (entire capital gain is deemed to accrue or arise in India)
₹12.00 crore
₹9.60 crore
₹8.00 crore
questions.explanation: Under Explanation 7 to Section 9(1)(i) of the Income-tax Act, 1961, where all the assets owned, directly or indirectly, by a foreign company or entity are not located in India, the income of the non-resident transferor from transfer outside India of a share or interest deemed to accrue or arise in India shall be ONLY such part of the income as is reasonably attributable to assets located in India and determined in the prescribed manner (Rule 11UC). The proportionality formula is: Deemed Capital Gain = Total Capital Gain × (FMV of assets located in India / FMV of all assets of the foreign entity). Here: Total Capital Gain = ₹20 crore; FMV of Indian assets = ₹48 crore; FMV of all global assets = ₹80 crore. Ratio = ₹48 crore / ₹80 crore = 60% (0.60). Deemed Capital Gain in India = ₹20 crore × 60% = ₹12.00 crore. The balance ₹8.00 crore relates to assets situated outside India and is not deemed to accrue or arise in India.

questions.question:
Apex Capital Ltd., a non-resident investment fund incorporated in Mauritius, held 3.5% of the total paid-up equity share capital and voting rights in Batavia BV (Netherlands). Batavia BV directly owns factory buildings and manufacturing plants located in Gujarat, India, valued at ₹150 crore (representing 70% of Batavia BV's total asset value). On 18th February 2026, Apex Capital Ltd. sold its entire 3.5% stake in Batavia BV to an overseas institutional investor for a capital gain of ₹6 crore.
Neither Apex Capital Ltd. nor any of its associated enterprises held any right of management or control in Batavia BV, nor did their aggregate voting power or share capital exceed 5% at any time in the 12 months preceding the date of transfer.
Examine the taxability of the capital gain of ₹6 crore in India under Section 9(1)(i) read with Explanation 7.
options: Taxable in India to the extent of 70% of ₹6 crore (₹4.20 crore) under the proportional attribution rule of Explanation 7.
Fully taxable in India at 20% because Batavia BV directly holds Indian assets exceeding ₹10 crore.

Exempt from tax in India; under Explanation 7, no income is deemed to accrue or arise from the transfer of shares in a foreign entity directly owning Indian assets if the transferor, along with associated enterprises, did not hold management/control rights and did not hold voting power or share capital exceeding 5% at any time in the 12 months preceding the transfer.
Exempt only if Apex Capital Ltd. reinvests the entire net sales consideration in specified Indian infrastructure bonds under Section 54EC.
questions.explanation: Explanation 7 to Section 9(1)(i) provides an explicit small shareholder exemption. Where a foreign company directly owns the assets situated in India, no income shall be deemed to accrue or arise to a non-resident from the transfer outside India of shares in such foreign company if the transferor (individually or along with associated enterprises), at any time in the 12 months preceding the date of transfer, does NOT hold: (i) the right of management or control in relation to the foreign company, OR (ii) voting power or share capital or interest exceeding 5% of the total voting power or total share capital of the foreign company. Apex Capital Ltd. held only 3.5% share capital/voting power (which is <= 5%) and held no right of management or control throughout the preceding 12 months. Therefore, Apex Capital Ltd. satisfies all conditions of the statutory carve-out under Explanation 7, and the capital gain of ₹6 crore is completely exempt from tax in India.

questions.question:
Cascade Holdings Inc. (Cayman Islands) holds 100% of the equity shares of Delta Overseas Ltd. (Dubai). Delta Overseas Ltd. in turn directly owns 100% shares and assets of an Indian operating company, Bharat Logistics Pvt Ltd. (FMV ₹300 crore, comprising 80% of Delta's total assets).
Mr. Frank, a non-resident investor, held 4% of the share capital and voting rights in Cascade Holdings Inc. Frank does not hold any right of management or control in Cascade Holdings Inc. Furthermore, Frank's rights in Cascade Holdings Inc. do not entitle him to exercise control or management of Delta Overseas Ltd., nor do they entitle him to voting power or share capital exceeding 5% in Delta Overseas Ltd. at any time in the preceding 12 months. Frank sold his 4% shares in Cascade Holdings Inc. on 14th November 2025 for a capital gain of ₹8 crore.
Assess the taxability of Frank's capital gain in India under Explanation 7 to Section 9(1)(i).
options: The capital gain is exempt from tax in India because where the foreign entity indirectly owns Indian assets, the transferor along with associated enterprises neither held management/control in the foreign company nor held rights entitling them to control or to more than 5% voting power/capital in the direct Indian-asset holding company.
The capital gain is fully taxable in India because the small shareholder exemption applies only to direct holding companies and not to multi-tier holding structures.
The capital gain is taxable in India because Delta Overseas Ltd. is incorporated in Dubai, which has no comprehensive capital gains article with India.
The capital gain is taxable to the extent of 80% of ₹8 crore (₹6.40 crore) by lifting the corporate veil under Section 9(1)(i).
questions.explanation: Explanation 7 to Section 9(1)(i) specifically addresses tiered / indirect holding structures in Category (2) of its exemption table. Where the foreign company or entity whose shares are transferred indirectly owns the assets situated in India (here, Cascade Holdings Inc. indirectly owns Indian assets through Delta Overseas Ltd.), the exemption applies if the transferor (individually or along with associated enterprises) at any time in the 12 months preceding the date of transfer: (i) does not hold the right of management or control in relation to such company (Cascade Holdings Inc.), AND (ii) does not hold any rights in such company which would entitle it to either exercise control or management of the direct holding company (Delta Overseas Ltd.) or entitle it to voting power or share capital exceeding 5% in the direct holding company. Frank held only 4% in Cascade Holdings Inc., had no management/control rights, and had no rights entitling him to control or >5% voting power in Delta Overseas Ltd. Thus, the indirect transfer is fully exempt in Frank's hands.

questions.question:
Which of the following statements regarding statutory carve-outs and administrative clarifications under the indirect transfer provisions of Section 9(1)(i) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 is INCORRECT?
Statement I: An asset or capital asset held by a non-resident by way of investment, directly or indirectly, in a Category-I Foreign Portfolio Investor (FPI) registered under the SEBI (FPI) Regulations, 2019 is not deemed to be situated in India under the third proviso to Explanation 5.
Statement II: An asset held by a non-resident by way of investment in a Category-II FPI registered under the SEBI (FPI) Regulations, 2019 is completely exempt from being deemed situated in India under Explanation 5.
Statement III: CBDT Circular No. 4/2015 clarifies that dividends declared and paid by a foreign company outside India do not constitute a transfer of underlying Indian assets, and are not deemed to accrue or arise in India under Section 9(1)(i), even if the foreign company derives its value substantially from assets situated in India.
Statement IV: CBDT Circular No. 28/2017 clarifies that indirect transfer provisions do not apply to redemption or buyback of shares/interest held indirectly by a non-resident in specified funds (VCF/AIF) to the extent proceeds do not exceed the pro-rata share in consideration realized from transfer of Indian securities.
options: Statements I and III
Statements III and IV
Statement I only
Statement II only
questions.explanation: Statement II is INCORRECT (making Option 3 the correct answer). Under the second proviso to Explanation 5, Category-I and Category-II FPIs were exempt under the earlier SEBI (FPI) Regulations, 2014. However, under the third proviso to Explanation 5 (inserted for SEBI (FPI) Regulations, 2019), the indirect transfer exemption is restricted ONLY to Category-I Foreign Portfolio Investors; Category-II FPIs under the 2019 regulations do NOT enjoy this statutory exemption. Statements I, III, and IV are correct: Statement I correctly states the third proviso; Statement III accurately reflects CBDT Circular No. 4/2015 (declaring foreign dividend is not a transfer of Indian assets); Statement IV accurately reflects CBDT Circular No. 28/2017 regarding redemption/buyback in specified funds (AIFs/VCFs).

questions.question:
Mr. Ethan, an Australian citizen and non-resident in India, was deputed by his Sydney-based employer, Pacific Mining Ltd., to execute a trial installation of mining robotics for an Indian client in Odisha. His assignment lasted from 1st July 2025 to 31st October 2025 (4 months). As per his service contract, he was entitled to a 10-day mid-assignment rest and recreation period from 11th September to 20th September 2025, which he spent vacationing in Sri Lanka. The rest period was both preceded and succeeded by active installation services rendered in Odisha. His monthly remuneration was AUD 15,000 (equivalent to ₹8,00,000 per month), which was credited directly into his bank account in Sydney, Australia. The Assessing Officer asserts that the entire salary for the 4-month period (₹32,00,000), including salary for the 10-day leave spent in Sri Lanka, is deemed to accrue or arise in India.
Analyze the validity of the Assessing Officer's assertion under Section 9(1)(ii).
options: The AO's assertion is invalid; since the salary was paid in Australia in Australian Dollars by a foreign employer, no salary is deemed to accrue or arise in India.

The AO's assertion is valid; under Section 9(1)(ii) and the Explanation thereto, salary payable for services rendered in India is deemed to accrue or arise in India, and salary payable for a rest/leave period which is preceded and succeeded by services rendered in India and forms part of the employment contract is regarded as earned in India.

The AO's assertion is partially valid; salary for the active working period in India is taxable, but salary corresponding to the 10-day rest period spent in Sri Lanka (₹2,66,667) must be excluded because services were not rendered in India.
The AO's assertion is invalid unless Ethan stayed in India for more than 182 days during the previous year.
questions.explanation: Under Section 9(1)(ii) of the Income-tax Act, 1961, income falling under the head 'Salaries' is deemed to accrue or arise in India if it is earned in India. Salary payable for services rendered in India is regarded as earned in India regardless of the place of receipt or the currency of payment. Crucially, the Explanation to Section 9(1)(ii) explicitly provides that salary payable for a rest period or leave period which is preceded and succeeded by services rendered in India and forms part of the service contract of employment shall be regarded as income earned in India. Here, Ethan rendered services in Odisha from 1st July to 31st October, and his 10-day rest period in September was preceded and succeeded by active services in India pursuant to his employment contract. Consequently, the entire salary for the 4-month period of ₹32,00,000 (including the salary attributable to the 10 days spent in Sri Lanka) is deemed to accrue or arise in India under Section 9(1)(ii). The AO's assertion is valid.

questions.question:
Mr. Devendra, a citizen of India, was posted as a Senior Counselor at the Embassy of India in Berlin, Germany, throughout Previous Year 2025-26. His residential status for Assessment Year 2026-27 is Non-Resident. During the previous year, he received the following emoluments and benefits from the Government of India:
- Basic Salary: ₹20,00,000 (paid in foreign currency in Berlin).
- Foreign compensatory allowances: ₹15,00,000 (paid in Berlin).
- Value of rent-free furnished official accommodation in Berlin provided by the Government (perquisite value under Rule 3): ₹5,00,000.
- Car with chauffeur provided by the Government in Berlin for official and personal use (perquisite value): ₹1,80,000.
- Interest on German savings bank account: ₹1,20,000.
Devendra is taxed under the default tax regime under Section 115BAC (standard deduction of ₹75,000 under Section 16(ia) is available for AY 2026-27).
Compute the Total Income chargeable to tax in India in the hands of Mr. Devendra for AY 2026-27.
options: Nil (as a non-resident rendering services outside India, no salary is taxable in India)
questions.explanation: Under Section 9(1)(iii) of the Income-tax Act, 1961, income chargeable under the head 'Salaries' payable by the Government to a citizen of India for services rendered outside India is deemed to accrue or arise in India. Therefore, the basic salary of ₹20,00,000 is deemed to accrue or arise in India, even though Devendra is a non-resident and rendered services in Berlin. However, Section 10(7) explicitly provides that any allowances or perquisites paid or allowed as such outside India by the Government to a citizen of India for rendering services outside India are completely exempt from tax. This exemption applies to the foreign compensatory allowance (₹15,00,000) as well as the perquisites of rent-free accommodation (₹5,00,000) and motor car (₹1,80,000). The Note to Illustration 4 clarifies that exemption u/s 10(7) is available irrespective of the tax regime chosen. Interest on the German bank account (₹1,20,000) accrues and is received outside India by a non-resident, hence not taxable in India. Gross Salary = ₹20,00,000. Less: Standard deduction u/s 16(ia) under default regime = ₹75,000. Net Total Income = ₹20,00,000 - ₹75,00,00 = ₹19,25,000.

questions.question:
A multidisciplinary tax advisory firm is reviewing the tax liability of four non-resident corporate clients for Previous Year 2025-26 under Section 9(1)(i):
Client 1 (Siberian Mining PJSC, Russia): Confined its Indian operations strictly to displaying uncut and unassorted rough diamonds at the notified Special Zone at Bharat Diamond Bourse, Mumbai.
Client 2 (Agence France Presse SA, France): Confined its Indian operations strictly to collecting political news and photos in New Delhi and transmitting them to Paris for international publication.
Client 3 (Rhine Engineering GmbH, Germany): Appointed an Indian agent who habitually maintains a stock of industrial valves in a warehouse in Pune and regularly delivers valves from this stock to Indian buyers on behalf of Rhine Engineering.
Client 4 (Caspian Garments Ltd., UK): Appointed a local sourcing agent in Tirupur whose operations are strictly confined to purchasing cotton t-shirts in India solely for export to London.
For which of the above non-resident clients is income deemed to accrue or arise in India under Section 9(1)(i)?
options: Clients 1, 2, 3 and 4
Clients 2 and 3 only
Clients 1 and 4 only
Client 3 only
questions.explanation: Client 1 is covered by the statutory exemption under Explanation 1(e) to Section 9(1)(i): display of uncut and unassorted rough diamonds in a notified Special Zone by a foreign diamond mining company is not deemed to accrue or arise in India. Client 2 is covered by the statutory exemption under Explanation 1(c) to Section 9(1)(i): collection of news and views in India for transmission outside India by a non-resident in the news/publishing business does not constitute a taxable deemed accrual. Client 4 is covered by the statutory exemption under Explanation 1(b) to Section 9(1)(i): operations confined to the purchase of goods in India solely for the purpose of export do not give rise to deemed accrual of income in India. Client 3, however, falls squarely under Explanation 2(b) to Section 9(1)(i): where a person acting on behalf of a non-resident habitually maintains in India a stock of goods or merchandise from which he regularly delivers goods or merchandise on behalf of the non-resident, a business connection is established. Only income attributable to operations carried out in India by Client 3 will be deemed to accrue or arise in India. Therefore, income is deemed to accrue or arise in India only in the case of Client 3.

questions.question: Bharat Infotech Ltd., an Indian company whose entire business operations and revenue arise from software development branches in Munich (Germany) and Zurich (Switzerland), declares and pays an interim dividend of USD 500,000 out of profits accumulated exclusively in foreign bank accounts directly into the Swiss bank accounts of its non-resident shareholders (Mr. Klaus and Mr. Hans, residents of Germany). The shareholders contend that since the business is carried on wholly outside India, the profits arose outside India, and the dividend was declared and paid outside India, no income accrues or arises or is received in India under Section 5(2). Examine the validity of the shareholders' contention under the provisions of the Income-tax Act, 1961.
options: The contention is valid because the profits out of which the dividend is paid arose wholly outside India and payment was made outside India into a foreign bank account.
The contention is valid provided the foreign branches of the Indian company have paid corporate tax in Germany and Switzerland under the respective DTAAs.
The contention is invalid only to the extent the dividend is remitted to India by the non-resident shareholders within the same financial year.

The contention is invalid because under Section 9(1)(iv), any dividend paid by an Indian company outside India is deemed to accrue or arise in India in all cases and is taxable in the hands of non-resident shareholders.
questions.explanation: Under Section 9(1)(iv) of the Income-tax Act, 1961, any dividend paid by an Indian company outside India is deemed to accrue or arise in India. This deeming provision creates an absolute statutory nexus with India based solely on the status of the paying company being an Indian company. The location where the company's business is carried on, where its profits are derived, where the dividend is declared, or where the dividend warrants/remittances are received is completely immaterial. Consequently, even though the profits arose exclusively in Germany and Switzerland and payments were made directly in Zurich, the dividend is deemed to accrue or arise in India and is chargeable to tax in the hands of the non-resident shareholders under Section 5(2)(b) read with Section 9(1)(iv). The shareholders' contention is therefore wholly invalid, making Option D the correct answer.

options: USD 90,000 (15% of the total interest)
USD 240,000 (40% of the total interest)
USD 600,000 (The entire interest is deemed to accrue or arise in India as the borrower is an Indian resident company)
Nil (Since the loan was disbursed and received outside India by a foreign bank)
questions.explanation: Under Section 9(1)(v)(b) of the Income-tax Act, 1961, interest payable by a person who is a resident is deemed to accrue or arise in India, EXCEPT where it is payable in respect of any debt incurred or moneys borrowed and used: (1) for the purposes of a business or profession carried on by him outside India; or (2) for the purposes of making or earning any income from any source outside India. In this case: (i) USD 6,000,000 (60% of corpus) was used for an active manufacturing business carried on outside India (Dhaka), so corresponding interest of USD 360,000 is exempt from Indian deeming fiction; (ii) USD 2,500,000 (25% of corpus) was used for earning interest income from a source outside India (Singapore corporate bonds), so corresponding interest of USD 150,000 also falls squarely under the statutory exception; (iii) USD 1,500,000 (15% of corpus) was used for its domestic processing mill in Surat (business in India). Therefore, only 15% of the total interest, i.e., USD 90,000 (15% of USD 600,000), is deemed to accrue or arise in India. Options B, C, and D are incorrect because they fail to properly apply both limbs of the statutory exception under Section 9(1)(v)(b).

questions.question:
Mr. Robert, a non-resident individual based in New York, borrows USD 2,000,000 from Ms. Claire, also a non-resident individual based in London. During the previous year 2024-25, Mr. Robert utilizes the borrowed funds in India as follows:
(1) USD 1,200,000 is invested in equity shares of listed Indian companies, yielding dividend income of INR 15,00,000;
(2) USD 800,000 is utilized as working capital in an active proprietary wholesale textile trading business carried on by him in Mumbai.
Mr. Robert pays annual interest of USD 100,000 (proportionately USD 60,000 for equity investments and USD 40,000 for the Mumbai trading business) to Ms. Claire in London. Determine the taxability of the interest income of USD 100,000 in the hands of Ms. Claire under Section 9(1)(v) of the Income-tax Act, 1961.
options: The entire interest of USD 100,000 is deemed to accrue or arise in India since both the shares and the trading business are located in India.
Nil interest is deemed to accrue or arise in India because both the borrower and the lender are non-residents and the loan contract was executed outside India.

Only USD 40,000 is deemed to accrue or arise in India, as interest payable by a non-resident is deemed to accrue or arise in India ONLY IF the borrowed funds are used for the purpose of a business or profession carried on by him in India.
Only USD 60,000 is deemed to accrue or arise in India because investment in Indian corporate securities represents a capital asset situated in India.
questions.explanation: Under Section 9(1)(v)(c) of the Income-tax Act, 1961, interest payable by a non-resident is deemed to accrue or arise in India ONLY WHEN it is payable in respect of any debt incurred or moneys borrowed and used for the purposes of a business or profession carried on by such person in India. Noticeably, unlike Section 9(1)(vi)(c) (royalty) and Section 9(1)(vii)(c) (fees for technical services), the legislature deliberately did NOT include the phrase 'or for the purposes of making or earning any income from any source in India' in Section 9(1)(v)(c). Consequently, if a non-resident borrows money from another non-resident and invests it in Indian company shares or other passive investment sources in India, the interest payable is NOT deemed to accrue or arise in India. Here, USD 1,200,000 was invested in Indian shares (other source), so interest of USD 60,000 is not deemed to accrue or arise in India. Only USD 800,000 was used for a business carried on by Mr. Robert in India (Mumbai wholesale trading), making only the proportionate interest of USD 40,000 deemed to accrue or arise in India. Thus, Option C is correct and Options A, B, and D are incorrect.

questions.question: Sumitomo Tokyo Bank (a banking company incorporated in Japan) operates an authorized branch in Mumbai, which constitutes its Permanent Establishment (PE) in India. During P.Y. 2024-25, the Mumbai branch pays interest of INR 50,00,000 to its Tokyo Head Office and INR 30,00,000 to its Singapore overseas branch for inter-branch credit facilities. The Mumbai branch claims that under general principles of corporate law, a branch cannot pay interest to itself (no one can earn income from oneself), and therefore this internal remittance does not constitute income accruing or arising in India, nor is it subject to TDS under Section 195. Evaluate the legal validity of the branch's contention under the Income-tax Act, 1961.
options: The claim of the Mumbai branch is legally sound under the doctrine of mutuality, and inter-branch interest is exempt from Indian tax.

Under the Explanation to Section 9(1)(v), the Mumbai PE is deemed to be a person separate and independent of the foreign bank, the interest of INR 80,00,000 is deemed to accrue or arise in India, and the PE is obligated to deduct TDS u/s 195; failure to deduct TDS will attract disallowance u/s 40(a)(i).
Only the interest of INR 30,00,000 paid to the Singapore branch is deemed to accrue or arise in India, whereas interest paid to the Tokyo Head Office is exempt from withholding tax.
The interest of INR 80,00,000 is taxable in India only if the Tokyo Head Office opts for the presumptive taxation scheme under Section 44BB.
questions.explanation: To resolve conflicts surrounding inter-branch interest payments by foreign banks, an Explanation was inserted in Section 9(1)(v) of the Income-tax Act, 1961. Under this Explanation, in the case of a non-resident engaged in the business of banking, any interest payable by the Permanent Establishment (PE) in India to the head office or any other PE or part of such non-resident outside India is deemed to accrue or arise in India. The PE in India is deemed to be a person separate and independent of the non-resident enterprise of which it is a PE. Consequently, the Indian branch must deduct tax at source under Section 195 on interest paid to both the Tokyo Head Office (INR 50 lakh) and the Singapore branch (INR 30 lakh), totaling INR 80,00,000. Non-deduction results in statutory disallowance of the interest expenditure in the hands of the Indian branch under Section 40(a)(i), along with interest under Section 201(1A) and penalties. Hence, Option B is correct and Options A, C, and D are legally untenable.

options: Only the regular interest of INR 85,00,000 qualifies as interest under Section 2(28A), while the arrangement fee and commitment fee are general business profits exempt in the absence of a PE.
The arrangement fee and commitment fee are technical fees governed by Section 9(1)(vii), whereas only interest on drawn funds is covered under Section 9(1)(v).
The commitment fee on unutilized funds is a capital receipt outside the charging scope of Section 4.

All three payments—regular interest, arrangement fee, and commitment fee on unutilized credit—fall within the statutory definition of 'interest' under Section 2(28A) and are deemed to accrue or arise in India under Section 9(1)(v).
questions.explanation: Under Section 2(28A) of the Income-tax Act, 1961, 'interest' means interest payable in any manner in respect of any moneys borrowed or debt incurred (including a deposit, claim or other similar right or obligation) AND INCLUDES any service fee or other charge in respect of the moneys borrowed or debt incurred OR in respect of any credit facility which has not been utilized. Therefore, the statutory definition specifically and expressly encompasses: (i) regular interest on drawn debt (INR 85,00,000); (ii) service, arrangement, and processing fees in respect of the debt (INR 25,00,000); and (iii) commitment fees or charges in respect of credit facilities that have not been utilized (INR 15,00,000). Since all three payments fall within the definition of 'interest' under Section 2(28A) and are payable by an Indian resident for a project in India, all three items are deemed to accrue or arise in India under Section 9(1)(v). Thus, Option D is correct and Options A, B, and C are incorrect.

questions.question: Tata Technologies Ltd., an Indian resident company, enters into an intellectual property licensing agreement with Dassault Corp., a French engineering design software enterprise. Under the contract, Tata Technologies pays an annual royalty of EUR 400,000 for the right to use specialized automotive CAD software. Tata Technologies uses this software exclusively in its design and development centre located in Munich, Germany, for designing automobile chassis for BMW AG, generating engineering service fees billed and received in Germany. Dassault Corp. has no branch or PE in India. Is the royalty of EUR 400,000 paid by Tata Technologies Ltd. deemed to accrue or arise in India under Section 9(1)(vi) of the Income-tax Act, 1961?
options: No, because under Section 9(1)(vi)(b), royalty payable by a resident is NOT deemed to accrue or arise in India if it is payable in respect of any right, property or information used for the purposes of a business or profession carried on by such resident outside India.
Yes, because royalty payable by an Indian resident person is always deemed to accrue or arise in India irrespective of where the property is utilized.
Yes, because Dassault Corp. does not have a Permanent Establishment in Germany and therefore the income reverts to Indian sourcing rules.
No, but only if Tata Technologies Ltd. obtains a prior nil withholding certificate under Section 195(2) from the Assessing Officer in India.
questions.explanation: Under Section 9(1)(vi)(b) of the Income-tax Act, 1961, income by way of royalty payable by a resident is deemed to accrue or arise in India, EXCEPT where it is payable in respect of any right, property or information used or services utilized for the purposes of a business or profession carried on by such person outside India or for the purposes of making or earning any income from any source outside India. In the given scenario, Tata Technologies Ltd. (an Indian resident) pays royalty for CAD software that is utilized exclusively in its business carried on outside India (its Munich development centre) and for earning income from a source outside India (designing automobile chassis for BMW AG in Germany). Therefore, the payment falls squarely within the statutory exception carved out in Section 9(1)(vi)(b). The royalty is not deemed to accrue or arise in India, and no withholding tax under Section 195 is attracted. Thus, Option A is the correct answer and Options B, C, and D are incorrect.

questions.question:
Consider the following independent transactions during P.Y. 2024-25:
Case X: Mr. John (a non-resident living in the UK) pays royalty of USD 50,000 to Mr. David (a non-resident living in the US) for using a patented manufacturing process in his bicycle manufacturing factory in Pune, India.
Case Y: Alpha LLC (a US company) pays royalty of USD 80,000 to Beta Corp (a Canadian company) for using a specialized software platform to manage a commercial shopping complex in Mumbai that earns rental income for Alpha LLC in India.
Case Z: Gamma Inc. (a French company) pays royalty of USD 60,000 to Delta Ltd. (a German company) for patent rights used in an assembly plant located in Paris, which manufactures luxury watches exported worldwide, including 15% of production exported directly to retail buyers in India.
In which of the above cases is the royalty deemed to accrue or arise in India under Section 9(1)(vi)(c) of the Income-tax Act, 1961?
options: Case X only
Case X, Case Y, and Case Z
Case X and Case Y only
Case Y and Case Z only
questions.explanation: Under Section 9(1)(vi)(c) of the Income-tax Act, 1961, royalty payable by a non-resident is deemed to accrue or arise in India ONLY WHEN the royalty is payable in respect of any right, property or information used or services utilized: (1) for the purposes of a business or profession carried on by such person in India; OR (2) for the purposes of making or earning any income from any source in India. Analyzing each case: In Case X, the patented process is used for a bicycle manufacturing business carried on by Mr. John in Pune, India (qualifies under limb 1). In Case Y, the software is used for earning rental income from a commercial complex in Mumbai, India (qualifies under limb 2, earning income from a source in India). In Case Z, the patent is used in an assembly plant in Paris (outside India); the mere subsequent export of finished watches to Indian customers does not mean the patent was used in a business in India or used for earning income from an Indian source. Hence, royalty is deemed to accrue or arise in India in Case X and Case Y only. Option C is correct.

questions.question:
GeoSeismic Corp., a non-resident company incorporated in Norway, enters into two distinct contracts with Indian entities during P.Y. 2024-25:
Contract 1: Leases deep-sea seismic survey vessels and specialized marine acoustic equipment to ONGC Ltd. for prospecting and exploring mineral oil reserves offshore of Andhra Pradesh, receiving hire charges of INR 4,00,00,000.
Contract 2: Leases advanced automated packaging machinery to MedLife Healthcare Ltd. (an Indian pharmaceutical company) for use in its formulations factory in Baddi, Himachal Pradesh, receiving hire charges of INR 60,00,000.
Determine the classification and tax treatment of the consideration received under Contract 1 and Contract 2 with reference to Section 9(1)(vi), Explanation 2(v) of the Income-tax Act, 1961.
options: Both Contract 1 and Contract 2 are classified as 'Royalty' under Explanation 2(v) to Section 9(1)(vi) and taxed under Section 115A.

Contract 1 is excluded from the definition of 'Royalty' under Explanation 2(v) as it relates to amounts referred to in Section 44BB, whereas Contract 2 constitutes 'Royalty' as consideration for the use of industrial/commercial equipment.
Contract 1 constitutes 'Royalty', whereas Contract 2 is treated as business profits because pharmaceutical manufacturing is an industrial activity under Section 28.
Neither contract constitutes 'Royalty' because the bare leasing of tangible physical equipment without transfer of technology is outside the scope of Section 9(1)(vi).
questions.explanation: Under Explanation 2(v) to Section 9(1)(vi) of the Income-tax Act, 1961, 'royalty' includes consideration for the use or right to use any industrial, commercial or scientific equipment, 'but not including the amounts referred to in section 44BB'. Section 44BB deals with presumptive taxation of non-resident taxpayers engaged in the business of providing services or facilities in connection with, or supplying plant and machinery on hire used, or to be used, in the prospecting for, or extraction or production of, mineral oils. Therefore, Contract 1 (leasing deep-sea seismic vessels to ONGC for mineral oil exploration) is specifically and expressly excluded from 'Royalty' by virtue of the carve-out in Explanation 2(v), and is governed by Section 44BB. On the other hand, Contract 2 represents consideration for the use of industrial/commercial packaging machinery by a pharmaceutical manufacturer, which is squarely covered under Explanation 2(v) as royalty. Thus, Option B is correct and Options A, C, and D are incorrect.

options: (ii) only, because theatrical exhibition of films and outright assignment of copyright are excluded from royalty.
(i) only, because television broadcasting rights are classified as telecommunication fees and not copyright royalties.
(i), (ii), and (iii), because any consideration received by a non-resident for intellectual property is deemed to be royalty.

(i) and (ii) only, because consideration for sale, distribution or exhibition of cinematographic films is expressly covered as royalty, while consideration chargeable under 'Capital Gains' is specifically excluded.
questions.explanation: Under Explanation 2(vi) to Section 9(1)(vi) of the Income-tax Act, 1961, 'royalty' includes consideration for the transfer of all or any rights (including granting of a license) in respect of any copyright, literary, artistic or scientific work including films or video tapes for use in connection with television or tapes for use in connection with radio broadcasting. Furthermore, the statutory Note clarifies: 'Consideration for sale, distribution or exhibition of cinematographic films is covered within the scope of royalty.' Therefore, both theatrical distribution rights of films (Item i) and television broadcasting rights (Item ii) constitute royalty. However, the opening clause of Explanation 2 explicitly states: 'royalty means consideration (including any lump sum consideration but excluding any consideration which would be the income of the recipient chargeable under the head Capital gains)'. Since Item (iii) involves an outright permanent transfer chargeable under the head 'Capital Gains', it is specifically excluded from royalty. Hence, only items (i) and (ii) constitute royalty. Option D is the correct answer.

questions.question: SoftTech India Pvt. Ltd. imports shrink-wrapped, off-the-shelf antivirus computer software packages and end-user licenses from Norton Systems Inc., a US resident corporation. The transaction falls under an End-User Licence Agreement (EULA) where SoftTech India simply resells the packaged software to Indian customers without having any right to copy, reverse-engineer, modify, or commercially exploit the underlying source code or copyright. The Assessing Officer asserts that Explanation 4 to Section 9(1)(vi) deems any right for use or right to use computer software (including a license) as royalty, and therefore SoftTech was bound to deduct tax under Section 195. What is the legal position regarding the taxability and requirement of TDS on this software payment under the Indo-US DTAA in light of the landmark Supreme Court decision in Engineering Analysis Centre of Excellence P. Ltd v. CIT (2021)?
options: The payment is for a 'copyrighted article' and not for the 'use of copyright'; under the DTAA (which is narrower than Explanation 4 and prevails under Section 90(2)), such payment is business profit and not royalty, hence no TDS u/s 195 is attracted in the absence of a PE in India.
The payment is royalty under domestic law as well as the DTAA because Explanation 4 overrides bilateral tax treaties under Section 90(2).
The payment constitutes royalty, but TDS under Section 195 is restricted to a concessional flat rate of 2% under Section 194J.
The payment is treated as Fees for Technical Services (FTS) under Article 12 of the Indo-US DTAA and subject to 15% withholding tax.
questions.explanation: In the landmark ruling of Engineering Analysis Centre of Excellence P. Ltd v. CIT (2021) 432 ITR 471, the Supreme Court analyzed the four categories of computer software transactions (including direct end-user purchase and distributor resale of shrink-wrap/off-the-shelf software under EULAs). The Apex Court held that the definition of 'royalty' under Article 12 of the DTAA (such as India's DTAA with the US, Singapore, etc.) requires the payment to be consideration for 'the use of, or the right to use, any copyright'. A payment for acquiring a computer software product or copyrighted article does not confer any right to exploit the copyright itself. Although Explanation 4 to Section 9(1)(vi) was inserted in the domestic Act to widen the definition to include the right to use computer software, Section 90(2) gives the non-resident the right to be governed by the beneficial provisions of the DTAA. Since the DTAA definition does not cover copyrighted articles and treaties cannot be unilaterally amended by domestic explanations, the payment constitutes business profits and is not taxable in India in the absence of a PE. Consequently, no TDS under Section 195 is required. Thus, Option A is correct.

questions.question: Delta Infotech Ltd., a resident distributor, purchases packaged enterprise resource planning (ERP) software from Microsoft India Ltd. (a resident transferor) for resale to domestic corporate clients. Microsoft India Ltd. had originally imported the software and deducted tax under Section 195 at the time of remittance to its foreign parent company. Delta Infotech purchases and resells the software without making any modification whatsoever. Delta Infotech seeks to know whether it must deduct TDS under Section 194J when making payment to Microsoft India Ltd. Under Notification No. 21/2012 dated 13.06.2012, which set of cumulative conditions must be satisfied so that Delta Infotech is NOT required to deduct tax under Section 194J on this acquisition?
options: (1) The software license is valid for less than 12 months; (2) Delta Infotech furnishes Form 15CA/15CB; and (3) The software is hosted on a government-approved cloud server.
(1) The software is a customized ERP software; (2) The payment is below INR 50,00,000; and (3) An advance ruling is obtained from the Board for Advance Rulings.

(1) The software is acquired in a subsequent transfer without any modification by the transferor; (2) Tax has been deducted either under Section 194J or Section 195 on payment for any previous transfer; and (3) The transferee obtains a declaration from the transferor that tax has been so deducted along with the PAN of the transferor.
(1) The transferor is a public sector undertaking; (2) The software is sold exclusively to educational institutions; and (3) Payment is made via electronic clearing system.
questions.explanation: To prevent multi-stage cascading TDS on software distribution, the Central Government issued Notification No. 21/2012 dated 13.6.2012 (effective 1st July 2012). This notification exempts subsequent transfers of software from tax deduction under Section 194J if three cumulative conditions are met: (1) The software is acquired in a subsequent transfer without any modification by the transferor; (2) Tax has been deducted either under Section 194J or under Section 195 on payment for any previous transfer of such software; and (3) The transferee obtains a declaration from the transferor that tax has been so deducted along with the Permanent Account Number (PAN) of the transferor. If all three conditions are satisfied, Delta Infotech is relieved of the obligation to deduct tax under Section 194J. Hence, Option C correctly articulates these statutory conditions.

options: Explanation 5 accepts CloudHost's argument and exempts any equipment hosted outside India where physical control remains with the foreign vendor.
Explanation 5 applies only to intangible secret formulas, and tangible server hardware remains strictly governed by physical situs in the USA.
Explanation 5 requires that at least 50% of the data processed on the server must relate to Indian citizens for it to be deemed as royalty.

Explanation 5 clarifies that consideration in respect of any right, property or information is royalty whether or not: (a) possession or control is with the payer; (b) used directly by the payer; or (c) the location of such right, property or information is in India.
questions.explanation: Explanation 5 to Section 9(1)(vi) was inserted by Finance Act, 2012 with retrospective effect from 1.6.1976 to clarify the scope of royalty. It expressly provides that royalty includes and has always included consideration in respect of any right, property or information, whether or not: (a) the possession or control of such right, property or information is with the payer; (b) such right, property or information is used directly by the payer; (c) the location of such right, property or information is in India. Consequently, the fact that the dedicated cryptographic hardware/servers are located in Virginia, USA, and that physical possession and custody remain with CloudHost Inc. does not remove the payment from the ambit of royalty under domestic law. Explanation 5 overrides all three objections raised by CloudHost. Thus, Option D is the correct answer.

questions.question: StarTelecast Ltd., an Indian resident television broadcasting company, pays USD 2,500,000 per annum to AsiaSat Ltd., a Hong Kong-based satellite operating company. AsiaSat provides transponder capacity on its geostationary satellite stationed over the Indian Ocean. The process involves receiving telecast signals beamed up from StarTelecast's earth station in Noida, amplifying the signals on the satellite transponder, shifting frequency, and downlinking them back across the Indian subcontinent. AsiaSat contends that transponder transmission is a standard, non-secret telecommunication service, and since the process is not secret, it cannot be classified as consideration for a 'secret formula or process' under Explanation 2 to Section 9(1)(vi). Examine the validity of AsiaSat Ltd.'s contention in light of Explanation 6 to Section 9(1)(vi) of the Income-tax Act, 1961.
options: The contention is valid because satellite technology is public scientific knowledge and only secret formulas or processes constitute royalty.

The contention is invalid because under Explanation 6, the term 'process' includes and is deemed to have always included transmission by satellite (including up-linking, amplification, conversion for down-linking), cable, optic fibre or similar technology, WHETHER OR NOT SUCH PROCESS IS SECRET.
The contention is valid provided AsiaSat Ltd. holds a telecommunications operator license granted by the Telecom Regulatory Authority of India (TRAI).
The contention is invalid, but the consideration is taxable under Section 44B as shipping and air transport operations rather than royalty.
questions.explanation: Under Explanation 6 to Section 9(1)(vi) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 (inserted with retrospective effect from 1.6.1976), the term 'process' includes and shall be deemed to have always included transmission by satellite (including up-linking, amplification, conversion for down-linking of any signal), cable, optic fibre or by any other similar technology, WHETHER OR NOT SUCH PROCESS IS SECRET. Prior to this amendment, taxpayers frequently argued that transponder fees were for standard telecommunication processes that were not secret. Explanation 6 neutralizes this argument completely by declaring that satellite transmission constitutes a 'process' under Explanation 2(i), (ii), and (iii), regardless of secrecy. Therefore, AsiaSat's contention is legally untenable under domestic law, and the transponder hire fees are deemed to be royalty accruing or arising in India. Option B is correct.

questions.question:
Narmada Hydro Power Corporation (an Indian resident entity) engages two foreign companies for its multi-purpose dam and hydro-electric project in Madhya Pradesh during P.Y. 2024-25:
1. Alpine GeoEng GmbH (Germany) is paid EUR 1,000,000 for undertaking the physical excavation, tunneling, civil construction, and on-site assembly of the underground turbine powerhouse cavern (a turnkey construction and assembly project).
2. Zurich Financial & Risk Advisory AG (Switzerland) is paid CHF 300,000 for providing macro-financial risk modeling, tariff consultancy, and project debt-structuring advisory services.
Which of the following correctly describes the characterization of these payments under Section 9(1)(vii) of the Income-tax Act, 1961?
options: The payment to Alpine GeoEng GmbH is excluded from FTS as consideration for a 'construction, assembly, mining or like project', whereas the payment to Zurich Financial & Risk Advisory AG constitutes FTS as managerial and consultancy services.
Both payments constitute Fees for Technical Services (FTS) because both involve highly specialized engineering and financial knowledge.
The payment to Alpine GeoEng GmbH constitutes FTS, while the payment to Zurich Financial & Risk Advisory AG is exempt from tax in India as financial advisory is not technical.
Neither payment constitutes FTS because neither foreign company has an established place of business in India.
questions.explanation: Under Explanation 2 to Section 9(1)(vii) of the Income-tax Act, 1961, 'fees for technical services' means any consideration (including any lump sum consideration) for the rendering of any managerial, technical or consultancy services (including the provision of services of technical or other personnel). However, the definition expressly EXCLUDES: (1) consideration for any construction, assembly, mining or like project undertaken by the recipient; or (2) consideration which would be income of the recipient chargeable under the head 'Salaries'. The civil excavation, tunneling, and assembly undertaken by Alpine GeoEng GmbH falls squarely within the statutory exclusion for a 'construction, assembly, mining or like project'. Conversely, the debt structuring, financial risk modeling, and tariff advisory provided by Zurich Financial & Risk Advisory AG constitute 'managerial or consultancy services' and are not covered by any exclusion. Hence, the payment to Alpine GeoEng is excluded from FTS, while the payment to Zurich Financial constitutes FTS. Option A is correct.

questions.question: Miss Ananya, an Indian resident entrepreneur, pays USD 25,000 to Mr. Fernando, an independent financial and management consultant practising in Colombo, Sri Lanka. The consultancy was engaged to formulate a financial feasibility report and capital-raising strategy for a new greenfield eco-resort project being developed by Ananya in Kerala, with potential foreign venture capital collaboration. Mr. Fernando performed the entire consultancy work in Colombo, never visited India, has no office, residence, or business connection in India, and received the payment in Colombo. Is the sum of USD 25,000 received by Mr. Fernando chargeable to income-tax in India under the Income-tax Act, 1961?
options: No, because Mr. Fernando is a non-resident, the services were rendered entirely in Sri Lanka, and the payment was received outside India.
No, because Section 9(1)(vii) requires the non-resident service provider to maintain a fixed place of business or permanent establishment in India.

Yes, because under Section 9(1)(vii) read with the Explanation to Section 9, fees for technical services are deemed to accrue or arise in India if utilized in a business in India, irrespective of whether the non-resident has a residence, place of business, or business connection in India, or whether the services were rendered in India.
Yes, but only if Miss Ananya fails to claim the expense as a deduction in her Indian income-tax return.
questions.explanation: Under Section 9(1)(vii)(b) of the Income-tax Act, 1961, fees for technical services payable by a resident are deemed to accrue or arise in India, except where payable in respect of services utilized in a business/profession carried on outside India or for earning income from a source outside India. Here, the consultancy was utilized for a resort project in Kerala, India. Furthermore, the Explanation to Section 9 (inserted by Finance Act, 2010 with retrospective effect from 1.6.1976) explicitly provides that income by way of interest, royalty, or fees for technical services deemed to accrue or arise in India under clauses (v), (vi), and (vii) of Section 9(1) shall be included in the total income of the non-resident, WHETHER OR NOT: (i) the non-resident has a residence or place of business or business connection in India; or (ii) the non-resident has rendered services in India. Therefore, even though Mr. Fernando rendered all services in Colombo, has no PE in India, and received payment in Sri Lanka, the payment is deemed to accrue or arise in India and is taxable in his hands. This directly reflects Illustration 5 in the Study Material. Option C is correct.

questions.question:
Mr. Rajesh, an Indian resident individual, made the following transfers outside India during P.Y. 2024-25:
(1) Wired a pure cash gift of USD 10,000 (equivalent to INR 8,30,000) from his Dubai bank account to the overseas bank account of his college friend, Mr. Arthur (a non-resident individual living in the UK), with no consideration and on no specific occasion.
(2) Transferred title of a luxury residential apartment in London valued at GBP 500,000 (INR 5.25 crore) to his foreign business associate, Mr. Smith (a non-resident), without any consideration.
(3) Gifted diamond jewelry situated in Singapore valued at SGD 30,000 (INR 18,50,000) to a foreign company, Pacific Holdings Ltd. (incorporated in Hong Kong), without consideration.
Which of the above transfers is/are deemed to accrue or arise in India under Section 9(1)(viii) read with Section 56(2)(x) of the Income-tax Act, 1961?
options: All three transfers (1, 2, and 3)
Transfer 1 and Transfer 2 only
Transfer 2 and Transfer 3 only
Transfer 1 only
questions.explanation: Under Section 9(1)(viii) of the Income-tax Act, 1961, income arising outside India, being ANY SUM OF MONEY paid without consideration, by a person resident in India to a non-corporate non-resident or to a foreign company or to a resident but not ordinarily resident, is deemed to accrue or arise in India if it is chargeable to tax under Section 56(2)(x) (i.e., aggregate sum exceeding INR 50,000). A crucial statutory nuance of Section 9(1)(viii) is that it applies ONLY to a 'sum of money paid without consideration'. The legislature did NOT extend this deeming fiction to transfers of movable or immovable property situated outside India transferred without consideration or for inadequate consideration.
