Therefore, while Transfer 1 (wire of USD 10,000) is a sum of money and is deemed to accrue or arise in India under Section 9(1)(viii), Transfer 2 (immovable residential apartment in London) and Transfer 3 (jewelry in Singapore) do not fall under Section 9(1)(viii). Thus, only Transfer 1 is deemed to accrue or arise in India, making Option D the correct answer.

Let us compute the Total Income of Mr. Kevin (non-resident) for A.Y. 2025-26 item by item:
1. Dividend from Indian company (Infosys Ltd.) paid outside India: Deemed to accrue or arise in India under Section 9(1)(iv) = INR 45,000.
2. Interest from Indian resident (Mr. Alok): Money was borrowed and used exclusively for a business carried on outside India (restaurant in London); covered by the exception in Section 9(1)(v)(b), so it is NOT deemed to accrue or arise in India = INR Nil.
3. Royalty from Government of India: Sourced under Section 9(1)(vi)(a), royalty payable by the Government is unconditionally deemed to accrue or arise in India = INR 1,20,000.
4. Fees for Technical Services (FTS) from French company (non-resident): The consultancy services were utilized for a business in India (Jamnagar refinery), so it is deemed to accrue or arise in India under Section 9(1)(vii)(c) read with the Explanation to Section 9 = INR 1,50,000.
5. Cash gift from Indian resident friend paid outside India: Being a sum of money paid without consideration exceeding INR 50,000 by a resident to a non-resident, it is deemed to accrue or arise in India under Section 9(1)(viii) and taxable under Section 56(2)(x) = INR 75,000.
Total Income = INR 45,000 + INR Nil + INR 1,20,000 + INR 1,50,000 + INR 75,000 = INR 3,90,000. Therefore, Option B is correct.

questions.question:
Global Horizons Fund, an offshore investment fund based in Mauritius, is planning to appoint Apex Asset Advisors LLP, an independent Mumbai-based portfolio manager, to manage its portfolio of investments across South Asia (including India). The trustees of Global Horizons Fund are apprehensive that:
(1) Having a fund manager in India will lead to the fund having a 'business connection' in India under Section 9(1)(i);
(2) The fund could be treated as a resident of India under Section 6(3) on the ground that its place of effective management (POEM) or fund manager is in India.
How do the safe harbour provisions of Section 9A(1) and Section 9A(2) protect an Eligible Investment Fund against these risks?
options: Section 9A(1) ensures that fund management activity carried out through an eligible fund manager shall not constitute a business connection in India, and Section 9A(2) ensures the fund will not be deemed resident in India merely because the eligible fund manager is located in India.
Section 9A provides a complete tax holiday on all capital gains and dividends earned by the fund in India for a period of 10 consecutive assessment years.
Section 9A mandates that the fund manager must be an employee of the fund and hold a minimum 51% voting equity in the fund.
Section 9A eliminates the requirement for the offshore fund to obtain a Permanent Account Number (PAN) or comply with transfer pricing documentation in India.
questions.explanation: Section 9A was introduced as a specific safe harbour regime to encourage offshore fund management from India without exposing the foreign fund to adverse Indian tax consequences. Section 9A(1) provides that in the case of an eligible investment fund, the fund management activity carried out through an eligible fund manager acting on behalf of such fund shall not constitute a business connection in India of the said fund. Complementing this, Section 9A(2) provides that an eligible investment fund shall not be said to be resident in India merely because the eligible fund manager undertaking fund management activities on its behalf is located in India. Together, these two provisions shield the foreign fund from having a taxable business connection or being classified as a tax resident of India due to the fund manager's physical presence. Option A is correct, whereas Options B, C, and D are factually and legally inaccurate.

questions.question: Olympus Global Growth Fund is an offshore investment fund incorporated in Luxembourg. As of 1st April 2024, the aggregate direct and indirect participation interest held by persons resident in India in Olympus Global Growth Fund is 7.5% of the total corpus (exceeding the normal statutory threshold of 5%). The fund management activities are conducted through an eligible fund manager in Mumbai. The fund takes active steps and successfully reduces the aggregate participation of Indian residents to 4.2% by 15th July 2024. Does Olympus Global Growth Fund violate the condition regarding Indian resident participation under Section 9A(3)(c) for P.Y. 2024-25?
options: Yes, because the 5% threshold is an absolute statutory ceiling that cannot be breached at any point during the financial year.
No, because Section 9A allows Indian residents to hold up to 25% participation interest if the fund is incorporated in a DTAA country.

No, because under the proviso to Section 9A(3)(c), if the aggregate participation of Indian residents exceeds 5% as on 1st April or 1st October of the previous year, the condition is deemed to be satisfied if the fund reduces its aggregate participation to 5% or less within 4 months from such date.
Yes, because remediation is only permissible if prior written approval is obtained from the CBDT before 30th April.
questions.explanation: Under Section 9A(3)(c) of the Income-tax Act, 1961, the aggregate participation or investment in the eligible investment fund, directly or indirectly, by persons resident in India should not exceed 5% of the corpus of the fund. However, recognizing market fluctuations and redemption cycles, the Proviso to Section 9A(3)(c) provides that if the aggregate participation or investment in the fund exceeds 5% as on 1st April and 1st October of the previous year, the condition shall be deemed to be satisfied if the fund reduces its aggregate participation or investment to 5% or less within 4 months from 1st April or 1st October of such previous year, as the case may be. In the present case, the participation was 7.5% on 1st April 2024, but the fund reduced it to 4.2% (below 5%) by 15th July 2024, which is within 4 months (i.e., before 31st July 2024). Consequently, the condition is deemed satisfied. Option C is correct.

questions.question:
Consider two offshore funds seeking safe harbour under Section 9A for P.Y. 2024-25:
Fund Alpha: A private equity fund incorporated in Ireland with 30 unconnected members. One member, Mr. Higgins, along with his wholly-owned investment company (connected person), holds a 12% participation interest.
Fund Beta: An investment fund set up by a Category-I Foreign Portfolio Investor (FPI) registered with SEBI under the SEBI (Foreign Portfolio Investors) Regulations, 2019, incorporated in Singapore, where 4 sovereign institutional investors collectively hold 70% of the corpus.
Evaluate the eligibility of Fund Alpha and Fund Beta under Section 9A(3) with respect to the member concentration conditions.
options: Both Fund Alpha and Fund Beta satisfy all conditions under Section 9A(3).
Fund Alpha is eligible because it has 30 members, but Fund Beta is ineligible because its top 4 members hold more than 50%.
Neither fund is eligible because Ireland and Singapore are not notified territories under Section 90A.

Fund Alpha is ineligible because a member along with connected persons holds > 10% (12%), while Fund Beta is eligible because the conditions regarding minimum 25 members, 10% single-member cap, and 50% top-10 cap do NOT apply to a Category-I FPI under the proviso to Section 9A(3).
questions.explanation: Under Section 9A(3) of the Income-tax Act, 1961, the general rules for an eligible investment fund require: (e) a minimum of 25 unconnected members; (f) no member along with connected persons shall hold participation interest exceeding 10%; and (g) aggregate participation of 10 or fewer members along with connected persons shall be less than 50%. Fund Alpha breaches clause (f) because Mr. Higgins and his connected entity hold 12% (> 10%), rendering Fund Alpha ineligible. On the other hand, the Proviso to Section 9A(3) explicitly carves out an exception: conditions (e), (f), and (g) DO NOT APPLY in the case of an investment fund set up by the Government or Central Bank of a foreign State, a sovereign fund, or a Category-I FPI registered under the SEBI (FPI) Regulations, 2019 (or Cat-I/Cat-II under 2014 Regulations). Therefore, Fund Beta, being a registered Category-I FPI, is entirely exempt from the 25-member, 10% single-member, and 50% top-10 concentration limits. Hence, Option D is the correct answer.

options: No, because the investment in Zenora Biotech Ltd. violates clause (i) of Section 9A(3), which strictly prohibits any investment in an 'associate entity' (defined as an entity where a director/trustee/member holds > 15% interest).
Yes, because the corpus exceeds INR 100 crore and no single investment exceeds 20% of the corpus.
No, because the fund must maintain a minimum corpus of at least INR 500 crore for foreign funds investing in Indian equities.
Yes, provided the director with the 18% interest recuses himself from the investment committee meetings.
questions.explanation: Section 9A(3) lays down specific investment and portfolio constraints for an eligible investment fund: (h) investment in any single entity shall not exceed 20% of the corpus of the fund (satisfied here, as maximum is 16.67%); (j) monthly average corpus shall not be less than INR 100 crore (satisfied, monthly average is INR 240 crore). However, clause (i) mandates that 'no investment shall be made by the fund in its associate entity'. Section 9A defines an 'associate' as an entity in which a director, trustee, partner, member, or fund manager of the investment fund holds, either individually or collectively, share or interest of MORE THAN 15% of its share capital or interest. Since a director of Vanguard Orient Fund holds an 18% equity interest in Zenora Biotech Ltd., Zenora is an associate entity. The investment of INR 25 crore in Zenora violates Section 9A(3)(i), disqualifying Vanguard Orient Fund from safe harbour. Option A is correct.

questions.question:
Helios India AMC Ltd., an Asset Management Company approved by SEBI under the SEBI (Mutual Funds) Regulations, 1996, acts as fund manager for Orion Global Fund (an eligible offshore fund). The Assessing Officer challenges Helios India's status as an 'eligible fund manager' on two grounds:
Ground 1: Helios India is an Asset Management Company (AMC) and not an individually registered portfolio manager;
Ground 2: Helios India, along with its wholly-owned advisory subsidiary, is entitled to a management fee plus a 15% profit-sharing carry from the transactions carried out by Orion Global Fund through Helios.
Are the Assessing Officer's objections sustainable under Section 9A(4) and relevant CBDT circulars?
options: Both objections are sustainable: AMCs cannot be fund managers under Section 9A, and any profit sharing disqualifies the manager.

Neither objection is sustainable: CBDT Circular No. 8/2019 clarifies that SEBI-approved AMCs are eligible fund managers, and Section 9A(4)(d) permits profit-sharing entitlement up to 20% along with connected persons.
Ground 1 is sustainable, but Ground 2 is not, because profit sharing up to 25% is permissible.
Ground 2 is sustainable because Section 9A strictly mandates fixed-fee remuneration only with zero profit participation.
questions.explanation: Under Section 9A(4) of the Income-tax Act, 1961, an eligible fund manager must satisfy specific conditions: (b) the person should be registered as a fund manager or investment advisor in accordance with specified regulations. CBDT Circular No. 8/2019 dated 10.5.2019 specifically clarified that an Asset Management Company (AMC) approved by SEBI under the SEBI (Mutual Funds) Regulations, 1996 is engaged in fund management of Mutual Funds and qualifies as an eligible fund manager. Hence, Ground 1 is unsustainable. Further, under Section 9A(4)(d), the fund manager along with connected persons shall not be entitled, directly or indirectly, to more than 20% of the profits accruing or arising to the eligible investment fund from transactions carried out by the fund through such fund manager. Since Helios India and its subsidiary are entitled to a 15% profit share (which is within the 20% statutory limit), Ground 2 is also unsustainable. Thus, Option B is correct.

questions.question: Pacific Crest Investment Fund, an eligible investment fund operating under Section 9A, concluded its financial year on 31st March 2024. Under Section 9A(5), the fund is required to furnish a statement in the prescribed form regarding fulfillment of eligibility conditions. Due to administrative delay in compiling audit certificates from its overseas custodians, the fund furnished the statement on 15th October 2024 (198 days after the end of the financial year). What is the statutory time limit under Section 9A(5) for furnishing the prescribed statement, and what penalty can the prescribed income-tax authority levy under Section 271FAB for the delay?
options: Time limit: Within 30 days from FY end; Penalty: INR 50,000 per month of delay.
Time limit: On or before the due date of filing return of income u/s 139(1) (31st October); Penalty: 1% of the fund corpus.
Time limit: Within 90 days from the end of the financial year; Penalty: A fixed sum of INR 5,00,000.
Time limit: Within 180 days from the end of the calendar year; Penalty: INR 10,000.
questions.explanation: Section 9A(5) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 provides that every eligible investment fund shall, in respect of its activities in a financial year, furnish within 90 days from the end of the financial year, a statement in the prescribed form to the prescribed income-tax authority. The statement must contain information relating to fulfillment of the conditions specified in Section 9A and other prescribed particulars. If an eligible investment fund fails to furnish such statement, information or document within the stipulated 90 days from the end of the financial year, Section 271FAB empowers the prescribed income-tax authority to direct that such fund shall pay, by way of penalty, a fixed sum of INR 5,00,000. Hence, Option C correctly specifies both the 90-day time limit and the INR 5,00,000 penalty under Section 271FAB.

options: The notification only relaxes the corpus requirement to INR 50 crore, but all member limits and day-to-day operation bars continue to apply strictly.
The notification exempts the fund only if all investors are non-resident Indian (NRI) individuals holding valid OCI cards.
The notification requires the fund to pay an IFSC facilitation surcharge of 10% in lieu of complying with Section 9A(3).

For an eligible fund manager located in an IFSC commencing on or before 31.03.2030, the conditions of minimum 25 members, 10% single-member cap, and 50% top-10 cap do NOT apply; and the monitoring mechanism (including appointment of directors) to protect investment is explicitly NOT considered as participating in day-to-day operations.
questions.explanation: Under Section 9A(8A) of the Income-tax Act, 1961, the Central Government notified special modifications via Notification No. 59/2022 dated 06.06.2022 for eligible investment funds whose fund manager is located in an IFSC and has commenced operations on or before 31.3.2030. Under this notification: (1) Clauses (e) [minimum 25 members], (f) [single member <= 10%], and (g) [top 10 members < 50%] of Section 9A(3) DO NOT APPLY to the fund; and (2) Clause (k) is modified to provide that the fund shall not participate in day-to-day operations of any person in India, BUT the monitoring mechanism to protect investment (including the right to appoint directors or executive directors) shall NOT be considered as participation in day-to-day operations. Furthermore, the fund manager is registered under IFSCA regulations. Thus, all three objections raised by the Assessing Officer are overridden by Notification No. 59/2022. Option D is the correct answer.

options: The fund's claim is valid because the sole purpose of the Section 9A safe harbour regime is to grant complete tax exemption to offshore funds.

The fund's claim is invalid because Section 9A(6) clarifies that the safe harbour regime has NO impact on the taxability of any income of the eligible investment fund which would have been chargeable to tax irrespective of whether the fund manager's activity constituted a business connection or not.
The fund's claim is valid for capital gains but invalid for dividend income which is always subject to gross basis withholding.
The fund's claim is invalid only if the fund manager fails to file Form 3CEFA before 30th November.
questions.explanation: Section 9A is merely a safe harbour designed to insulate an offshore fund from being deemed to have a business connection or tax residency in India solely by reason of having an Indian fund manager. Sub-section (6) of Section 9A explicitly provides that nothing contained in this section shall affect the taxability of any income of the eligible investment fund which would have been chargeable to tax irrespective of whether the activity of the eligible fund manager constituted the business connection in India of such fund or not. Capital gains on Indian shares and dividends from Indian companies are taxable under Section 5(2) read with Section 9(1)(i) and Section 9(1)(iv) on the ground of source and location of assets in India, completely independent of any business connection. Therefore, Neptune Global Fund remains fully taxable in India on its Indian capital gains and dividends; only its foreign income (Indonesian bond gains) is shielded from Indian taxation. Option B is correct.

questions.question: Mr. Rohan, an Indian citizen, has been residing and working in Dubai since 2018. He qualifies as a 'person resident outside India' under FEMA, 1999 as well as a non-resident under the Income-tax Act, 1961. He maintains a Non-Resident (External) [NRE] Savings Account with State Bank of India, Mumbai Branch, which earned interest of ₹4,20,000 during P.Y. 2025-26. His father, Mr. Dinakar, who is a resident and ordinarily resident in India under FEMA and the Income-tax Act, was added as a joint holder in the NRE account on a 'Former or Survivor' basis as permitted under RBI regulations, but has not contributed any funds. During P.Y. 2025-26, Mr. Rohan also earned interest of ₹65,000 from an ordinary domestic savings account with SBI. Which of the following statements correctly states the taxability of the interest income for A.Y. 2026-27?
options: Both the NRE interest of ₹4,20,000 and the domestic savings interest of ₹65,000 are fully taxable in India in the hands of Mr. Rohan, since the inclusion of an Indian resident joint holder automatically revokes the NRE account's tax-exempt status under the Foreign Exchange Management Act and Income-tax Act.
50% of the NRE interest (₹2,10,000) is exempt in the hands of Mr. Rohan, while the remaining 50% (₹2,10,000) is taxable in the hands of Mr. Dinakar as a resident joint holder.

The entire NRE interest of ₹4,20,000 is exempt from income-tax in the hands of Mr. Rohan under section 10(4)(ii), whereas the domestic savings bank interest of ₹65,000 is taxable in India (subject to deduction under section 80TTA).
The entire NRE interest of ₹4,20,000 is taxable in the hands of Mr. Dinakar because RBI regulations do not permit any tax exemption where an Indian resident is a joint signatory.
questions.explanation: As per section 10(4)(ii) of the Income-tax Act, 1961, any income by way of interest on moneys standing to the credit of an individual in an NRE Account in any bank in India is exempt, provided the individual is a person resident outside India under FEMA, 1999 (or permitted by the RBI). Under RBI regulations, an NRI can include a resident close relative as a joint holder on a 'Former or Survivor' basis, but the funds belong beneficially to the non-resident individual. Since Mr. Rohan is a person resident outside India under FEMA and the beneficial owner of the deposit, the entire NRE interest of ₹4,20,000 is exempt under section 10(4)(ii). Adding a resident joint holder for operational convenience on a former/survivor basis does not taint the exemption for the non-resident owner. Conversely, the domestic savings bank interest of ₹65,000 accrues and arises in India and is taxable under Section 5(2), eligible for deduction up to ₹10,000 under section 80TTA.

questions.question:
Mr. Alok, an individual citizen of India, has resided in the United Kingdom since 2015 and qualifies as a non-resident under the Income-tax Act, 1961 as well as a person resident outside India under FEMA. During P.Y. 2025-26, he derived the following receipts in India:
(i) Interest of ₹1,80,000 on notified Central Government savings certificates, subscribed to by him in convertible foreign exchange through official banking channels.
(ii) Interest of ₹2,40,000 on his NRE fixed deposit with HDFC Bank in India.
(iii) Interest of ₹90,000 on Foreign Currency Non-Resident [FCNR(B)] deposit with ICICI Bank in India.
Examine the taxability of the above receipts in the hands of Mr. Alok for A.Y. 2026-27 under the Income-tax Act, 1961:
options: All three receipts totaling ₹5,10,000 are completely exempt from income-tax under section 10(4B), section 10(4)(ii), and section 10(15)(iv)(fa) respectively.
Only the NRE interest of ₹2,40,000 is exempt under section 10(4)(ii); interest on notified savings certificates (₹1,80,000) and FCNR(B) interest (₹90,000) are fully taxable at normal slab rates.
Interest on notified savings certificates (₹1,80,000) and NRE interest (₹2,40,000) are exempt, but FCNR(B) interest of ₹90,000 is taxable in India because it was credited by an Indian scheduled bank.
Only FCNR(B) interest of ₹90,000 is exempt; NRE interest and savings certificate interest are taxable at a flat rate of 20% under Chapter XII-A.
questions.explanation: All three receipts are specifically exempt under the Income-tax Act, 1961. First, under section 10(4B), in the case of an individual citizen of India or a person of Indian origin who is a non-resident, any income by way of interest on notified savings certificates issued by the Central Government is exempt, provided such certificates were subscribed to in convertible foreign exchange. Second, under section 10(4)(ii), interest on moneys standing to the credit in an NRE account is exempt for an individual resident outside India under FEMA. Third, under section 10(15)(iv)(fa), interest payable by any scheduled bank on deposits in foreign currency (such as FCNR accounts) is exempt in the hands of a non-resident or an RNOR. Therefore, all three receipts are entirely exempt.

questions.question: Under section 10(4C) of the Income-tax Act, 1961, interest payable by an Indian company or a business trust in respect of monies borrowed from a source outside India is exempt in the hands of certain non-resident lenders. Which of the following statements correctly specifies the eligible lenders, borrowing instruments, and qualifying issuance window under section 10(4C)?
options: The exemption is available to all non-residents on any foreign currency denominated convertible bonds or foreign currency external commercial borrowings issued between 1st April 2018 and 31st March 2023.
The exemption is available only to a non-corporate non-resident or a foreign company, in respect of rupee denominated bonds issued during the period from 17th September 2018 to 31st March 2019.
The exemption is available to sovereign wealth funds and foreign pension funds in respect of external commercial borrowings contracted between 1st April 2020 and 31st March 2025.
The exemption is available to any non-resident entity in respect of rupee denominated bonds listed on an IFSC exchange and issued on or after 1st April 2019.
questions.explanation: As per section 10(4C) of the Income-tax Act, 1961, any income by way of interest payable by an Indian company or a business trust in respect of money borrowed from a source outside India by way of issue of rupee denominated bonds (popularly called Masala Bonds) during the period beginning on 17th September, 2018 and ending on 31st March, 2019 is exempt from tax. The exemption is specifically restricted to lenders who are either a non-corporate non-resident or a foreign company. The other options are incorrect as they misstate the borrowing instrument, the issuance dates, or the eligible classes of assessees.

questions.question:
'Alpha Capital Fund' is a Category III Alternative Investment Fund established as a trust and located in GIFT City IFSC. It qualifies as a 'Specified Fund' under section 10(4D). In Alpha Capital Fund, 90% of the units are held by non-residents (having no permanent establishment in India), while the remaining 10% of the units are held by the Indian sponsor/manager. During P.Y. 2025-26, the fund earned the following income streams:
1. Capital gains on transfer of Rupee Denominated Bonds of an Indian company on a recognized stock exchange in IFSC, settled in convertible foreign exchange: ₹50,00,000.
2. Capital gains on transfer of equity shares of an Indian resident operating company on BSE: ₹30,00,000.
3. Capital gains on transfer of foreign currency bonds issued by a foreign company (transacted on IFSC exchange in foreign currency): ₹20,00,000.
4. Business income received from a securitisation trust chargeable under the head 'Profits and gains of business or profession': ₹10,00,000.
Assuming the fund furnishes its annual statement of exempt income within the due date specified under section 139(1), compute the amount of income exempt in the hands of the fund under section 10(4D) for A.Y. 2026-27:
options: ₹1,10,00,000 (100% of all incomes earned by the fund are exempt u/s 10(4D) irrespective of unit-holding composition).
₹99,00,000 (90% of all four income streams earned by the fund, including domestic company shares).
₹70,00,000 (Entire capital gains of ₹50,00,000 + ₹20,00,000, excluding securitisation trust income and domestic shares).
questions.explanation: Under section 10(4D), the exempt incomes of a specified fund include: (i) transfer of capital assets being bonds/GDRs/rupee denominated bonds/derivatives/notified securities on an IFSC exchange settled in convertible foreign exchange (₹50,00,000); (ii) transfer of securities other than shares in a company resident in India (hence, transfer of foreign currency bonds of ₹20,00,000 is eligible, but transfer of equity shares of an Indian resident company of ₹30,00,000 is expressly excluded); and (iii) income from a securitisation trust chargeable under PGBP (₹10,00,000). Thus, eligible income pool = ₹50,00,000 + ₹20,00,000 + ₹10,00,000 = ₹80,00,000. Under section 10(4D), the exemption applies to the extent such income is attributable to units held by non-residents (not having a PE in India). Here, non-residents hold 90% of the units. Therefore, the exempt income is 90% of ₹80,00,000 = ₹72,00,000. The units held by the sponsor/manager (10%) are excluded from exemption.

questions.question: Under section 10(4D) of the Income-tax Act, 1961, all units of a Category III AIF located in an IFSC must generally be held by non-residents (other than units held by a sponsor or manager). However, the Act provides a specific relaxation where a non-resident unit holder subsequently becomes an Indian resident. Which of the following statements accurately describes this relaxation and the procedural compliance required to sustain the exemption under Section 10(4D)?
options: The fund retains its specified fund status if a unit holder who was a non-resident when units were issued becomes resident under section 6(1) or 6(1A) in a subsequent year, provided the aggregate value and number of units held by such resident unit holder(s) do not exceed 5% of the total units issued, and the fund furnishes an annual statement of exempt income on or before the due date u/s 139(1).

The fund retains its specified fund status provided that such resident unit holder disposes of all units within 180 days of becoming resident in India, and the fund files an audit report along with an undertaking to that effect before the end of the previous year under section 139(4A), failing which entire fund earnings become taxable.
Up to 15% of the units can be held by individuals who become resident in India, provided they do not participate in fund distribution meetings and hold non-voting preference shares.
The relaxation applies only if the unit holder becomes resident under section 6(6) as an RNOR, and no statement is required to be filed if tax has been withheld at source under section 196D.
questions.explanation: As per the third proviso to clause (i) of Explanation to Section 10(4D), the condition that all units must be held by non-residents (other than units held by sponsor or manager) does not apply where any unit holder, who was a non-resident during the previous year when such units were issued, becomes resident under section 6(1) or section 6(1A) in any subsequent previous year, provided the aggregate value and number of units held by such resident unit holder(s) do not exceed 5% of the total units issued and prescribed conditions are fulfilled. Furthermore, under section 10(4D) and Notification No. 64/2022, the income attributable to units held by non-residents shall NOT be exempt unless the specified fund furnishes an annual statement of exempt income on or before the due date specified under section 139(1). Thus, Option 0 is correct.

questions.question: An investment division of an Offshore Banking Unit (OBU) located in an International Financial Services Centre (IFSC) can qualify as a 'Specified Fund' eligible for exemption under section 10(4D). Which of the following statutory requirements must be satisfied by such an investment division to be recognized as an eligible specified fund?
options: It must be registered as a Category-II AIF under SEBI regulations, maintain at least 75% of its portfolio in sovereign green bonds, and commence banking operations on or before 31st March 2026.
It must be incorporated as a subsidiary of a foreign central bank, hold all investments in debt instruments, and invest 100% of its funds in Indian infrastructure projects.

It must be granted a certificate of registration as a Category-I Foreign Portfolio Investor (FPI) under the SEBI (FPI) Regulations, 2019, commence its operations on or before 31st March 2030, and maintain separate accounts for its investment division.
It must hold a banking license under the Banking Regulation Act, 1949 and restrict its operations solely to currency derivatives traded on the IFSC exchange.
questions.explanation: Explanation clause (c)(ii) to Section 10(4D) defines a specified fund to include an investment division of an offshore banking unit which has been: (I) granted a certificate of registration as a Category-I foreign portfolio investor under the SEBI (Foreign Portfolio Investors) Regulations, 2019 made under the SEBI Act, 1992 and which has commenced its operations on or before 31st March 2030; and (II) fulfils such conditions including maintenance of separate accounts for its investment division, as may be prescribed. Furthermore, under Notification No. 64/2022, it must furnish the annual statement of exempt income and report of audit on or before the due date u/s 139(1). Option 2 accurately captures these statutory conditions.

questions.question:
Apex Global Holdings Inc., a company incorporated in the Cayman Islands and a non-resident in India, entered into several Non-Deliverable Forward Contracts (NDFCs) and Over-The-Counter (OTC) derivative transactions with an IFSC Banking Unit (IBU) of an Indian bank located in GIFT City. During P.Y. 2025-26, Apex Global earned net gains of ₹1.25 crores from the settlement of these NDFCs in US Dollars.
The Assessing Officer seeks to tax this income in India contending that the transactions were settled through an Indian bank's unit. Apex Global points out that although it has a liaison office in Mumbai (which constitutes a PE for certain unrelated marketing activities in India), the derivative contracts were negotiated, executed, and settled directly from its Cayman headquarters without any connection to its Indian PE.
Considering Section 10(4E) read with Rule 21AK, determine the taxability of this income for A.Y. 2026-27:
options: The income of ₹1.25 crores is fully taxable in India at 40% plus surcharge and cess as business profits attributed to the Indian permanent establishment under section 44DA, because any non-resident having any PE in India is strictly barred from claiming exemption under Section 10(4E).

The income of ₹1.25 crores is completely exempt under Section 10(4E) read with Rule 21AK, since the contracts were entered into with a registered IFSC Banking Unit and were not entered into through or on behalf of its permanent establishment in India.
50% of the income (₹62.5 lakhs) is exempt, while the balance 50% is deemed to be business profits attributable to the Indian PE and taxed under Section 44DA.
The income is exempt under Section 10(4E) only if Apex Global agrees to settle all derivative transactions in Indian Rupees rather than US Dollars.
questions.explanation: Under section 10(4E), any income accrued or arisen to, or received by a non-resident as a result of the transfer of non-deliverable forward contracts, offshore derivative instruments (ODIs), or over-the-counter (OTC) derivatives entered into with an offshore banking unit of an IFSC (or an FPI being a unit of an IFSC) is exempt. Rule 21AK specifies the conditions for this exemption: (i) the contract must be entered into with an OBU holding a valid registration under IFSCA (Banking) Regulations, 2020; and (ii) such contract or derivative is NOT entered into by the non-resident through or on behalf of its permanent establishment in India. Merely having an unrelated PE does not disqualify the non-resident; as long as the derivative was not entered into through or on behalf of that PE, the exemption is available. Thus, the income of ₹1.25 crores is fully exempt.

questions.question:
Skyline Aviation Leasing Ltd., a tax resident of Ireland and non-resident in India, entered into an aircraft dry lease agreement on 1st June 2025 with 'Vimaan IFSC Pvt. Ltd.', an entity located in GIFT City IFSC eligible for deduction under section 80LA(1A). Vimaan IFSC commenced its commercial operations on 15th January 2025.
During P.Y. 2025-26, Skyline Aviation Leasing Ltd. received the following amounts from Vimaan IFSC:
1. ₹8,00,00,000 as lease rentals for leasing two commercial passenger aircraft.
2. ₹1,50,00,000 as lease rentals for leasing three spare aircraft engines.
3. ₹50,00,000 as interest on delayed lease rental payments.
Examine the taxability of these sums in the hands of Skyline Aviation Leasing Ltd. under the Income-tax Act, 1961 for A.Y. 2026-27:
options: Only the aircraft lease rental of ₹8,00,00,000 is exempt; spare engine rentals and interest on delay are taxable as royalty and interest u/s 115A at 20% plus surcharge and cess.
All amounts are taxable in India as Royalty and Interest under section 9(1)(vi) and 9(1)(v) since the lessee is an Indian company carrying on operations in India.
Lease rentals of aircraft (₹8,00,00,000) and engines (₹1,50,00,000) are exempt under section 10(4F); however, interest of ₹50,00,000 is taxable at 20% under section 115A.
The entire amount of ₹10,00,00,000 (aircraft lease rental, engine lease rental, and interest) is exempt from income-tax in India under section 10(4F).
questions.explanation: As per section 10(4F), any income of a non-resident by way of royalty or interest, on account of lease of an aircraft or a ship in a previous year, paid by a unit of an IFSC referred to in section 80LA(1A), is exempt from tax, provided the IFSC unit has commenced its operations on or before 31st March 2030. Vimaan IFSC commenced operations in January 2025 (well before 31.3.2030). The Explanation to section 10(4F) defines 'Aircraft' as an aircraft or a helicopter, or an engine of an aircraft or a helicopter, or any part thereof. Thus, lease rental of spare aircraft engines is squarely covered as lease of an aircraft. Furthermore, section 10(4F) expressly covers income by way of royalty OR interest on account of lease of an aircraft. Therefore, all three amounts (₹8 crores + ₹1.5 crores + ₹0.5 crore = ₹10 crores) are fully exempt.

questions.question: Under section 10(4G) of the Income-tax Act, 1961, certain income received by a non-resident in an account maintained with an Offshore Banking Unit (OBU) in an IFSC is exempt from tax. Which of the following statements correctly states the scope and statutory conditions governing this exemption?
options: Any income received by a non-resident from a portfolio of securities, financial products, or funds managed or administered by a portfolio manager on behalf of such non-resident in an account maintained with an OBU in an IFSC is exempt, to the extent such income accrues or arises outside India and is not deemed to accrue or arise in India.

Any dividend or interest income received by a non-resident from securities of Indian companies or units of mutual funds held in an account maintained with an Offshore Banking Unit in an IFSC is completely exempt up to an aggregate monetary cap of ₹50,00,000 in each financial year, provided the portfolio manager holds a license from IFSCA.
Any interest income received by a non-resident from lending to Indian public sector entities through an account maintained with an OBU in an IFSC is completely exempt without any conditions.
All capital gains arising to a non-resident from trading in Indian securities through an IFSC portfolio manager are exempt, regardless of whether they accrue or arise in India.
questions.explanation: Under section 10(4G), any income received by a non-resident from: (i) portfolio of securities or financial products or funds, managed or administered by any portfolio manager on behalf of such non-resident; or (ii) such activity carried out by such person as may be notified by the Central Government, in an account maintained with an Offshore Banking Unit in any IFSC (referred to in section 80LA(1A)) is exempt from tax, to the extent such income accrues or arises outside India and is not deemed to accrue or arise in India. This provision ensures that foreign income passing through an IFSC OBU account for portfolio management is not brought into the Indian tax net merely by virtue of receipt in India.

questions.question:
'AeroLease IFSC Pvt. Ltd.' is a domestic company and a registered unit in GIFT City IFSC, engaged primarily in the business of leasing of aircraft. The company commenced its commercial operations on 1st November 2024 (P.Y. 2024-25, relevant to A.Y. 2025-26).
'Global Aviation Partners', a corporate non-resident entity based in Luxembourg, held 1,00,000 equity shares in AeroLease IFSC Pvt. Ltd. In July 2027 (P.Y. 2027-28 / A.Y. 2028-29), Global Aviation Partners transferred 40,000 equity shares, realizing capital gains of ₹4,50,00,000.
Examine the taxability of the capital gains in A.Y. 2028-29 and determine the statutory holiday window available under Section 10(4H):
options: The capital gains are taxable in A.Y. 2028-29 because section 10(4H) provides exemption only on the transfer of units of an AIF, and not on equity shares of a domestic company.
The capital gains are exempt, but only for a maximum period of 5 assessment years from incorporation, expiring in A.Y. 2029-30.
The capital gains of ₹4,50,00,000 are exempt under section 10(4H) for A.Y. 2028-29, and the exemption is available for a period of ten assessment years starting from A.Y. 2025-26 to A.Y. 2034-35.

The capital gains are exempt for a statutory period of ten assessment years beginning strictly from A.Y. 2024-25 and ending on A.Y. 2033-34, irrespective of the actual financial year in which the domestic company commenced its commercial operations in the IFSC.
questions.explanation: As per section 10(4H), any income of a non-resident or a Unit of IFSC engaged primarily in the business of leasing of an aircraft or a ship, by way of capital gains on transfer of equity shares of a domestic company, being a Unit of an IFSC, engaged primarily in the business of lease of an aircraft or a ship which has commenced operations on or before 31.3.2030, is exempt from tax. The exemption is available for a period of ten assessment years: (i) from the A.Y. relevant to the P.Y. in which the domestic company has commenced its operations; or (ii) from A.Y. 2024-25, where the period of 10 A.Ys. under (i) ends before 1.4.2034. Since AeroLease commenced operations in P.Y. 2024-25 (A.Y. 2025-26), the 10 assessment year period runs from A.Y. 2025-26 to A.Y. 2034-35. The transfer in P.Y. 2027-28 (A.Y. 2028-29) falls squarely within this window, and the entire gain of ₹4,50,00,000 is exempt.

questions.question:
During P.Y. 2025-26, the following three individuals served as officials or staff in the Embassy of the United States in New Delhi, each receiving an annual remuneration of ₹18,00,000 from the US Government:
1. Mr. David Clark, a citizen and national of the United States of America. Indian diplomatic officials stationed in Washington D.C. enjoy reciprocal income-tax exemption under US law. Mr. Clark did not engage in any other business or employment in India.
2. Mr. Suresh Nair, an individual born in Kochi who holds Indian citizenship. He had lived abroad for 12 years and was a non-resident for tax purposes before being recruited in India by the US Embassy.
3. Mr. Liam O'Connor, an Irish citizen who was recruited as embassy staff by the US Embassy. He was not engaged in any other business or employment in India, and the Irish government provides reciprocal tax exemption to Indian diplomats.
Evaluate the taxability of their remuneration under Section 10(6)(ii) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 for A.Y. 2026-27:
options: Remuneration of all three individuals is exempt under Section 10(6)(ii) because the employer paying the salary is a foreign sovereign government embassy.
Remuneration of Mr. David Clark and Mr. Liam O'Connor is exempt under Section 10(6)(ii), whereas the remuneration of Mr. Suresh Nair is fully taxable in India because he is an Indian citizen.

Only Mr. David Clark's remuneration is exempt; Mr. Liam O'Connor's remuneration is taxable because he is an Irish citizen serving in the United States Embassy rather than a diplomatic mission of Ireland, violating statutory mission affiliation.
None of the remuneration is exempt because the services were rendered physically on Indian soil and are deemed to accrue or arise in India under section 9(1)(ii).
questions.explanation: Section 10(6)(ii) provides exemption for remuneration received by an individual who is NOT a citizen of India for services as an official of an embassy, high commission, consulate, etc., of a foreign state, subject to reciprocal exemption enjoyed by Indian officials in that country and provided staff members are subjects of the respective countries (or foreign states) and not engaged in any other business, profession, or employment in India. The overarching condition of Section 10(6) is that the individual must NOT be a citizen of India. Suresh Nair is a citizen of India; hence, Section 10(6) is completely unavailable to him, and his salary is taxable under Section 9(1)(ii). Mr. David Clark (US citizen) and Mr. Liam O'Connor (Irish citizen fulfilling conditions of reciprocity and no other business) are non-citizens and meet all conditions, making their remuneration exempt under Section 10(6)(ii).

questions.question:
Hans Becker, a German national and non-citizen of India, is a regular employee of 'Berlin Engineering GmbH' (a German company). Berlin Engineering GmbH has no permanent establishment, trade, or business in India. Hans Becker was deputed to India during P.Y. 2025-26 to inspect technical plant specifications for an independent Indian client.
Consider the following three independent scenarios regarding his stay and remuneration in India:
Scenario 1: Hans stays in India for 82 days during P.Y. 2025-26. His salary of ₹12,00,000 for this period is paid in Germany by Berlin Engineering GmbH and is not claimed as a deduction by any entity against income chargeable under the Indian Income-tax Act.
Scenario 2: Hans stays in India for 94 days during P.Y. 2025-26. All other facts are identical to Scenario 1.
Scenario 3: Hans stays in India for 75 days during P.Y. 2025-26. However, Berlin Engineering GmbH operates an unrelated project office in Mumbai which is taxable in India as a PE, and the salary of ₹10,00,000 paid to Hans is cross-charged and deducted in computing the taxable profits of that Mumbai PE.
Which of the following correctly determines the availability of exemption under Section 10(6)(vi) for each scenario?
options: Scenario 1: Taxable; Scenario 2: Exempt; Scenario 3: Exempt.
Scenario 1: Exempt; Scenario 2: Exempt (since stay is less than 182 days); Scenario 3: Taxable.
Scenario 1: Taxable; Scenario 2: Taxable; Scenario 3: Taxable.
Scenario 1: Exempt; Scenario 2: Taxable; Scenario 3: Taxable.
questions.explanation: Section 10(6)(vi) exempts remuneration received by a foreign national as an employee of a foreign enterprise for services rendered during his stay in India, subject to three cumulative conditions: (a) the foreign enterprise is not engaged in any trade or business in India; (b) the employee's stay in India does not exceed in aggregate 90 days in the previous year; and (c) the remuneration is not liable to be deducted from the income of the employer chargeable under the Income-tax Act. In Scenario 1, all three conditions are satisfied (82 days <= 90 days, no business in India, no deduction claimed in India), so the salary is EXEMPT. In Scenario 2, stay is 94 days (> 90 days), violating condition (b), so the salary is TAXABLE. In Scenario 3, the foreign enterprise is engaged in business in India through a PE and the remuneration is deducted from the Indian PE's chargeable income, violating conditions (a) and (c), so the salary is TAXABLE. Thus, Scenario 1: Exempt; Scenario 2: Taxable; Scenario 3: Taxable.

questions.question:
Mr. Kartik is an Indian citizen who emigrated to the United States in 2017 and is employed by 'Texas Cloud Systems Inc.' (a US corporation having no branch, trade, or business in India). In P.Y. 2025-26, Kartik was deputed to India for 80 days to attend client meetings and provide technical integration support. His salary for the 80-day period amounted to ₹15,00,000, which was paid directly into his US bank account by Texas Cloud Systems Inc. No deduction was claimed for this remuneration by any employer under the Indian Income-tax Act. Kartik qualifies as a non-resident in India under Section 6 for P.Y. 2025-26.
Kartik contends that since his stay in India was only 80 days (not exceeding 90 days) and Texas Cloud Systems Inc. is not engaged in any trade or business in India, his salary is exempt under Section 10(6)(vi). Is Kartik's contention correct?
options: No, Kartik's contention is incorrect because exemption under Section 10(6)(vi) is available only to an individual who is not a citizen of India; since Kartik is an Indian citizen, the exemption is barred and his salary is deemed to accrue or arise in India under section 9(1)(ii).

Yes, Kartik's contention is fully correct because residential status as a non-resident under Section 6 overrides citizenship, and where physical presence is under 90 days without domestic business presence, Section 10(6)(vi) applies squarely to protect NRI employees.
No, Kartik's contention is incorrect because Section 10(6)(vi) applies exclusively to employees of foreign philanthropic bodies and diplomatic missions.
Yes, Kartik's contention is correct provided he obtains a No Objection Certificate (NOC) from the Reserve Bank of India prior to leaving India.
questions.explanation: The opening words of Section 10(6) unambiguously provide that exemptions under its clauses are available only to 'individuals, who are not citizens of India'. Mr. Kartik is an Indian citizen. Therefore, he is ineligible for exemption under Section 10(6)(vi), regardless of his residential status under Section 6 and despite satisfying the stay threshold (80 days <= 90 days) and the non-business condition of the foreign enterprise. Under section 9(1)(ii), income under the head 'Salaries' is deemed to accrue or arise in India if it is earned in India, i.e., for services rendered in India. Because Kartik rendered services in India during his 80-day stay, the salary of ₹15,00,000 is deemed to accrue or arise in India and is fully taxable.

questions.question:
Captain Pierre Dubois, a French citizen and non-resident in India, is employed as a navigational officer on an ocean cargo vessel flying the flag of Liberia and owned by a Greek shipping company. During P.Y. 2025-26, the vessel docked at the Indian ports of JNPT (Mumbai), Cochin, and Visakhapatnam to load and discharge commercial freight. Captain Pierre's total stay within the territorial waters and ports of India during the previous year aggregated to 78 days. His salary for this period amounting to ₹14,00,000 was credited directly to his bank account in Paris.
Examine the taxability of Captain Pierre's salary in India for A.Y. 2026-27:
options: The salary of ₹14,00,000 is deemed to accrue or arise in India under section 9(1)(ii) and is fully taxable at regular individual slab rates because the navigation services were performed physically within the territorial waters and ports of India.
The salary is taxable on a presumptive basis at the rate of 7.5% under Section 44B of the Income-tax Act.

The salary of ₹14,00,000 is completely exempt from income-tax in India under Section 10(6)(viii) because he is a non-citizen and a non-resident whose total stay in India did not exceed 90 days in the previous year.
The salary is exempt only if the Liberian flag authority and the Greek shipowner submit a reciprocal tax exemption treaty certificate to the Indian maritime board.
questions.explanation: Under section 10(6)(viii) of the Income-tax Act, 1961, any income chargeable under the head 'Salaries' received by or due to an individual who is not a citizen of India and is a non-resident, as remuneration for services rendered in connection with his employment on a foreign ship, is exempt from income-tax, provided his total stay in India does not exceed 90 days during the previous year. In this case, Captain Pierre Dubois is a French national (non-citizen of India), a non-resident, employed on a foreign ship, and his total stay in India was 78 days (which does not exceed 90 days). Therefore, the entire salary of ₹14,00,000 is exempt from tax under Section 10(6)(viii).

questions.question: Under section 10(6)(xi) of the Income-tax Act, 1961, remuneration received by an employee of the Government of a foreign state from that foreign Government during his stay in India is exempt from tax, if such remuneration is received in connection with his training in specified establishments in India. Which of the following is NOT an eligible establishment for the purpose of claiming exemption under Section 10(6)(xi)?
options: Any company owned by the Central Government or any State Government, or partly by the Central Government and partly by one or more State Governments, or its subsidiary.
A privately owned Indian commercial bank listed on the National Stock Exchange.
Any statutory corporation established by or under a Central, State, or Provincial Act.
Any society registered under the Societies Registration Act, 1860, wholly or partly financed by the Central Government or one or more State Governments.
questions.explanation: Section 10(6)(xi) exempts remuneration received by an employee of a foreign Government from that Government during his stay in India in connection with his training in any establishment or office of, or in any undertaking owned by: (a) the Government; (b) any Government company (Central or State); (c) any subsidiary of such Government company; (d) any statutory corporation; or (e) any society registered under the Societies Registration Act, 1860, or any other law, wholly or partly financed by Central or State Governments. A privately owned commercial bank is not a government undertaking, statutory corporation, or government-financed society, and therefore training in such an entity does not qualify for exemption under Section 10(6)(xi).

questions.question:
Consider the statutory provisions of Section 10(15A) and Section 10(6BB) governing lease payments and taxes paid on lease payments for aircraft or aircraft engines acquired on lease by an Indian company engaged in the business of operation of aircraft:
Which of the following statements correctly distinguishes the scope and operational mechanics of Section 10(15A) and Section 10(6BB)?
options: Section 10(15A) exempts lease rentals under agreements entered into between 1-4-1997 and 31-3-1999, whereas Section 10(6BB) exempts lease rentals entered into at any time after 31-3-2007, provided the lease agreement is certified by the Director General of Civil Aviation.
Section 10(6BB) exempts the lease rentals directly in the hands of the foreign lessor, while Section 10(15A) exempts the Indian airline from deducting tax at source under section 195.
Section 10(15A) applies to payments for providing spares and maintenance services, whereas Section 10(6BB) applies strictly to bare hull charter rentals.

Section 10(15A) exempts the lease rental itself paid to a foreign enterprise under an approved agreement NOT entered into between 1-4-1997 and 31-3-1999 or after 31-3-2007; whereas Section 10(6BB) exempts the tax paid by the Indian company on behalf of the foreign enterprise on lease rentals under an approved agreement entered into between 1-4-1997 and 31-3-1999 or after 31-3-2007.
questions.explanation: Under section 10(15A), any payment made by an Indian company engaged in the business of operation of aircraft, to acquire an aircraft or an aircraft engine on lease (other than payment for spares or services) from the Government of a foreign State or a foreign enterprise under an agreement approved by the Central Government, is exempt from tax, provided the agreement was NOT entered into between 1-4-1997 and 31-3-1999, or after 31-3-2007. For agreements entered into between 1-4-1997 and 31-3-1999, or after 31-3-2007, the lease rental itself is NOT exempt; however, under section 10(6BB), if the Indian company pays the income-tax on such lease rentals on behalf of the foreign enterprise under an agreement approved by the Central Government, the tax so paid is exempt in the hands of the foreign enterprise and not grossed up under section 195A. Option 3 precisely states this distinction.

questions.question:
During P.Y. 2025-26, 'DefTech Systems Corp.', a foreign company incorporated in France and non-resident in India, entered into two separate agreements:
1. An agreement with the Central Government of India to provide technical consultancy services outside India for specialized radar projects connected with the national security of India. The Central Government issued a formal notification in the Official Gazette notifying DefTech Systems Corp. for the purpose of this project. DefTech received fees for technical services (FTS) of ₹15 crores under this agreement.
2. An agreement with the National Technical Research Organisation (NTRO) for rendering cyber security technical services in India, under which DefTech received royalty of ₹8 crores.
Examine the taxability of the above receipts in India in the hands of DefTech Systems Corp. for A.Y. 2026-27:
options: Both the FTS of ₹15 crores from the Central Government and the royalty of ₹8 crores from NTRO are exempt from income-tax in India under Section 10(6C) and Section 10(6D) respectively.

Only the FTS of ₹15 crores is exempt under Section 10(6C); the royalty of ₹8 crores from NTRO is taxable at 20% plus surcharge and cess under Section 115A as standard royalty income derived from an Indian entity.
Both receipts are taxable in India under Section 9(1)(vi) and Section 9(1)(vii) as Royalty and FTS at the rate of 20% plus surcharge and cess.
The royalty of ₹8 crores from NTRO is exempt under Section 10(6D), but the FTS of ₹15 crores is taxable because the consultancy services were rendered outside India.
questions.explanation: Both receipts are specifically exempt under the Income-tax Act, 1961. Under section 10(6C), any income arising to a foreign company (notified by the Central Government in this behalf) by way of royalty or fees for technical services received under an agreement entered into with the Central Government for providing services in or outside India in projects connected with security of India is exempt. Since DefTech was notified by the Central Government, the ₹15 crores FTS is exempt. Under section 10(6D), any income arising to a non-corporate non-resident or a foreign company by way of royalty from, or fees for technical services rendered in or outside India to, the National Technical Research Organisation (NTRO) is exempt. Hence, the ₹8 crores royalty from NTRO is also exempt. Both receipts are completely exempt.

questions.question:
Evaluate the taxability of the following three interest receipts earned during P.Y. 2025-26 under the provisions of Section 10(15) of the Income-tax Act, 1961:
1. Mr. Kenji, a Japanese citizen and non-resident in India, earned interest of ₹3,50,000 on foreign currency deposits maintained with Punjab National Bank (a scheduled commercial bank approved by the RBI to accept foreign currency deposits).
2. Mr. Tarun, an Indian citizen who returned to India after 14 years in Canada and qualifies as a 'Resident but Not Ordinarily Resident' (RNOR) for P.Y. 2025-26, earned interest of ₹2,80,000 on his FCNR deposit maintained with Bank of Baroda.
3. 'Zurich Capital LLC', a foreign corporation and non-resident in India, lent US$ 10,000,000 on 15th October 2023 to 'FinTech IFSC Ltd.' (a registered unit located in GIFT City IFSC) and received interest of ₹75,00,000 during P.Y. 2025-26 on such borrowing.
Which of the following statements is correct regarding the taxability of these three interest incomes for A.Y. 2026-27?
options: Only Mr. Kenji's interest is exempt; Mr. Tarun's interest is taxable because he has become an Indian tax resident under section 6, and Zurich Capital's interest is taxable under Section 115A at 20% plus applicable surcharge and cess.
Interest earned by Mr. Kenji and Zurich Capital LLC is exempt, but Mr. Tarun's interest is taxable because Section 10(15)(iv)(fa) does not apply to RNOR individuals.

All three interest incomes (Mr. Kenji: ₹3,50,000, Mr. Tarun: ₹2,80,000, and Zurich Capital LLC: ₹75,00,000) are completely exempt from income-tax in India under Section 10(15)(iv)(fa) and Section 10(15)(ix).
Only Zurich Capital LLC's interest is exempt under Section 10(15)(ix); both Kenji and Tarun are taxable under section 56(2) at applicable slab rates.
questions.explanation: Under section 10(15)(iv)(fa), interest payable by any scheduled bank on deposits in foreign currency where acceptance of such deposits is duly approved by the RBI is exempt in the hands of: (a) a non-resident, or (b) an individual or HUF who is a resident but not ordinarily resident (RNOR). Therefore, Mr. Kenji (non-resident) and Mr. Tarun (RNOR) are both entitled to exemption under Section 10(15)(iv)(fa) on their foreign currency deposit interest. Under section 10(15)(ix), interest payable by a unit located in an IFSC in respect of monies borrowed by it on or after 1st September 2019 is exempt in the hands of a non-resident. Zurich Capital LLC lent money to an IFSC unit in October 2023 (after 1.9.2019), so its interest of ₹75,00,000 is exempt under section 10(15)(ix). Consequently, all three interest incomes are completely exempt.

questions.question:
'Oceanic Cruises Ltd.', a foreign company incorporated in Bermuda, leases two luxury cruise ships to 'Voyager Maritime Services Pvt. Ltd.', a foreign company that operates cruise ships in Indian coastal waters. Both Oceanic Cruises Ltd. and Voyager Maritime Services Pvt. Ltd. are wholly owned subsidiaries of 'Global Seas Holdings Plc' (a UK holding company).
Voyager Maritime Services Pvt. Ltd. opts to pay tax on its cruise shipping profits in India in accordance with the presumptive taxation provisions of Section 44BBC for P.Y. 2025-26 (A.Y. 2026-27).
During P.Y. 2025-26, Oceanic Cruises Ltd. received lease rentals of ₹25 crores from Voyager Maritime Services Pvt. Ltd. for the cruise ships operated in India.
The Assessing Officer contends that Oceanic Cruises Ltd. is liable to tax in India on the ₹25 crores lease rental as royalty under Section 9(1)(vi).
Assess the validity of the Assessing Officer's contention in light of Section 10(15B):
options: The AO's contention is valid because lease rentals for the use of commercial vessels in Indian territorial waters are deemed to accrue in India under Section 9(1)(vi) without any statutory exemption.

The AO's contention is invalid because the lease rentals are exempt under Section 10(15B), since the foreign lessor and the operating lessee are subsidiaries of the same holding company, the lessee is a specified company opting for Section 44BBC, and the income arises on or before A.Y. 2030-31.
The AO's contention is invalid only if Voyager Maritime Services Pvt. Ltd. is an Indian domestic company registered under the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958.
The lease rentals are exempt under Section 10(15B) only to the extent of 50%, while the remaining 50% is subject to 10% withholding tax under Section 195.
questions.explanation: As per section 10(15B) of the Income-tax Act, 1961, any income of a foreign company from lease rentals of cruise ships received from a 'specified company' which operates such ship or ships in India is exempt from tax. A 'specified company' means any company, other than a domestic company, which operates cruise ships in India and opts to pay tax in accordance with the provisions of section 44BBC. The exemption applies where such foreign company and the specified company are subsidiaries of the same holding company, and such income is received or accrues or arises in India for any assessment year on or before 1st April 2030 (i.e., up to A.Y. 2030-31). Here, both companies are foreign companies and subsidiaries of Global Seas Holdings Plc, Voyager opts for Section 44BBC, and the year is A.Y. 2026-27. Thus, all conditions of section 10(15B) are met and the AO's contention is invalid.

questions.question: Section 10(23FBC) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 provides an exemption to unitholders of a Specified Fund located in an IFSC. Which of the following statements correctly represents the scope and nature of income exempted under Section 10(23FBC)?
options: Exemption is granted exclusively in respect of dividend distributions received by resident individual unitholders from the specified fund, subject to a maximum cap of ₹10,00,000 per assessment year.
Exemption is limited to short-term capital gains arising to non-resident unitholders on the redemption of units held for less than 12 months.
Exemption is available only to the sponsor or manager of the specified fund in respect of performance fees received from managing the portfolio.
Any income accruing or arising to or received by a unit holder from a specified fund or on transfer of units in a specified fund is exempt from tax.
questions.explanation: Section 10(23FBC) provides that any income accruing or arising to or received by a unit holder from a specified fund or on transfer of units in a specified fund would be exempt from income-tax. A 'specified fund' has the same meaning as assigned to it in clause (c) of the Explanation to section 10(4D), namely a Category III AIF in an IFSC or an eligible investment division of an offshore banking unit. Thus, both distribution of income by the specified fund to its unitholders and capital gains arising on transfer of units in such specified fund are exempt under section 10(23FBC).

questions.question: Under section 10(23FE) of the Income-tax Act, 1961, specified persons (including a wholly owned subsidiary of the Abu Dhabi Investment Authority, a notified Sovereign Wealth Fund, or a notified Pension Fund) enjoy exemption on specified incomes arising from investments in Indian infrastructure. Which combination of statutory criteria regarding eligible income streams, qualifying investment period, and minimum holding period is correct?
options: Eligible incomes: Dividend, interest, specified sum under section 56(2)(xii), and long-term capital gains (whether or not deemed as STCG u/s 50AA); Investment period: Made between 1st April 2020 and 31st March 2030; Minimum holding period: At least 3 years.

Eligible incomes: Only dividend and interest from infrastructure SPVs; Investment period: Made between 1st April 2019 and 31st March 2025; Minimum holding period: At least 5 continuous years from the end of the financial year in which the debt or equity investment was subscribed.
Eligible incomes: All capital gains, business profits, and management fees; Investment period: Made between 1st April 2021 and 31st March 2035; Minimum holding period: At least 1 year.
Eligible incomes: Dividend, interest, and short-term capital gains under section 111A; Investment period: Made between 1st April 2020 and 31st March 2028; Minimum holding period: At least 2 years.
questions.explanation: Under section 10(23FE): (1) The eligible categories of income are: dividend, interest, any sum referred to in section 56(2)(xii) (specified sum received by a unit holder from a business trust), and long-term capital gains (whether or not such capital gains are deemed as short-term capital gains under section 50AA). (2) The investment in debt, share capital, or units in India must be made on or after 1st April, 2020 but on or before 31st March, 2030. (3) The investment must be held for a minimum period of at least three years. Option 0 correctly states all these statutory parameters.

questions.question:
A notified Sovereign Wealth Fund seeks to make indirect investments in the Indian infrastructure sector to claim exemption under Section 10(23FE). To qualify as an eligible investee, different intermediary investment vehicles must satisfy specific statutory minimum deployment thresholds in eligible infrastructure entities. Match the intermediary vehicle with its required statutory threshold:
(I) Category-I or Category-II Alternative Investment Fund (AIF)
(II) Domestic company set up and registered on or after 01.04.2021
(III) Non-Banking Financial Company registered as an Infrastructure Finance Company (NBFC-IFC) or Infrastructure Debt Fund (IDF-NBFC)
Statutory minimum thresholds:
(P) Minimum 75% investments in eligible infrastructure entities
(Q) Minimum 90% lending to eligible infrastructure entities
(R) Not less than 50% investment in eligible infrastructure entities or in an Infrastructure Investment Trust (InvIT)
Select the correct combination:
questions.explanation: Under Section 10(23FE)(ii): (c) Category-I or Category-II AIF must have not less than 50% investment in eligible infrastructure companies/entities or in an InvIT -> (I) matches (R); (d) Domestic company set up and registered on or after 1.4.2021 must have minimum 75% investments in eligible infrastructure companies/entities -> (II) matches (P); (e) NBFC registered as an Infrastructure Finance Company or Infrastructure Debt Fund must have minimum 90% lending to eligible infrastructure companies/entities -> (III) matches (Q). Therefore, the correct matching is (I)-(R), (II)-(P), (III)-(Q).

questions.question:
'Gulf Sovereign Infrastructure Fund' (GSIF) is a notified Sovereign Wealth Fund satisfying all conditions of Section 10(23FE). On 1st May 2021, GSIF invested ₹200 crores in units of 'Bharath Infra AIF', a SEBI-registered Category-I Alternative Investment Fund.
During P.Y. 2025-26, Bharath Infra AIF deployed its corpus as follows:
- 70% in operating entities developing toll highways and greenfield ports (eligible infrastructure facilities under Section 80-IA(4)(i));
- 30% in commercial retail shopping complexes (non-infrastructure).
GSIF held these units continuously for more than 3 years. During P.Y. 2025-26, GSIF received the following amounts from Bharath Infra AIF:
- Dividend income: ₹14,00,000;
- Long-term capital gains on redemption of a portion of its units: ₹36,00,000.
Calculate the amount of income exempt from tax in the hands of GSIF under Section 10(23FE) for A.Y. 2026-27:
options: ₹50,00,000 (100% of the income is exempt because Bharath Infra AIF satisfies the minimum 50% threshold for Category-I AIFs under section 10(23FE)).
Nil (Exemption is entirely denied because Bharath Infra AIF did not maintain 100% of its corpus in eligible infrastructure facilities).
₹35,00,000 [70% proportionate exemption on the total eligible income of ₹50,00,000 (70% of ₹14,00,000 dividend + 70% of ₹36,00,000 LTCG)].
₹25,00,000 (Exemption is restricted strictly to 50% of total income, representing the baseline statutory threshold).
questions.explanation: Under Section 10(23FE)(ii)(c), a Category-I or Category-II AIF qualifies as an eligible investee if it has not less than 50% investment in eligible infrastructure entities or InvIT. Here, Bharath Infra AIF has 70% investment in eligible infrastructure, which exceeds 50%, so it qualifies. However, as per Section 10(23FE)(v)(a), where a Category-I or Category-II AIF has investment of less than 100% in eligible entities, the income accrued, arisen, or received by the specified person which is exempt shall be calculated PROPORTIONATELY to the investment made in eligible infrastructure entities. Total income received = ₹14,00,000 (dividend) + ₹36,00,000 (LTCG) = ₹50,00,000. Exempt income = 70% of ₹50,00,000 = ₹35,00,000. The remaining ₹15,00,000 (30%) is taxable in India.

questions.question:
'Nordic Pension Board' (NPB) is a notified foreign pension fund established in Sweden. In June 2022, NPB made an equity investment of ₹500 crores in 'National Expressways Ltd.', an Indian infrastructure entity, fulfilling the 3-year holding requirement.
During scrutiny assessment for A.Y. 2026-27, the Assessing Officer discovered that in 2021, NPB's global central treasury entity in Stockholm had issued commercial paper and floating-rate bonds in Europe for general liquidity and balance-sheet treasury management across global operations. The AO proposes to deny exemption under Section 10(23FE) on dividend of ₹35 crores received by NPB during P.Y. 2025-26, citing the statutory bar on direct or indirect borrowings for making investments in India.
NPB proves conclusively with banking records that the borrowings raised by its central treasury were not specifically raised for making investments in India, and the actual source of funding for the Indian equity investment was entirely from accumulated statutory retirement contributions of Swedish pension scheme participants.
In light of CBDT Circular No. 19/2021, is the Assessing Officer's action to deny the exemption tenable in law?
options: Yes, the AO's action is tenable because Section 10(23FE) imposes an absolute, strict bar prohibiting any borrowing by the fund or any associate entity in the chain of holding, without admitting any commercial explanation or tracing of fund sources.
Yes, because pension funds are statutorily required to maintain zero financial liabilities worldwide to qualify for tax exemption in India.
No, but NPB is required to pay a compounding fee equal to 5% of the borrowing before the exemption can be restored.

No, the AO's action is not tenable; as per CBDT Circular No. 19/2021, where borrowings are taken by a group concern not specifically for the purposes of making investment in India, it shall not be presumed that the investment in India has been made out of such borrowings, provided the source of investment is not from such borrowings.
questions.explanation: As per clause (vi) of Section 10(23FE), if a sovereign wealth fund or pension fund has loans or borrowings, directly or indirectly, for the purposes of making investment in India, it is deemed ineligible for exemption. To resolve practical difficulties regarding group debt, CBDT Circular No. 19/2021 dated 26.10.2021 clarified that: (a) if loans and borrowings have been taken by the specified fund or any group concern specifically for making investment in India, the exemption is denied; but (b) if loans and borrowings have been taken by the specified fund or any of its group concerns not specifically for the purposes of making investment in India, it shall NOT be presumed that the investment in India was made out of such borrowings, and the fund remains eligible for exemption under section 10(23FE), provided that the source of the investment in India is not from such borrowings. Since NPB's investment was funded from pension contributions and not from the general borrowings, the AO's action is legally untenable.

questions.question:
'Pacific Ocean Fund', an offshore investment fund based in Mauritius, relocated to GIFT City IFSC by transferring all its assets to 'Pacific Bharat IFSC Fund' (a resultant fund / specified fund) in accordance with Section 47(viiac). In the relocation, shares of 'IndoTech Ltd.' (an Indian resident company) were transferred to the resultant fund.
In P.Y. 2025-26, Pacific Bharat IFSC Fund sold the shares of IndoTech Ltd., realizing long-term capital gains of ₹20,00,000. Non-residents hold 80% of the units of Pacific Bharat IFSC Fund (having no PE in India). Had the relocation not taken place, capital gains on such shares would not have been chargeable to tax in the hands of the original Mauritius fund under the DTAA.
The due date for filing return of income u/s 139(1) for the fund is 31st October 2026.
Which of the following procedural compliance requirements MUST be strictly satisfied for the capital gains attributable to non-resident unitholders (₹16,00,000) to be exempt under Section 10(23FF)?
options: The fund must obtain prior approval from the SEBI Board within 30 days of the transaction, pay an equalisation levy of 2%, and deposit the proceeds in an escrow account with the Reserve Bank of India.

The fund must furnish an annual statement of exempt income in the prescribed form electronically under digital signature on or before 31st October 2026, which must be certified by an accountant before 30th September 2026 (one month prior to the due date u/s 139(1)) and filed by that date.
The non-resident unitholders must individually file returns of income in India and furnish Tax Residency Certificates along with Form 10F.
The fund is automatically exempt without any filing requirement because fund relocations are governed by the statutory doctrine of continuous neutrality.
questions.explanation: Under section 10(23FF), capital gains arising on transfer of shares of an Indian resident company by a resultant fund or specified fund, to the extent attributable to units held by non-residents (not having a PE in India), are exempt where such capital gains were not chargeable to tax had the relocation not taken place. However, the section mandates strict procedural compliance: (1) The income is exempt ONLY when the specified fund furnishes an annual statement of exempt income in the prescribed form electronically under digital signature on or before the due date specified under section 139(1). If not filed, the exempt income is treated as NIL! (2) Further, such annual statement must be certified by an accountant before the specified date [one month prior to the due date u/s 139(1), i.e., 30th September] and the accountant must furnish the certificate in the prescribed form electronically under digital signature by that date. Option 1 accurately states both mandatory requirements.

questions.question:
'National Petroleum Corp. of Emirates' (NPCE), a foreign company wholly owned by a foreign government, entered into an agreement with the Government of India in the national interest (duly approved and notified by the Central Government). Under the agreement, NPCE stored crude oil in underground strategic petroleum reserve caverns located in Mangalore and Padur, India.
During P.Y. 2025-26, NPCE recorded the following receipts in India:
1. ₹120 crores from sale of stored crude oil to Indian Oil Corporation Ltd. (an Indian resident PSU) from the Indian underground storage facility.
2. Upon formal termination of the strategic storage arrangement in February 2026, NPCE sold the leftover stock of crude oil remaining in the storage caverns to Bharat Petroleum Corporation Ltd. for ₹45 crores in accordance with the notified terms.
NPCE was not engaged in any other commercial activity, trade, or business in India.
Determine the taxability of these receipts under the Income-tax Act, 1961 for A.Y. 2026-27:
options: Both the income of ₹120 crores from sale of stored crude oil and ₹45 crores from sale of leftover stock upon termination are completely exempt from tax under Section 10(48A) and Section 10(48B) respectively.

The sale of crude oil (₹120 crores) is exempt under Section 10(48A), but the sale of leftover stock (₹45 crores) is taxable as business income under Section 28 read with Section 9(1)(i) because termination sales are commercial liquidation transactions.
Both receipts are taxable on a presumptive basis at 10% under Section 44BB as income derived from the provision of services and facilities in connection with mineral oils.

Only the sale of leftover stock (₹45 crores) is exempt under Section 10(48B); regular sales from storage are taxable because maintaining storage caverns in India constitutes a permanent establishment.
questions.explanation: Both receipts are specifically exempt under the Income-tax Act, 1961. Under section 10(48A), any income accruing or arising to a foreign company on account of storage of crude oil in a facility in India and sale of crude oil therefrom to any person resident in India is exempt, provided the foreign company and the agreement/arrangement are notified by the Central Government in the national interest, and the foreign company is not engaged in any other activity in India. Under section 10(48B), any income accruing or arising to such foreign company from the sale of leftover stock of crude oil from the facility in India after the expiry of the agreement or arrangement referred to in section 10(48A) or on termination thereof, in accordance with the terms mentioned therein and subject to notified conditions, is also exempt. Since NPCE satisfies all statutory conditions, both receipts (₹120 crores and ₹45 crores) are fully exempt.

questions.question:
Ocean Carriers Inc., a foreign shipping enterprise resident in Greece, operates ocean cargo vessels across the globe (not being cruise ships). During the previous year 2025-26, the company earned/received the following gross revenues in connection with its cargo shipping operations:
(1) ₹150 lakhs paid in India for carriage of goods shipped at Mumbai port to Rotterdam.
(2) ₹80 lakhs payable in London for carriage of goods shipped at Chennai port to Singapore.
(3) ₹60 lakhs received in India on account of carriage of goods shipped at Dubai to Kandla.
