(4) ₹120 lakhs received in London on account of carriage of goods shipped at Antwerp to Visakhapatnam.
(5) Demurrage charges of ₹15 lakhs received in India for delay in unloading goods shipped at Mumbai port.
(6) Handling charges of ₹10 lakhs paid in Greece for cargo shipped at Chennai port.
During the year, the company incurred actual fleet operational expenses (fuel, crew salaries, port handling charges) of ₹210 lakhs attributable to Indian voyages.
What is the amount of income chargeable to tax under the head 'Profits and gains of business or profession' in the hands of Ocean Carriers Inc. under Section 44B for Assessment Year 2026-27?
options: ₹17.625 lakhs
₹23.625 lakhs
₹21.750 lakhs
₹31.125 lakhs
questions.explanation:
Under Section 44B of the Income-tax Act, 1961, the profits and gains of a non-resident engaged in shipping operations (other than cruise ships) are deemed to be 7.5% of the aggregate of: (i) amounts paid or payable (whether in or out of India) on account of carriage of passengers, livestock, mail, or goods shipped at ANY port in India; and (ii) amounts received or deemed to be received in India on account of carriage of passengers, livestock, mail, or goods shipped at ANY port outside India. As established in CIT v. Japan Lines Ltd. (260 ITR 656) and Section 172(8), demurrage charges and handling charges are includible in these specified receipts. 
Here, specified receipts comprise: (1) ₹150 lakhs (shipped at Mumbai); (2) ₹80 lakhs (shipped at Chennai, payable in London); (3) ₹60 lakhs (shipped at Dubai, received in India); (5) ₹15 lakhs (demurrage for goods shipped at Mumbai); and (6) ₹10 lakhs (handling charges for goods shipped at Chennai) = Total ₹315 lakhs. Item (4) of ₹120 lakhs is excluded because goods were shipped outside India and freight was also received outside India (London). Presumptive profit = 7.5% of ₹315 lakhs = ₹23.625 lakhs. Since Section 44B is a non-obstante section overriding Sections 28 to 43A, actual expenses of ₹210 lakhs cannot be deducted.

questions.question: M/s Hellenic Lines Ltd., a non-resident foreign shipping company, opts for computation of its shipping income under the presumptive provisions of Section 44B for Assessment Year 2026-27. Its gross presumptive profit computed at 7.5% of specified receipts comes to ₹45 lakhs. Hellenic Lines Ltd. has an unabsorbed brought forward business loss of ₹30 lakhs pertaining to Assessment Year 2023-24 from its shipping operations in India. The Assessing Officer contends that since Section 44B starts with a non-obstante clause ('Notwithstanding anything to the contrary contained in sections 28 to 43A'), no deduction or set-off whatsoever is permissible, and the entire ₹45 lakhs must be taxed. Examine the validity of the Assessing Officer's contention.
options: The Assessing Officer is incorrect, because the non-obstante clause of Section 44B overrides only Sections 28 to 43A, leaving Chapter VI provisions (including Section 72 for set-off of brought forward business losses) fully operative against such presumptive income.
The Assessing Officer is correct, because presumptive taxation schemes under Chapter IV-D are self-contained codes that prohibit any deduction or set-off of past losses against deemed income.
The Assessing Officer is incorrect, but only 50% of the brought forward business loss can be set off against presumptive business income under general international tax rules.

The Assessing Officer is correct, because Section 44B was amended pari passu with Section 44BB and Section 44BBB to explicitly prohibit the set-off of unabsorbed depreciation and brought forward losses.
questions.explanation: The Assessing Officer's contention is legally untenable. Section 44B(1) contains a non-obstante clause that explicitly overrides only Sections 28 to 43A of the Income-tax Act, 1961 (which govern allowances, deductions, and computing business profits under Chapter IV-D). It does not override the provisions of Chapter VI relating to the aggregation of income and set-off and carry forward of losses. Therefore, brought forward business losses under Section 72(1) can legitimately be set off against the presumptive profits computed under Section 44B (as affirmed in CIT v. Japan Lines Ltd. and ICAI technical guidance). In contrast, specific statutory prohibitions against setting off brought forward losses exist under Sections 44BB, 44BBB, and 44BBD, but Parliament has intentionally not inserted any such restriction in Section 44B. Hence, Hellenic Lines Ltd. can set off ₹30 lakhs of brought forward loss, leaving a taxable business income of ₹15 lakhs.

questions.question:
S.S. Poseidon, a tramp cargo vessel owned by a foreign company incorporated in Panama, made an occasional voyage to Paradip port in India in December 2025. It loaded mineral ore destined for Japan and collected freight of ₹400 lakhs and demurrage of ₹20 lakhs before leaving the port. Regarding the tax assessment and port clearance under Section 172 of the Income-tax Act, 1961, consider the following statements:
I. The master of the ship is primarily liable to prepare and furnish a return of the full amount paid or payable on account of carriage of goods shipped at the Indian port before the departure of the ship.
II. If the Assessing Officer is satisfied that the master cannot furnish the return before departure, an authorized person may furnish the return within 30 days of departure, provided satisfactory arrangements for payment of tax have been made.
III. Port clearance may be granted by the customs authorities purely on the master undertaking to file a return under Section 139(1) by 31st October of the assessment year.
IV. The deemed profits chargeable to tax are 7.5% of the total amount of ₹420 lakhs, and tax is payable thereon at the rates applicable to a foreign company.
Which of the above statements are correct?
options: I and III only
II, III, and IV only
I, II, III, and IV
I, II, and IV only
questions.explanation: Statements I, II, and IV are correct, whereas Statement III is incorrect. Under Section 172(3), the master of an occasional/tramp ship is obligated to prepare and furnish to the Assessing Officer a return of the full amount paid or payable on account of carriage of goods shipped at an Indian port before the departure of the ship. However, under the proviso to Section 172(3), if the AO is satisfied that the master cannot furnish the return before departure and satisfactory arrangements have been made for filing the return and payment of tax by another person, the return may be furnished within 30 days of departure. Under Section 172(2) and Section 172(8), 7.5% of the total amount including demurrage (₹420 lakhs × 7.5% = ₹31.50 lakhs) is deemed to be taxable income, and tax is determined at the rates in force applicable to a foreign company. Statement III is false because under Section 172(6), port clearance shall NOT be granted by the customs authorities until the tax assessable under Section 172 has been duly paid or satisfactory guarantee/arrangement has been made; a mere undertaking to file a return under Section 139(1) is invalid.

questions.question:
A foreign tramp ship chartered by Neptune Marine LLC (a foreign corporation resident in Liberia) touches Kandla port on an occasional voyage in January 2026. The ship loads agricultural commodities for export to Egypt. The charterer receives freight of ₹200 lakhs paid in Singapore, freight of ₹100 lakhs paid in India, and demurrage charges of ₹20 lakhs payable in India. The company also collected freight of ₹80 lakhs in Mumbai for cargo shipped from Colombo to Dubai. Assuming the corporate tax rate for a foreign company is 35%, and Health & Education Cess is 4% (surcharge is Nil since deemed total income does not exceed ₹1 crore),
compute the total tax liability payable under Section 172(4) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 before port clearance is granted.
questions.explanation: Under Section 172(2), the tax base for an occasional shipping visit is restricted strictly to the amount paid or payable (whether in or out of India) on account of carriage of passengers, livestock, mail, or goods SHIPPED AT A PORT IN INDIA. Demurrage charges are includible under Section 172(8). Here, cargo shipped at Kandla comprises: ₹200 lakhs (paid in Singapore) + ₹100 lakhs (paid in India) + ₹20 lakhs (demurrage payable in India) = ₹320 lakhs. The freight of ₹80 lakhs for cargo shipped from Colombo to Dubai, even though received in Mumbai, is excluded from Section 172 because it was NOT shipped at an Indian port (unlike Section 44B, Section 172 does not tax goods shipped outside India). Deemed income under Section 172(2) = 7.5% of ₹320 lakhs = ₹24,00,000. Since total income is ₹24 lakhs (≤ ₹1 crore), surcharge is Nil. Tax @ 35% on ₹24,00,000 = ₹8,40,000. Add Health & Education Cess @ 4% = ₹33,600. Total tax payable = ₹8,73,600. Option 0 wrongly includes the Colombo freight; Option 1 applies 40% tax rate; Option 3 considers only Indian receipts.

questions.question: The master of an occasional foreign cargo ship, 'MV Atlantic Voyager', furnished a return of income under Section 172(3) to the Assessing Officer at Kochi port on 14th February 2025 in respect of freight earned on timber exported from India. The Assessing Officer proceeded to make an assessment under Section 172(4). According to Section 172(4A), what is the statutory time limit within which the Assessing Officer must pass the assessment order under Section 172?
options: Within 30 days from the date of departure of the ship from Kochi port.
Within 12 months from the date of filing the return under Section 172(3).
Within 9 months from the end of the financial year in which the return under Section 172(3) is furnished, i.e., on or before 31st December 2025.
Within 9 months from the end of the assessment year relevant to the previous year in which the ship departed, i.e., on or before 31st December 2026.
questions.explanation: Under Section 172(4A) of the Income-tax Act, 1961, it is incumbent on the Assessing Officer to pass the order of assessment within 9 months from the end of the financial year in which the return of income under Section 172(3) is filed. In this case, the return was furnished on 14th February 2025, which falls in Financial Year 2024-25. The end of the financial year is 31st March 2025. Adding 9 months to 31st March 2025 gives 31st December 2025. Therefore, the assessment order under Section 172(4) must be passed on or before 31st December 2025. Option 0 confuses this with the 30-day return filing window under the proviso to Section 172(3); Options 1 and 3 use incorrect time frames and base dates.

questions.question: A non-resident shipowner was assessed summarily under Section 172(4) on an occasional voyage during P.Y. 2025-26 and paid tax of ₹15 lakhs. Subsequently, within the time limit prescribed under Section 172(7), the shipowner exercised the option to have his total income assessed under the regular provisions of the Income-tax Act, 1961 (i.e. under Section 44B). With respect to this exercise of option and the legal nature of assessment under Section 172, which of the following statements correctly states the legal position as affirmed by the Supreme Court in CIT v. A.S. Glittre and CBDT Circular No. 9/2001?
options: The assessment made under Section 172(4) is a final and conclusive assessment; Section 172(7) merely permits an application for rectification of mistakes apparent from record within four years.

The assessment under Section 172(4) is an 'ad-hoc' assessment which is completely superseded when regular assessment is opted under Section 172(7); the tax paid under Section 172(4) is treated as advance tax, and provisions of interest under Sections 234B, 234C, and 244A become applicable.

Upon exercising the option under Section 172(7), the shipowner must be assessed under Sections 28 to 43A by maintaining detailed regular books of account, and the presumptive basis of Section 44B cannot be availed.
Any excess tax paid under Section 172(4) can only be adjusted against future tax liabilities arising from Indian shipping voyages within 5 years and cannot be refunded in cash.
questions.explanation: As held by the Supreme Court in CIT v. A.S. Glittre (1997) 225 ITR 739, an assessment made under Section 172(4) is an 'ad-hoc' summary assessment intended to secure immediate tax collection before a foreign vessel departs Indian waters. When the non-resident owner or charterer exercises the option under Section 172(7) before the expiry of the assessment year relevant to the previous year of departure, a regular assessment is made under the provisions of the Act (i.e. Section 44B). This regular assessment completely supersedes the ad-hoc assessment. Under Section 172(7), the tax paid under Section 172(4) is treated as advance tax paid for that assessment year, and the difference is paid by or refunded to the assessee. Furthermore, CBDT Circular No. 9/2001 clarifies that in such regular assessments, the assessee is liable to pay interest under Sections 234B and 234C, or entitled to receive interest on refund under Section 244A. Options 0, 2, and 3 mischaracterize the statutory mechanism.

questions.question: Which of the following represents a correct statutory distinction between the presumptive provisions of Section 44B and the special provisions of Section 172 of the Income-tax Act, 1961?
options: Section 44B applies only to foreign companies, whereas Section 172 applies exclusively to non-resident individual shipowners.

Section 44B provides a complete procedural code for assessment, port clearance, and immediate tax recovery, whereas Section 172 merely defines the taxable profit percentage without procedural machinery.
Under Section 44B, the presumptive rate of profit is 10%, whereas under Section 172, the presumptive profit is computed at 7.5%.

Section 44B applies to regular shipping business and taxes freight for carriage shipped outside India if received in India; whereas Section 172 applies to occasional shipping visits and taxes only amounts paid/payable on account of carriage of goods/passengers shipped at an Indian port.
questions.explanation: Option 3 correctly states the statutory distinction. Section 44B is a computational section for non-residents engaged regularly in the shipping business (other than cruise ships); its scope encompasses amounts paid/payable for carriage shipped at Indian ports (wherever received) PLUS amounts received or deemed received in India for carriage shipped at foreign ports. Conversely, Section 172 is a complete code for occasional voyages/tramp ships of non-residents and applies solely to amounts paid/payable for carriage of passengers, livestock, mail, or goods shipped AT a port in India. Section 172 does not tax freight for goods shipped outside India even if received in India. Option 0 is false because both sections apply to non-residents regardless of legal form. Option 1 is inverted because Section 172 contains the complete recovery and port clearance code, whereas Section 44B contains no procedural assessment machinery. Option 2 is false as both sections prescribe 7.5%.

questions.question:
DeepDrill Inc., a non-resident corporate entity incorporated in Norway, entered into two separate agreements with an Indian oil exploration public sector undertaking during P.Y. 2025-26:
Agreement 1: Provision of specialized offshore jack-up drilling rigs and marine crew for offshore exploratory drilling of crude oil in the Krishna-Godavari basin for a consideration of ₹12 crores.
Agreement 2: Conducting 3D seismic data geological analysis, interpreting reservoir geophysical models, and rendering strategic technical advisory opinions on hydrocarbon potential through Norwegian petroleum geologists for a fee of ₹3 crores (qualifying as Fees for Technical Services under Explanation 2 to Section 9(1)(vii)). DeepDrill Inc. has a Permanent Establishment (PE) in India with which Agreement 2 is effectively connected.
How should the revenues under Agreement 1 and Agreement 2 be taxed under the Income-tax Act, 1961?
options: Agreement 1 is taxable on a presumptive basis @ 10% under Section 44BB, whereas Agreement 2 (being Fees for Technical Services effectively connected with a PE) is excluded from Section 44BB and must be taxed on net income basis under Section 44DA.
Both Agreement 1 and Agreement 2 must be combined and taxed on a presumptive basis @ 10% under Section 44BB, as both relate to mineral oil exploration.
Agreement 1 is taxable under Section 44B @ 7.5% as shipping/marine operation, while Agreement 2 is exempt from tax under Section 10(15B).
Both Agreement 1 and Agreement 2 must be taxed on gross basis @ 20% under Section 115A.
questions.explanation: Agreement 1 involves supplying drilling plant/machinery on hire and providing facilities directly used in prospecting for and extraction of mineral oils, which squarely falls under Section 44BB (taxable on a presumptive basis @ 10%). Plant for Section 44BB explicitly includes drilling units and vessels. However, as clarified in Section 44BB(1) and statutory notes, Section 44BB does not apply to any income to which Section 44DA or Section 115A applies. Where the consideration received is in the nature of Fees for Technical Services (FTS), it cannot be assessed under Section 44BB irrespective of its connection to mineral oil exploration. Because DeepDrill Inc. has a PE in India and Agreement 2 is effectively connected with that PE, Agreement 2 is governed by Section 44DA (computed on net basis under Sections 28 to 44C after deducting wholly and exclusively incurred PE expenses). Therefore, Option 0 is correct.

questions.question:
Barents Drilling AG, a non-resident foreign company, is engaged in the business of providing services and facilities in connection with the extraction and production of mineral oils in India. During the previous year 2025-26, Barents Drilling AG received/accrued the following amounts:
(1) ₹800 lakhs paid in India for exploratory drilling services rendered in Bombay High.
(2) ₹300 lakhs paid in Germany for drilling and casing facilities provided at an offshore block in Gujarat.
(3) ₹150 lakhs received in India on account of supply of drilling rigs on hire used in an oilfield in Oman.
(4) ₹250 lakhs received in Germany on account of supply of plant and machinery on hire used in an oilfield in Dubai.
Actual operational costs incurred in India were ₹950 lakhs, and depreciation as per books was ₹120 lakhs.
Assuming Barents Drilling AG opts for the presumptive scheme under Section 44BB, what is the total deemed business income chargeable to tax under Section 44BB for Assessment Year 2026-27?
options: ₹110 lakhs
₹80 lakhs
₹125 lakhs
₹150 lakhs
questions.explanation:
Under Section 44BB of the Income-tax Act, 1961, presumptive profit is 10% of the aggregate of: (i) amounts paid or payable (whether in or out of India) on account of the provision of services and facilities in connection with prospecting for, or extraction or production of mineral oils in India; and (ii) amounts received or deemed to be received in India on account of such services/facilities/hire used outside India. 
In this case, the qualifying receipts are: (1) ₹800 lakhs (services in Bombay High); (2) ₹300 lakhs (facilities in Gujarat, paid in Germany); and (3) ₹150 lakhs (rigs used in Oman, but consideration received in India). Item (4) of ₹250 lakhs is excluded because the plant was used outside India and the consideration was also received outside India (Germany). Aggregate specified receipts = ₹800L + ₹300L + ₹150L = ₹1,250 lakhs. Deemed profits under Section 44BB @ 10% = ₹125 lakhs. Actual operational expenses (₹950L) and depreciation (₹120L) cannot be deducted because Section 44BB overrides Sections 28 to 43A.

questions.question: PetroTech Global LLC, a foreign company engaged in providing oilfield extraction facilities, received ₹500 lakhs during P.Y. 2025-26 from Indian exploration contracts. Its actual net profit after allowable business expenses and depreciation was only ₹20 lakhs (i.e. 4% of gross receipts). PetroTech Global LLC wishes to declare this lower income instead of the presumptive income of ₹50 lakhs (10%) under Section 44BB. Which of the following conditions must be fulfilled by PetroTech Global LLC to declare lower profits, and what is the consequence regarding brought forward losses?
options: It can declare lower profits simply by submitting an affidavit; brought forward losses can be set off without any limitation.

It must keep and maintain books of account under Section 44AA(2), get them audited and furnish an audit report under Section 44AB; the assessment shall be conducted by the Assessing Officer under Section 143(3). However, if an assessee declares profits under the 10% presumptive scheme, no set-off of unabsorbed depreciation and brought forward loss is allowable.
It can declare lower profits without maintaining books of account if it pays tax at 40% instead of 35%.
Non-residents engaged in mineral oil extraction are strictly barred from claiming lower profits under any circumstances, as Section 44BB is a mandatory non-rebuttable code.
questions.explanation: Under the proviso to Section 44BB(1) and Section 44BB(3), an assessee may claim lower profits than the 10% presumptive rate if he keeps and maintains books of account and other documents as required under Section 44AA(2), gets them audited, and furnishes a report of such audit under Section 44AB before the specified date. In all such cases, regular scrutiny assessment is conducted by the Assessing Officer under Section 143(3). Furthermore, the statute provides that where an assessee declares profits and gains @ 10% in accordance with the presumptive provisions of Section 44BB, no set-off of unabsorbed depreciation and brought forward loss is allowed for such previous year. Hence, Option 1 accurately reflects both the compliance requirements for claiming lower profits and the loss set-off restriction under Section 44BB. Options 0, 2, and 3 are legally inaccurate.

questions.question: Under sub-section (1) of Section 44BB of the Income-tax Act, 1961, the presumptive taxation scheme for mineral oil exploration/extraction does NOT apply to income covered under certain specified sections. Which of the following sets of sections represents the complete list of statutory exclusions from Section 44BB?
options: Sections 10(15B), 44B, 44BBA, and 115BB
Sections 40(a)(i), 40A(2), 43B, and 115JB
Sections 42, 44DA, 115A, and 293A
Sections 44AA, 44AB, 44AD, and 44ADA
questions.explanation: Section 44BB(1) contains an express exclusion clause: 'Provided that this sub-section shall not apply to any income to which the provisions of section 42 or section 44DA or section 115A or section 293A apply for the purposes of computing profits or gains or any other income referred to in those sections.' Section 42 deals with special deductions for mineral oil business agreements; Section 44DA deals with royalties and FTS effectively connected with an Indian PE; Section 115A deals with royalties and FTS without an Indian PE; and Section 293A empowers the Central Government to grant tax exemptions/reductions in connection with mineral oil businesses. Therefore, Option 2 is the exact and complete statutory list of exclusions.

questions.question:
SkyGulf Aviation, an airline enterprise operated by a non-resident individual, operates commercial flights connecting Dubai, Mumbai, and Bangkok. For the previous year 2025-26, SkyGulf Aviation reported the following receipts from air transportation of passengers, mail, and cargo:
1. ₹600 lakhs received in Mumbai on account of carriage of passengers and cargo from Mumbai to Dubai.
2. ₹400 lakhs received in Dubai on account of carriage of passengers from Mumbai to Bangkok.
3. ₹500 lakhs received in Mumbai on account of carriage of passengers from Bangkok to Dubai.
4. ₹700 lakhs received in Dubai on account of carriage of passengers from Dubai to Mumbai.
The actual operational expenditure incurred by SkyGulf Aviation for running these flights during the year was ₹1,850 lakhs.
Compute the business income chargeable to tax in India under Section 44BBA for Assessment Year 2026-27.
options: ₹110 lakhs
₹80 lakhs
₹50 lakhs
₹75 lakhs
questions.explanation:
Under Section 44BBA, the income of a non-resident engaged in the operation of aircraft is computed at a flat rate of 5% of the aggregate of: (a) amounts paid or payable, whether in or out of India, on account of carriage of passengers, livestock, mail, or goods FROM ANY PLACE IN INDIA; and (b) amounts received or deemed to be received in India on account of carriage of passengers, livestock, mail, or goods FROM ANY PLACE OUTSIDE INDIA. 
Here, eligible receipts under (a) are: ₹600 lakhs (carriage from Mumbai, received in Mumbai) + ₹400 lakhs (carriage from Mumbai, received in Dubai) = ₹1,000 lakhs. Eligible receipts under (b) are: ₹500 lakhs (carriage from Bangkok, received in Mumbai). Item 4 of ₹700 lakhs is excluded because carriage was from a place outside India (Dubai) and payment was also received outside India (Dubai). Total qualifying receipts = ₹1,000L + ₹500L = ₹1,500 lakhs. Presumptive income @ 5% = ₹75 lakhs. Since Section 44BBA overrides Sections 28 to 43A, actual operational expenses of ₹1,850 lakhs are completely disregarded.

questions.question:
Consider the applicability of Section 44BBA of the Income-tax Act, 1961 to the following two non-resident assessees:
Assessee A: Captain Ahmed, an individual resident of UAE, operating an air-taxi charter service between Abu Dhabi and New Delhi.
Assessee B: AeroTrans Global Ltd., a foreign corporate airline incorporated in the United Kingdom, operating scheduled passenger flights between London and Bengaluru.
The Assessing Officer contends that Section 44BBA applies only to foreign companies (like AeroTrans Global Ltd.) and that non-resident individuals (like Captain Ahmed) cannot avail of the 5% presumptive basis and must maintain books under Section 44AA. Evaluate the Assessing Officer's contention.
options: The Assessing Officer's contention is incorrect, because Section 44BBA applies to any 'assessee, being a non-resident, engaged in the business of operation of aircraft', without making any distinction between corporate and non-corporate non-residents.
The Assessing Officer's contention is entirely correct, as all non-resident presumptive taxation provisions in Chapter IV-D are exclusively reserved for foreign companies.
The Assessing Officer's contention is partially correct; Captain Ahmed can avail of Section 44BBA only if he incorporates a liaison office in India.
The Assessing Officer's contention is incorrect, but Captain Ahmed's presumptive profit rate is 10% under Section 44AD while AeroTrans Global Ltd. is taxed @ 5% under Section 44BBA.
questions.explanation: The Assessing Officer's contention is incorrect. The statutory wording of Section 44BBA(1) begins: 'in the case of an assessee, being a non-resident, engaged in the business of operation of aircraft'. Unlike Section 44BBB (which specifically uses the term 'foreign company'), Section 44BBA applies broadly to any 'assessee, being a non-resident'. As affirmed in Illustration 8 of the ICAI study material, Section 44BBA does not distinguish between corporate and non-corporate taxpayers who operate aircraft, provided their residential status is that of a non-resident. Therefore, both Captain Ahmed (an individual non-resident) and AeroTrans Global Ltd. (a foreign corporate entity) are fully entitled to compute their income under the presumptive scheme of Section 44BBA @ 5% of specified receipts. Option 0 is correct.

questions.question:
Volta Power GmbH, a foreign company incorporated in Germany, entered into a contract with NTPC Ltd. for civil construction, erection of plant and machinery, and testing and commissioning of a 1,000 MW super-thermal power plant approved by the Central Government. During P.Y. 2025-26, Volta Power GmbH received ₹80 crores for civil construction and erection works in India and ₹20 crores in Germany for overseas engineering design directly connected with the turnkey power project.
In this context, examine the applicability and provisions of Section 44BBB:
Statement 1: Section 44BBB applies only to an assessee being a foreign company and not to any other category of non-resident.
Statement 2: A sum equal to 10% of the amount paid or payable (whether in or out of India) on account of civil construction, erection, testing, or commissioning is deemed to be the profits and gains of business.
Statement 3: Volta Power GmbH can claim profits lower than 10% by maintaining books of account under Section 44AA and getting them audited under Section 44AB.
Statement 4: If Volta Power GmbH declares profits @ 10% under Section 44BBB, it is permitted to set off brought forward business losses and unabsorbed depreciation of prior years against this 10% deemed income.
Which of the statements are correct?
options: Statements 1, 2, 3, and 4 are all correct.
Statements 2 and 4 only are correct.
Statements 1, 2, and 3 only are correct.
Statements 1 and 3 only are correct.
questions.explanation: Statements 1, 2, and 3 are correct, while Statement 4 is incorrect. Under Section 44BBB: (1) The eligible assessee must strictly be a 'foreign company' engaged in civil construction or erection, testing, or commissioning of plant/machinery in connection with a turnkey power project approved by the Central Government. (2) The presumptive profit rate is 10% of the amount paid or payable (whether in or out of India) to the foreign company. (3) Under Section 44BBB(2), the assessee may claim lower profits by maintaining books under Section 44AA(2) and furnishing an audit report under Section 44AB, with assessment under Section 143(3). (4) Statement 4 is incorrect because the statute expressly mandates that where an assessee declares profits @ 10% under Section 44BBB, no set-off of unabsorbed depreciation and brought forward loss is allowed for such previous year. Hence, Option 2 is the correct answer.

questions.question:
Compare the statutory provisions of Section 44B (Shipping), Section 44BB (Mineral oils), Section 44BBA (Aircraft), and Section 44BBB (Turnkey power projects) regarding:
(i) The option to claim lower profits by maintaining books of account under Section 44AA and audit under Section 44AB; and
(ii) The set-off of unabsorbed depreciation and brought forward business losses against presumptive profits.
Which of the following summaries correctly states the law?
options: Lower profit option is available under Sections 44B, 44BB, 44BBA, and 44BBB; brought forward losses cannot be set off under any of these four sections.
Lower profit option is available only under Section 44B; set-off of brought forward loss is allowed under Section 44BB and 44BBB, but prohibited under Section 44B.
None of the sections allow a lower profit option, but all four sections permit full set-off of unabsorbed depreciation and brought forward losses.

Lower profit option is available under Section 44BB and Section 44BBB, but NOT under Section 44B and Section 44BBA. Furthermore, set-off of brought forward loss is prohibited when presumptive income is declared under Section 44BB and Section 44BBB, but brought forward business loss CAN be set off under Section 44B.
questions.explanation: Option 3 correctly summarizes the statutory scheme. Under Sections 44B (shipping) and 44BBA (aircraft), there is no statutory mechanism for the assessee to opt out and declare lower profits by maintaining books under Section 44AA and getting an audit under Section 44AB; the presumptive rates of 7.5% and 5% are mandatory and conclusive. Conversely, both Section 44BB(3) and Section 44BBB(2) contain explicit provisos permitting an assessee to claim lower profits by complying with Section 44AA and Section 44AB. In respect of brought forward losses: Sections 44BB and 44BBB contain express statutory bans disallowing the set-off of unabsorbed depreciation and brought forward loss in any year where the 10% presumptive rate is declared. In Section 44B, because the non-obstante clause overrides only Sections 28 to 43A, brought forward business losses under Section 72(1) can be set off against presumptive shipping profits (CIT v. Japan Lines Ltd.). Options 0, 1, and 2 misstate these critical distinctions.

questions.question:
Seven Seas Cruises Ltd., a non-resident foreign corporation, operates luxury ocean passenger cruise vessels. During P.Y. 2025-26, it operated a luxury cruise vessel 'Ocean Empress' on a scheduled leisure voyage with dining and cabin facilities. The vessel has a passenger carrying capacity of 350 passengers and an overall length of 90 meters. The voyage commenced at Goa port, touched Kochi port, and returned to Goa port for shore excursions, primarily carrying international tourists for leisure and recreation, and carrying zero cargo.
During the year, Seven Seas Cruises Ltd. earned gross passenger fares of ₹50 crores from this cruise operation. The company incurred ₹32 crores on ship charter, fuel, catering, and port levies.
Evaluate the taxability of Seven Seas Cruises Ltd. under Section 44BBC read with Rule 6GB for Assessment Year 2026-27.
options: The vessel fails the conditions of Rule 6GB because a cruise ship must carry both cargo and passengers; hence it is taxed under regular provisions at 35% on net profit of ₹18 crores.
Since it is a shipping business, it is governed by Section 44B, and presumptive profits are deemed @ 7.5% of ₹50 crores, i.e., ₹3.75 crores.

The vessel fulfills all conditions of Rule 6GB (passenger capacity > 200, length >= 75m, leisure/recreation, touching at least two Indian ports or same port twice, primarily for passengers); therefore, Section 44BBC applies and its profits are deemed to be 20% of passenger receipts, i.e., ₹10 crores.
Section 44BBC applies, but the presumptive rate is 10% of gross receipts, resulting in taxable profit of ₹5 crores.
questions.explanation: Option 2 is correct. Section 44BBC governs the presumptive taxation of non-residents operating cruise ships. Deemed profits are equal to 20% of amounts paid/payable or received/deemed received on account of carriage of passengers. Under Rule 6GB (inserted vide Notification No. 9/2025), an eligible cruise ship must: (i) have carrying capacity > 200 passengers or length of 75 meters or more, for leisure and recreation with appropriate dining and cabin facilities; (ii) operate on scheduled voyage or shore excursion touching at least two sea ports of India or the same sea port twice; (iii) operate primarily for passengers and NOT for cargo; and (iv) comply with Ministry of Tourism/Shipping guidelines. 'Ocean Empress' satisfies all these conditions (capacity 350, length 90m, Goa-Kochi-Goa, leisure only, no cargo). Hence, Section 44BBC applies @ 20% on ₹50 crores = ₹10 crores. Section 44B is inapplicable because Section 44B specifically excludes cruise ships referred to in Section 44BBC. Actual expenses of ₹32 crores cannot be deducted.

questions.question:
Coral Cruises Inc. (a foreign company) operates cruise ships in Indian waters and opts for presumptive taxation under Section 44BBC for P.Y. 2025-26. Coral Cruises Inc. has leased its cruise ship from Pacific Marine Leasing Ltd. (another foreign company). Both Coral Cruises Inc. and Pacific Marine Leasing Ltd. are 100% subsidiaries of Global Maritime Holdings Corp. (a foreign holding company). Coral Cruises Inc. paid lease rentals of ₹15 crores during P.Y. 2025-26 to Pacific Marine Leasing Ltd.
What is the tax treatment of the lease rentals of ₹15 crores in the hands of the recipient foreign company, Pacific Marine Leasing Ltd., under the Income-tax Act, 1961?
options: The lease rentals are exempt from income-tax in the hands of Pacific Marine Leasing Ltd. under Section 10(15B), provided both companies are subsidiaries of the same holding company; this exemption is available up to Assessment Year 2030-31.
The lease rentals are fully taxable in India in the hands of Pacific Marine Leasing Ltd. under Section 115A @ 20% as royalty.
The lease rentals are taxable @ 7.5% on presumptive basis under Section 44B in the hands of Pacific Marine Leasing Ltd.
The lease rentals are exempt under Section 10(15B) only if Pacific Marine Leasing Ltd. is an Indian company.
questions.explanation: Option 0 is correct. To foster cruise shipping in India, Section 10(15B) was amended to provide that lease rentals paid by a foreign company which opts for the presumptive regime under Section 44BBC are exempt in the hands of the recipient foreign company, provided both the lessee foreign company and the recipient foreign lessor company are subsidiaries of the same holding company. This statutory exemption is available up to Assessment Year 2030-31. Here, Coral Cruises Inc. and Pacific Marine Leasing Ltd. are both foreign corporations and 100% subsidiaries of the same foreign parent (Global Maritime Holdings Corp.). Consequently, the lease rentals of ₹15 crores received by Pacific Marine Leasing Ltd. are completely exempt under Section 10(15B). Options 1, 2, and 3 misstate the statutory exemption.

questions.question:
Under Section 44BBD of the Income-tax Act, 1961, presumptive taxation is available to non-residents providing services or technology for setting up electronics manufacturing facilities in India. Which of the following statements correctly captures the statutory framework of Section 44BBD?
I. The eligible assessee must be a non-resident providing services or technology in India to a resident company establishing or operating an electronics manufacturing facility under a scheme notified by MeitY.
II. The deemed profits and gains are computed at 25% of the amounts paid/payable or received/deemed to be received.
III. The provisions of Section 44DA and Section 115A do not apply in respect of income covered by Section 44BBD.
IV. The assessee declaring profits @ 25% under Section 44BBD is entitled to set off unabsorbed depreciation and brought forward business losses against such presumptive profits.
Which of the statements are correct?
options: I, II, and III only
II, III, and IV only
I, II, III, and IV
I and IV only
questions.explanation: Statements I, II, and III are correct, while Statement IV is incorrect. Under Section 44BBD: (1) The scheme applies to a non-resident providing services or technology in India for setting up an electronics manufacturing facility or manufacturing electronic goods to a resident company under a scheme notified by MeitY. (2) The presumptive profit rate is 25% of the aggregate amounts paid/payable or received/deemed to be received. (3) Under Section 44BBD(3), the provisions of Section 44DA (FTS with PE) and Section 115A (tax on royalty/FTS) do not apply to income covered under this section. (4) Statement IV is incorrect because Section 44BBD(4) explicitly provides that where an assessee declares profits and gains @ 25% under this section, no set-off of unabsorbed depreciation and brought forward loss would be allowed to the assessee for such previous year. Hence, Option 0 is correct.

questions.question:
Tokyo Trading Corp., a foreign company, has a branch office in Mumbai. For the previous year ended 31.03.2026, the Profit and Loss Account of the Mumbai branch shows a net loss of ₹150 lakhs. This net loss was arrived at after debiting ₹300 lakhs of executive and general administrative expenses incurred by the Head Office in Tokyo and allocated to the Mumbai branch. The actual head office expenditure incurred by the foreign company attributable to the Indian branch business was ₹300 lakhs.
Compute the business income to be declared by the Mumbai branch in its return of income for Assessment Year 2026-27 under the provisions of Section 44C.
options: Net Loss of ₹150 lakhs
Income of ₹142.50 lakhs
Income of ₹150 lakhs
Income of ₹135 lakhs
questions.explanation:
Under Section 44C of the Income-tax Act, 1961, deduction of head office expenditure in the case of a non-resident is restricted to the lower of: (a) 5% of the 'adjusted total income', or (b) actual head office expenditure attributable to the business in India. 
To compute Adjusted Total Income, the head office expenses of ₹300 lakhs debited to the profit and loss account must be added back to the net loss: 
Adjusted Total Income = Net Loss (-₹150 lakhs) + ₹300 lakhs = ₹150 lakhs. 
Allowable deduction under Section 44C is the lower of: (i) 5% of ₹150 lakhs = ₹7.50 lakhs; or (ii) Actual head office expenses attributable = ₹300 lakhs. 
Therefore, allowable head office deduction is ₹7.50 lakhs. 
Income to be declared in the return = Adjusted Total Income (₹150 lakhs) - Allowable Head Office deduction (₹7.50 lakhs) = ₹142.50 lakhs (or net loss of -₹150L + disallowance of ₹292.50L = ₹142.50 lakhs). This matches Illustration 9 in the ICAI material. Option 1 is correct.

questions.question:
For Assessment Year 2026-27, the Indian branch of a foreign banking corporation, Nippon Bank Ltd., has the following figures before giving effect to Section 44C:
- Net business profit (after debiting HO expenses of ₹80 lakhs): ₹400 lakhs
- Unabsorbed depreciation brought forward under Section 32(2): ₹60 lakhs
- Brought forward business loss under Section 72(1): ₹50 lakhs
- Deduction under Chapter VI-A (Section 80JJAA): ₹20 lakhs
- Actual head office expenditure incurred in Tokyo attributable to the Indian branch: ₹80 lakhs
Calculate the 'Adjusted Total Income' for the purpose of Section 44C and the maximum allowable deduction of head office expenses.
options: Adjusted Total Income = ₹350 lakhs; Allowable HO deduction = ₹17.50 lakhs
Adjusted Total Income = ₹420 lakhs; Allowable HO deduction = ₹21.00 lakhs
Adjusted Total Income = ₹400 lakhs; Allowable HO deduction = ₹20.00 lakhs
Adjusted Total Income = ₹480 lakhs; Allowable HO deduction = ₹24.00 lakhs
questions.explanation:
Under the Explanation to Section 44C, 'Adjusted Total Income' means the total income computed in accordance with the provisions of the Act without giving effect to: (i) allowance under Section 44C; (ii) unabsorbed depreciation under Section 32(2); (iii) capital family planning expenditure under Section 36(1)(ix); (iv) brought forward losses under Sections 72(1), 73(2), 74(1), 74A(3); and (v) deductions under Chapter VI-A. 
Here, starting from net profit of ₹400 lakhs, head office expenses of ₹80 lakhs are added back to compute income before Section 44C = ₹480 lakhs. Since unabsorbed depreciation (₹60L), brought forward business loss (₹50L), and Chapter VI-A deductions (₹20L) must NOT be deducted in arriving at Adjusted Total Income, the Adjusted Total Income is ₹480 lakhs. Maximum deduction under Section 44C = lower of: (a) 5% of ₹480 lakhs = ₹24 lakhs; or (b) Actual HO expenses = ₹80 lakhs. Thus, allowable deduction = ₹24 lakhs. Option 3 is correct; Options 0, 1, and 2 incorrectly give effect to b/f loss, unabsorbed depreciation, or Chapter VI-A deductions.

questions.question:
Frankfurt Capital GmbH, a German entity, operates a branch in Mumbai. For P.Y. 2025-26 (A.Y. 2026-27), after adding back head office expenses of ₹120 lakhs, the 'adjusted total income' of the Indian branch is still a net loss of (-) ₹50 lakhs. The adjusted total incomes of the branch for the three immediately preceding assessment years were:
- A.Y. 2025-26: ₹180 lakhs
- A.Y. 2024-25: ₹120 lakhs
- A.Y. 2023-24: ₹240 lakhs
Actual head office expenditure attributable to the Indian branch during P.Y. 2025-26 was ₹120 lakhs.
How much head office expenditure can Frankfurt Capital GmbH claim as a deduction under Section 44C for A.Y. 2026-27?
options: ₹9 lakhs, being 5% of the average adjusted total income of the three immediately preceding assessment years.
Nil, because when adjusted total income of the current year is negative, no head office expenditure deduction is allowable under Section 44C.
₹27 lakhs, being 5% of the aggregate adjusted total income of preceding 3 years.
₹120 lakhs, being the actual expenditure incurred, since ceiling applies only when there is positive income.
questions.explanation:
Section 44C(a) specifically provides that where the adjusted total income of the current year is a loss, the ceiling for head office expenditure deduction is 5% of the 'average adjusted total income'. Under clause (b) of the Explanation to Section 44C, 'average adjusted total income' means one-third of the aggregate amount of the adjusted total income of the three assessment years immediately preceding the relevant assessment year (where total income was assessable for all three preceding years). 
Here, aggregate adjusted total income of preceding three years = ₹180 lakhs + ₹120 lakhs + ₹240 lakhs = ₹540 lakhs. Average adjusted total income = ₹540 lakhs / 3 = ₹180 lakhs. Allowable deduction under Section 44C = lower of: (a) 5% of ₹180 lakhs = ₹9 lakhs; or (b) Actual HO expenses = ₹120 lakhs. Hence, the allowable deduction is ₹9 lakhs. Option 0 is correct; Option 1 ignores the statutory mechanism of average adjusted total income.

questions.question: For the purposes of Section 44C of the Income-tax Act, 1961, which of the following expenses incurred by a foreign company outside India are included within the statutory definition of 'Head Office Expenditure'?
options: Direct freight and import duties paid at Mumbai port for cargo dispatched to Indian customers.

Executive and general administration expenditure incurred outside India, including rent, rates, taxes, repairs or insurance of premises outside India, and salaries, travel expenses of employees managing the affairs of overseas offices.
Advertising and sales promotion expenses incurred in Indian media exclusively promoting the Indian branch's products.
Interest paid to Indian commercial banks for working capital loans utilized by the Indian branch.
questions.explanation: Under Explanation (c) to Section 44C, 'head office expenditure' means executive and general administration expenditure incurred by the assessee outside India, including expenditure incurred in respect of: (a) rent, rates, taxes, repairs or insurance of any premises outside India used for the business or profession; (b) salary, wages, bonus, commission, gratuity, perquisites paid to any employee or person managing the affairs of any office outside India; (c) travelling by any employee or person managing overseas offices; and (d) other prescribed executive/general administrative matters. Direct expenses incurred for the Indian branch (such as Indian import duties, Indian media advertisement, or Indian working capital interest in Options 0, 2, and 3) are governed by normal deduction provisions under Sections 28 to 37 and are not subject to the 5% cap under Section 44C. Hence, Option 1 is correct.

questions.question:
Apex Cybernetics Corp., a company incorporated in the USA, enters into an agreement on 1st June 2025 with an Indian enterprise to provide technical software consulting. Apex Cybernetics Corp. maintains a permanent establishment (PE) in Bengaluru through which its IT consultants operate, and the technical consulting agreement is effectively connected with this Bengaluru PE.
During P.Y. 2025-26, the gross Fees for Technical Services (FTS) received were ₹200 lakhs. The Bengaluru PE incurred administrative and salary expenses of ₹70 lakhs wholly and exclusively for its Indian business. Additionally, the PE remitted ₹30 lakhs to its US Head Office labeled as 'Management Oversight Fees'.
How should the income of Apex Cybernetics Corp. be assessed in India for Assessment Year 2026-27 under the provisions of Section 44DA versus Section 115A?
options: Section 115A applies on gross basis; ₹200 lakhs is taxed @ 20% without any deduction for expenses.
Section 44DA applies; taxable income is ₹100 lakhs after deducting both the ₹70 lakhs operational expenses and ₹30 lakhs management fees paid to Head Office.

Section 44DA applies on net basis; operational expenses of ₹70 lakhs incurred wholly and exclusively for the PE are allowed, but the remittance of ₹30 lakhs to Head Office is disallowed, resulting in taxable income of ₹130 lakhs taxed under PGBP.
Section 44BB applies on presumptive basis; taxable income is 10% of ₹200 lakhs, i.e., ₹20 lakhs.
questions.explanation: Under Section 44DA, where a non-resident or foreign company receives royalty or FTS pursuant to an agreement entered into after 31.03.2003, carries on business through a permanent establishment (PE) in India, and the contract is effectively connected with the PE, the income is taxable under the head 'Profits and gains of business or profession' (PGBP) on a net basis under Sections 28 to 44C. Deductions are allowed for expenses incurred wholly and exclusively for the business of the PE. However, Section 44DA(1) explicitly disallows any deduction for amounts paid (otherwise than reimbursement of actual expenses) by the PE to its head office or other overseas offices, such as royalties, commissions, or management fees. Therefore, the ₹70 lakhs operational expense is allowed, but the ₹30 lakhs management fee remittance to the US Head Office is disallowed. Taxable income under Section 44DA = ₹200L - ₹70L = ₹130 lakhs. Section 115A does not apply because Section 115A is strictly for cases where royalty/FTS is not effectively connected with a PE in India. Option 2 is correct.

questions.question:
Nordic Engineering AS, a foreign corporation, computes its income under Section 44DA for Assessment Year 2026-27 in respect of royalty and FTS effectively connected with its project office (PE) in Mumbai. The company is required to furnish a transfer pricing report under Section 92E in Form 3CEB in respect of international transactions.
Regarding statutory accounting and audit compliance under Section 44DA, consider the following statements:
Statement I: Nordic Engineering AS is mandatorily required to keep and maintain books of account and other documents in accordance with Section 44AA.
Statement II: The audit report for computation of income under Section 44DA must be furnished in the prescribed Form 3CE.
Statement III: Since Nordic Engineering AS is required to furnish a report under Section 92E, the specified date for getting its accounts audited and furnishing the audit report under Section 44DA(2) is 31st October of the assessment year.
Statement IV: In case of non-furnishing of the audit report, the Assessing Officer has power to unilaterally tax the entire gross royalty under Section 115A without allowing any expenses.
Which of the statements are correct?
options: Statement IV only
Statements I, II, and III only
Statements II and IV only
Statements I and IV only
questions.explanation: Statements I, II, and III are correct, while Statement IV is incorrect. Under Section 44DA(2): (1) An assessee computing income under Section 44DA is mandatorily required to keep and maintain books of account and documents under Section 44AA; (2) Get them audited by an accountant and furnish an audit report in Form 3CE; (3) The audit report must be furnished before the date one month prior to the due date for filing return under Section 139(1). Where an assessee is required to furnish a Section 92E transfer pricing report, the return filing due date under Section 139(1) is 30th November of the assessment year; hence, the specified date for furnishing the audit report is 31st October of the assessment year. Statement IV is incorrect because failure to furnish an audit report may attract penalty under Section 271B, but the Assessing Officer has no statutory power to convert PE-connected income into Section 115A, because Section 115A expressly excludes income effectively connected with a permanent establishment in India. Option 1 is correct.

questions.question:
Global Dynamics Conglomerate (a non-resident foreign entity group) undertook the following four independent commercial activities in India during P.Y. 2025-26:
Activity P: Operation of container ocean cargo vessels carrying goods shipped at Nhava Sheva port, earning ₹200 lakhs freight.
Activity Q: Operation of scheduled passenger aircraft landing at New Delhi airport, collecting ₹300 lakhs from passengers departing from New Delhi to Frankfurt.
Activity R: Supply of jack-up drilling units and marine services used in Krishna-Godavari basin for extraction of crude oil, earning ₹500 lakhs gross receipts.
Activity S: Civil construction and erection of machinery for an approved turnkey thermal power project executed by a foreign subsidiary, receiving ₹400 lakhs.
Assuming none of the entities maintained books of account to claim lower profits, what is the correct presumptive profit percentage applicable to Activities P, Q, R, and S respectively under the Income-tax Act, 1961?
questions.explanation:
Option 3 correctly maps each non-resident business activity to its corresponding presumptive provision and percentage: 
- Activity P (Shipping business of non-residents): Governed by Section 44B at 7.5% of specified receipts. 
- Activity Q (Operation of aircraft by non-residents): Governed by Section 44BBA at 5% of specified receipts. 
- Activity R (Mineral oil exploration/extraction facilities and services): Governed by Section 44BB at 10% of specified receipts. 
- Activity S (Turnkey power projects civil construction/erection by foreign company): Governed by Section 44BBB at 10% of specified receipts. 
Options 0, 1, and 2 misstate the presumptive rates across one or more of these sections.

questions.category: Capital Gains & Chapter XII-A for NRIs
questions.question: Under the first proviso to Section 48 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 read with Rule 115A, capital gains arising to a non-resident from the transfer of shares in, or debentures of, an Indian company acquired utilizing foreign currency are computed by converting the amounts into foreign currency and reconverting the net capital gains into Indian currency. What are the specific exchange rates adopted by the State Bank of India (SBI) prescribed for these conversions?
options: Cost of acquisition, transfer expenses, and sale consideration are all converted using the SBI Telegraphic Transfer Buying Rate (TTBR); and resultant capital gains are reconverted into INR using the SBI Telegraphic Transfer Selling Rate (TTSR).

Cost of acquisition is converted using SBI TTBR; transfer expenses and sale consideration are converted using SBI TTSR; and resultant capital gains are reconverted into INR using the average of TTBR and TTSR.

Cost of acquisition, transfer expenses, and sale consideration are converted into foreign currency using the average of SBI TTBR and TTSR on their respective dates; whereas resultant capital gains are reconverted into INR using the SBI TTBR on the date of transfer.

All elements including cost of acquisition, transfer expenditure, sale consideration, and resultant capital gains are converted and reconverted using the SBI TTBR on the respective dates of transaction.
questions.explanation: Under Rule 115A of the Income-tax Rules, 1962, read with the first proviso to Section 48, the conversion of rupees into foreign currency for: (a) cost of acquisition (as on date of acquisition), (b) expenditure incurred wholly and exclusively in connection with transfer (as on date of transfer), and (c) full value of consideration (as on date of transfer), is made using the average of the telegraphic transfer buying rate (TTBR) and telegraphic transfer selling rate (TTSR) adopted by the State Bank of India. However, for reconverting the net capital gains computed in foreign currency into Indian rupees, the telegraphic transfer buying rate (TTBR) of such currency as on the date of transfer must be used. Option 2 correctly specifies this statutory rule, whereas other options incorrectly interchange TTBR, TTSR, or the average rate.

questions.category: Capital Gains & Chapter XII-A for NRIs
questions.question:
Mr. David, a non-resident, remitted foreign currency to India and purchased 10,000 equity shares of an unlisted Indian company on 03.10.2015 for ₹60 per share (total cost ₹6,00,000). On 20.02.2026, he sold all 10,000 shares outside a recognized stock exchange for ₹170 per share (total consideration ₹17,00,000) and incurred transfer expenses of ₹34,000.

The SBI exchange rates (₹ per US$) were as follows:
- On 03.10.2015: TTBR = ₹58; TTSR = ₹62
- On 20.02.2026: TTBR = ₹83; TTSR = ₹87

Ignoring Chapter XII-A, what is the Long-Term Capital Gain chargeable to tax in the hands of Mr. David for AY 2026-27 under the first proviso to Section 48?
questions.explanation:
As per the first proviso to Section 48 read with Rule 115A:
1. Cost of acquisition in US$ = ₹6,00,000 / Average rate on 03.10.2015 [(₹58 + ₹62) / 2 = ₹60] = US$ 10,000.
2. Sale consideration in US$ = ₹17,00,000 / Average rate on 20.02.2026 [(₹83 + ₹87) / 2 = ₹85] = US$ 20,000.
3. Transfer expenses in US$ = ₹34,000 / Average rate on 20.02.2026 (₹85) = US$ 400.
4. Net Long-Term Capital Gain in US$ = US$ 20,000 - US$ 400 - US$ 10,000 = US$ 9,600.
5. Reconversion into INR = US$ 9,600 × SBI TTBR on date of transfer (₹83) = ₹7,96,800.
Hence, Option 0 (₹7,96,800) is correct. Option 1 incorrectly reconverts at the average rate of ₹85 (US$ 9,600 × ₹85 = ₹8,16,000). Option 2 computes normal capital gains in INR without foreign currency conversion (₹17,00,000 - ₹34,000 - ₹6,00,000 = ₹10,66,000).

questions.category: Capital Gains & Chapter XII-A for NRIs
questions.question: Ms. Jennifer, a non-resident individual, remitted foreign exchange into India and purchased 2,000 listed equity shares of Zenith Ltd. through a recognized stock exchange in July 2017, paying Securities Transaction Tax (STT). She sold these shares on 10.02.2026 through the BSE, again paying STT. In computing her capital gains, she insists on applying the foreign currency fluctuation conversion mechanism provided in the first proviso to Section 48. Is her contention tenable?
options: Yes, because the first proviso to Section 48 is mandatory for all non-residents investing foreign currency in any Indian company's shares.

No, because the benefit of foreign currency fluctuation under the first proviso to Section 48 is specifically not available in respect of capital gains arising from the transfer of long-term capital assets referred to in Section 112A.
Yes, provided she foregoes the benefit of grandfathering of cost of acquisition as on 31.01.2018 under Section 55(2)(ac).
No, because the first proviso to Section 48 applies exclusively to debentures of Indian companies and not to equity shares.
questions.explanation: As per the specific statutory exclusion under Section 48, the benefit of currency fluctuation under the first proviso to Section 48 is NOT available in respect of capital gains arising from the transfer of long-term capital assets referred to in Section 112A, viz. (i) equity shares in a company on which STT is paid both at the time of acquisition and transfer, and (ii) units of an equity-oriented fund or business trust on which STT is paid at the time of transfer. Consequently, Ms. Jennifer must compute her LTCG under Section 112A directly in Indian rupees (availing grandfathering u/s 55(2)(ac) if applicable), with long-term capital gains exceeding ₹1,25,000 taxed at 12.5%. Hence, her contention is untenable and Option 1 is the correct answer.

questions.category: Capital Gains & Chapter XII-A for NRIs
questions.question:
Consider the following capital assets acquired by a non-resident utilizing convertible foreign exchange:
I. Equity shares of an unlisted Indian public company
II. Debentures of an Indian private limited company
III. Capital index bonds issued by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI)
IV. Sovereign Gold Bonds issued by the Government of India
V. Preference shares of a Government company incorporated under the Companies Act in India

Which of the above capital assets are eligible for the foreign currency conversion mechanism provided in the first proviso to Section 48 upon transfer?
options: I, II, III, IV, and V
I, III, and V only
I, II, and III only
I, II, and V only
questions.explanation: The first proviso to Section 48 applies strictly to capital gains arising to a non-resident from the transfer of 'shares in, or debentures of, an Indian company' acquired utilizing foreign currency. An Indian company includes a private company, public company, or Government company incorporated in India. Therefore, equity shares of an unlisted public company (I), debentures of a private company (II), and preference shares of a Government company (V) are all eligible. However, bonds or securities issued by the RBI (III) or Government of India (IV) are not shares or debentures of an Indian company, and thus are statutorily outside the purview of the first proviso to Section 48. Hence, Option 3 (I, II, and V only) is correct.

questions.category: Capital Gains & Chapter XII-A for NRIs
questions.question: Foxconn Global Pte Ltd., a non-resident corporate entity, sold unlisted equity shares of an Indian closely held private company during PY 2025-26, which were held for 36 months. How will the resulting long-term capital gains be taxed under Section 112(1)(c)(iii) of the Income-tax Act, 1961?
options: At 20% with the benefit of cost indexation under the second proviso to Section 48.
At 12.5% without giving effect to the first proviso (forex conversion) and second proviso (indexation) to Section 48.
At 10% after applying the foreign currency fluctuation computation under the first proviso to Section 48.
At 12.5% with the benefit of the second proviso (indexation) but without foreign currency fluctuation.
questions.explanation: Under Section 112(1)(c)(iii) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 (as amended), in the case of a non-resident (not being a company) or a foreign company, long-term capital gains arising from the transfer of a capital asset, being unlisted securities or shares of a company not being a company in which the public are substantially interested, are chargeable to tax at the rate of 12.5% without giving effect to the first proviso (foreign currency fluctuation) and the second proviso (cost indexation) to Section 48. Therefore, Option 1 is the accurate statement of law.

questions.category: Capital Gains & Chapter XII-A for NRIs
questions.question:
Mr. William, a non-resident, subscribed to Rupee Denominated Bonds (RDBs / Masala Bonds) issued outside India by an Indian company for ₹50,00,000 on 01.07.2020, by remitting US$ 66,667 (exchange rate: US$ 1 = ₹75). On 01.07.2025, upon maturity, the Indian company redeemed the bonds at par for ₹50,00,000. Owing to the appreciation of the Indian Rupee against the US Dollar at redemption (US$ 1 = ₹62.50), Mr. William converted the ₹50,00,000 proceeds into US$ 80,000, thereby realizing a foreign currency gain of US$ 13,333.

How is this gain treated under the fifth proviso to Section 48 of the Income-tax Act, 1961?
options: The entire gain arising on account of rupee appreciation is ignored and not included in the full value of consideration, resulting in no taxable capital gains in India.
The gain of US$ 13,333 is chargeable as Long-Term Capital Gains at a concessional rate of 12.5% in India.
The gain is treated as income from other sources and taxed at normal applicable slab rates.
The gain is taxable only if the non-resident fails to reinvest the proceeds into specified Indian assets within 6 months.
questions.explanation: As a measure to facilitate Indian companies raising funds abroad and to protect foreign investors who bear currency risk on Rupee Denominated Bonds (RDBs), the fifth proviso to Section 48 provides that any gains arising on account of appreciation of the rupee between the date of purchase and the date of redemption of RDBs of an Indian company held by a non-resident against foreign currency shall not be included in the computation of the full value of consideration. Since redemption is at par in INR (₹50,00,000 proceeds against ₹50,00,000 cost) and the currency appreciation gain is statutorily excluded, no taxable capital gains arise in India. Thus, Option 0 is correct.

questions.category: Capital Gains & Chapter XII-A for NRIs
questions.question:
Matrix Capital Inc., a US-based investment firm (non-resident), holds Rupee Denominated Bonds issued outside India by an Indian public company. Matrix Capital Inc. transfers these bonds outside India to Apex Global Ltd., a UK-based investment firm (non-resident), for a consideration payable in US Dollars.

What are the Indian capital gains tax implications of this transaction?
options: It is taxable in India as capital gains under Section 9(1)(i) because the underlying asset is an obligation of an Indian company.
It is exempt from capital gains tax only if the approval of the Reserve Bank of India has been obtained prior to the transfer.
It is not regarded as a transfer under Section 47(viiaa), and hence no capital gains tax arises in India.
It is taxable in India at a flat rate of 12.5% without indexation under Section 112(1)(c).
questions.explanation: Under Section 47(viiaa) of the Income-tax Act, 1961, any transfer of a capital asset, being a rupee denominated bond of an Indian company issued outside India, made outside India by a non-resident to another non-resident, is not regarded as a 'transfer' for the purposes of Section 45. Since Matrix Capital Inc. (transferor) and Apex Global Ltd. (transferee) are both non-residents and the transaction was executed outside India, no capital gains arise in India. Option 2 is correct, and Option 0 is incorrect because Section 47 provides an express exemption overriding Section 9(1)(i) and Section 45.

questions.category: Capital Gains & Chapter XII-A for NRIs
questions.question: Under Section 47(viiab) of the Income-tax Act, 1961, any transfer of specified securities by a non-resident on a recognized stock exchange located in an International Financial Services Centre (IFSC) is not regarded as a transfer, subject to certain conditions. In which of the following scenarios will the exemption under Section 47(viiab) NOT be available?
options: Transfer of foreign currency denominated equity shares of an Indian company on an IFSC exchange where consideration is payable in US Dollars.
Transfer of Rupee Denominated Bonds of an Indian company on an IFSC exchange where consideration is payable in Euros.
Transfer of derivative contracts on an IFSC exchange where consideration is payable in Singapore Dollars.
Transfer of GDRs of an Indian company on an IFSC exchange where consideration is paid or payable in Indian Rupees.
questions.explanation: Section 47(viiab) provides that any transfer of specified securities (which include bonds, GDRs, RDBs, derivatives, or foreign currency denominated shares) by a non-resident on a recognized stock exchange located in an International Financial Services Centre (IFSC) is not regarded as a transfer, provided the consideration for such transaction is paid or payable in foreign currency. If the consideration is paid or payable in Indian Rupees, the mandatory statutory condition is violated, and the exemption under Section 47(viiab) is unavailable. Thus, Option 3 is correct.

questions.category: Capital Gains & Chapter XII-A for NRIs
questions.question:
Examine the correctness of the following statements regarding capital gains exemptions available to non-residents under Section 47:
Statement 1: Transfer of Capital Indexed Bonds issued by the Government outside India by a non-resident to another non-resident is not regarded as a transfer under Section 47(viia).
Statement 2: Transfer of Global Depository Receipts (GDRs) referred to in Section 115AC(1) made outside India by a non-resident to another non-resident is not regarded as a transfer under Section 47(viib).
Statement 3: Transfer of GDRs referred to in Section 115AC(1) made outside India by a non-resident to an Indian resident company is not regarded as a transfer under Section 47(viib).

Which of the above statements is/are correct?
options: Statement 1 only
Statements 1 and 2 only
Statements 2 and 3 only
Statements 1, 2, and 3
questions.explanation: Statement 1 is correct because Section 47(viia) provides that any transfer of a capital asset being a Capital Indexed Bond issued by the Government, made outside India by a non-resident to another non-resident, is not regarded as a transfer. Statement 2 is correct because Section 47(viib) provides that any transfer of a capital asset being Global Depository Receipts referred to in Section 115AC(1), made outside India by a non-resident to another non-resident, is not regarded as a transfer. Statement 3 is incorrect because Section 47(viib) strictly requires both the transferor and the transferee to be non-residents; a transfer made to an Indian resident is not exempt under Section 47(viib). Thus, Option 1 (Statements 1 and 2 only) is correct.

questions.category: Capital Gains & Chapter XII-A for NRIs
questions.question:
Mr. Karl, a non-resident, sells unquoted equity shares of an Indian company acquired in foreign currency for an agreed consideration of ₹5,00,000. The Fair Market Value (FMV) of these shares determined in the prescribed manner under Section 50CA is ₹8,00,000.

How does Section 50CA operate in conjunction with the first proviso to Section 48 for computing Mr. Karl's capital gains?
options: Section 50CA does not apply to non-residents whose capital gains are governed by the first proviso to Section 48.
The agreed consideration of ₹5,00,000 is converted into foreign currency, but the difference of ₹3,00,000 is taxed as deemed dividend.
The deemed full value of consideration of ₹8,00,000 under Section 50CA must be converted into foreign currency using the SBI average of TTBR and TTSR on the date of transfer.
The deemed full value of consideration of ₹8,00,000 under Section 50CA must be reconverted directly at the TTBR without converting cost into foreign currency.
questions.explanation: Under Section 50CA, where the consideration received or accruing as a result of the transfer of a capital asset, being unquoted shares of a company, is less than the fair market value (FMV) determined in the prescribed manner, such FMV is deemed to be the full value of consideration. For a non-resident whose computation is governed by the first proviso to Section 48, this statutory deemed full value of consideration (₹8,00,000) replaces the actual consideration and is converted into foreign currency using the average of SBI TTBR and TTSR on the date of transfer as per Rule 115A. Therefore, Section 50CA operates fully, making Option 2 correct.

questions.category: Capital Gains & Chapter XII-A for NRIs
questions.question:
Chapter XII-A of the Income-tax Act, 1961 contains special provisions relating to certain incomes of Non-Resident Indians (NRIs). In this context, consider the following individuals/entities:
1. Mr. Alex, a British citizen born in London, whose parents and grandparents were all born in the UK.
2. Mr. Brian, a US citizen born in New York, whose maternal grandmother was born in Lahore in 1938 (undivided India).
3. Orion Holdings LLC, a Delaware incorporated foreign company.
4. Mr. Chetan, an Indian citizen employed in Singapore who qualifies as a non-resident for the previous year.

Which of the above qualify as a 'Non-Resident Indian' within the meaning of Section 115C(e)?
options: Mr. Brian and Mr. Chetan only
Mr. Chetan only
Mr. Alex, Mr. Brian, and Mr. Chetan
Mr. Brian, Mr. Chetan, and Orion Holdings LLC
questions.explanation: Under Section 115C(e), a 'Non-Resident Indian' means an individual, being a citizen of India or a person of Indian origin, who is not a 'resident'. A person is deemed to be of Indian origin if he, or either of his parents or any of his grandparents, was born in undivided India. Non-individuals (such as foreign corporate Orion Holdings LLC) are strictly excluded. Mr. Alex has no ancestry born in undivided India, so he is not an NRI. Mr. Brian is a person of Indian origin (maternal grandmother born in undivided India) and a non-resident individual, so he qualifies. Mr. Chetan is an Indian citizen and non-resident individual, so he qualifies. Thus, only Mr. Brian and Mr. Chetan qualify (Option 0).

questions.category: Capital Gains & Chapter XII-A for NRIs
questions.question:
An NRI acquired various investments in India utilizing convertible foreign exchange. Which of the following qualify as 'Specified Assets' under Section 115C(f) of Chapter XII-A?
I. Shares in an Indian private limited company
II. Debentures issued by an Indian private limited company
III. Debentures issued by an Indian public limited company
IV. Deposits with an Indian public limited company
V. Securities of the Central Government
VI. Deposits with an Indian private limited company
options: I, II, III, IV, and V
I, III, IV, and V only
III, IV, and V only
I, II, IV, and VI only
questions.explanation: Under Section 115C(f), 'specified asset' means any of the following assets: (i) Shares in an Indian company (whether public or private); (ii) Debentures issued by an Indian company which is NOT a private company (i.e., public company only); (iii) Deposits with an Indian company which is NOT a private company (i.e., public company only); (iv) Any security of the Central Government; and (v) Any other notified asset. Notice that while shares of any Indian company (including private companies) qualify, debentures and deposits qualify ONLY if issued by an Indian company which is NOT a private company. Therefore, I, III, IV, and V are specified assets; II and VI are excluded. Hence, Option 1 is correct.

questions.category: Capital Gains & Chapter XII-A for NRIs
questions.question:
Mr. Vikram, a Non-Resident Indian, subscribed to debentures of Bharat Heavy Infra Ltd. (a public Indian company) utilizing convertible foreign exchange. During PY 2025-26, he earned gross interest of ₹5,00,000 on these debentures. To fund this investment, Vikram had borrowed funds abroad and paid interest of ₹1,50,000 to a foreign bank during the year, and incurred ₹5,000 as bank collection charges in India.

How much income will be chargeable to tax under the head 'Income from Other Sources' as investment income under Section 115D(1)?
options: ₹3,45,000, after deducting interest expenditure of ₹1,50,000 and bank charges of ₹5,000 under Section 57.
₹3,50,000, after deducting interest expenditure of ₹1,50,000 under Section 57, but disallowing bank charges.
₹4,95,000, after deducting bank collection charges of ₹5,00,000 only.
₹5,00,000, with no deduction allowed in respect of any expenditure or allowance whatsoever.
questions.explanation: Section 115D(1) explicitly provides that in computing the investment income of a non-resident Indian, no deduction shall be allowed under any provision of the Act in respect of any expenditure or allowance thereabout. Therefore, the general deductions allowable under Section 57 (such as interest on borrowed capital or bank collection charges) are completely barred. Investment income under Chapter XII-A is taxed strictly on a gross basis. Hence, the entire ₹5,00,000 is chargeable to tax, making Option 3 correct.

questions.category: Capital Gains & Chapter XII-A for NRIs
questions.question:
Mr. Rajesh, an NRI governed by Chapter XII-A, has the following income particulars for AY 2026-27:
- Investment income from specified foreign exchange assets: ₹4,00,000
- Long-Term Capital Gains from transfer of foreign exchange assets: ₹3,00,000
- Interest on NRO Savings Bank account: ₹1,00,000

He deposited ₹1,50,000 in a Public Provident Fund (PPF) account eligible for deduction under Section 80C and claimed ₹10,000 deduction under Section 80TTA.

What is the total allowable Chapter VI-A deduction and Rajesh's Total Income for AY 2026-27 under Section 115D(2)?
options: Chapter VI-A deduction of ₹1,60,000; Total Income = ₹6,40,000
Chapter VI-A deduction is NIL; Total Income = ₹8,00,000
Chapter VI-A deduction of ₹1,00,000; Total Income = ₹7,00,000
Chapter VI-A deduction of ₹80,000; Total Income = ₹7,20,000
questions.explanation: Under Section 115D(2), where the gross total income of an NRI includes investment income or long-term capital gains, deductions under Chapter VI-A are not allowed against such investment income or LTCG. Chapter VI-A deductions are allowed ONLY against that portion of gross total income which does not include investment income and LTCG. Here, the other income is ₹1,00,000 (NRO interest). Total eligible Chapter VI-A deductions are ₹1,50,000 (80C) + ₹10,000 (80TTA) = ₹1,60,000. However, this deduction is capped at the available other income of ₹1,00,000. Thus, allowable Chapter VI-A deduction is ₹1,00,000, reducing other income to Nil. Total Income = ₹4,00,000 + ₹3,00,000 + Nil = ₹7,00,000. Hence, Option 2 is correct.

questions.category: Capital Gains & Chapter XII-A for NRIs
questions.question: Under Section 115E of the Income-tax Act, 1961, what are the special rates of income-tax applicable to a Non-Resident Indian on his investment income and long-term capital gains derived from foreign exchange assets?
options: Investment income is taxed at 20%; Long-term capital gains from specified assets are taxed at 12.5%; and other total income is taxed at normal applicable rates.
Investment income is taxed at 10%; Long-term capital gains from specified assets are taxed at 10%; and other total income is taxed at 30%.
Investment income is taxed at 20%; Long-term capital gains from specified assets are taxed at 20%; and other total income is taxed at normal applicable rates.
Investment income is taxed at 15%; Long-term capital gains from specified assets are taxed at 12.5%; and other total income is exempt.
questions.explanation: Section 115E prescribes that the tax payable by a Non-Resident Indian shall be the aggregate of: (a) income-tax on investment income at 20%; (b) income-tax on long-term capital gains arising from the transfer of specified assets (acquired in foreign currency) at 12.5%; and (c) income-tax on his other total income at the normal rates applicable to individuals. Hence, Option 0 correctly states the statutory tax rates.

questions.category: Capital Gains & Chapter XII-A for NRIs
questions.question:
Mr. Anand, a Non-Resident Indian, acquired shares in an Indian company on 01.01.2012 for ₹2,00,000 in convertible foreign exchange. He sold these shares on 01.11.2025 for ₹6,00,000 and paid transfer brokerage of ₹20,000 (net consideration ₹5,80,000). On 20.02.2026 (within 4 months of transfer), he invested ₹5,80,000 in debentures of a public Indian company.

Ignoring the first proviso to Section 48, what is the Long-Term Capital Gain chargeable to tax in the hands of Mr. Anand for AY 2026-27 under Section 115F?
options: NIL
questions.explanation:
Under Section 115F, where a Non-Resident Indian transfers a foreign exchange asset and within 6 months invests the net consideration in any specified asset (which includes debentures of a public Indian company), exemption is available. Here:
- Net consideration = ₹6,00,000 - ₹20,000 = ₹5,80,000.
- Cost of acquisition of original asset = ₹2,00,000.
- Long-term capital gains before exemption = ₹5,80,000 - ₹2,00,000 = ₹3,80,000.
- Cost of new specified asset = ₹5,80,000.
Since the cost of the new asset is equal to (not less than) the net consideration, the ENTIRE capital gain of ₹3,80,000 is exempt under Section 115F(1)(a). The taxable LTCG is NIL. Option 1 is correct.

questions.category: Capital Gains & Chapter XII-A for NRIs
questions.question:
Mr. Kevin, a Non-Resident Indian, purchased unlisted shares of an Indian company on 01.07.2012 for ₹1,50,000 in convertible foreign exchange.
