On 15.09.2025, he sold these shares for a consideration of ₹6,00,000 and incurred expenditure of ₹30,000 wholly and exclusively in connection with the transfer. On 10.01.2026 (within 6 months), he invested ₹3,80,000 in Central Government securities.

Ignoring the first proviso to Section 48, what is the taxable Long-Term Capital Gain for AY 2026-27 after claiming exemption under Section 115F?
questions.explanation:
As per Section 115F of the Income-tax Act, 1961:
1. Full value of consideration = ₹6,00,000
2. Less: Transfer expenses = ₹30,000
3. Net Consideration = ₹5,70,000
4. Less: Cost of acquisition = ₹1,50,000
5. Long-term capital gain = ₹4,20,000
6. Since the cost of the new asset (₹3,80,000) is less than the net consideration (₹5,70,000), proportionate exemption u/s 115F applies:
Exemption = LTCG × (Cost of new asset / Net consideration)
= ₹4,20,000 × (₹3,80,000 / ₹5,70,000) = ₹4,20,000 × (2 / 3) = ₹2,80,000.
7. Taxable LTCG = ₹4,20,000 - ₹2,80,000 = ₹1,40,000.
Hence, Option 0 (₹1,40,000) is correct. Option 1 represents the exempt portion, not the taxable gain.

questions.category: Capital Gains & Chapter XII-A for NRIs
questions.question:
Mr. Suresh, an NRI, earned long-term capital gains on transfer of foreign exchange assets during PY 2023-24 and claimed full exemption of ₹4,00,000 under Section 115F by investing the net consideration in Central Government securities on 01.12.2023 for ₹10,00,000. On 15.11.2025 (within 24 months of acquisition), he sold these Central Government securities for ₹11,20,000.

What are the capital gains tax implications in the hands of Mr. Suresh for AY 2026-27 (PY 2025-26)?
options: Only the capital gain of ₹1,20,000 on the sale of Central Government securities is taxable in AY 2026-27.
The assessment for AY 2024-25 will be reopened under Section 147 to tax the earlier exempted LTCG of ₹4,00,000.
The earlier exempted LTCG of ₹4,00,000 is deemed to be Short-Term Capital Gain in AY 2026-27, while the gain of ₹1,20,000 is long-term.
The earlier exempted LTCG of ₹4,00,000 is deemed to be Long-Term Capital Gain of PY 2025-26 (AY 2026-27), in addition to the capital gain of ₹1,20,000 arising from the transfer of the securities.
questions.explanation: Under Section 115F(2), where the new specified asset is transferred or converted into money within a period of 3 years from the date of its acquisition, the amount of capital gains arising from the transfer of the original asset which was not charged to tax earlier shall be deemed to be income chargeable under the head 'Capital Gains' relating to long-term capital assets of the previous year in which the new asset is transferred or converted into money. It is NOT taxed retrospectively by reopening AY 2024-25. Therefore, in AY 2026-27, the previously exempted LTCG of ₹4,00,000 is deemed as LTCG of PY 2025-26, and the fresh gain of ₹1,20,000 (₹11,20,000 - ₹10,00,000) on the sale of Government securities is also taxable in AY 2026-27. Thus, Option 3 is correct.

questions.category: Capital Gains & Chapter XII-A for NRIs
questions.question:
An NRI sold equity shares of an Indian company acquired in convertible foreign exchange on 15.06.2025, realizing long-term capital gains. To claim exemption under Section 115F, he must reinvest the net consideration within 6 months in 'specified assets' defined under Section 115C(f).

Which of the following reinvestment options will entitle him to exemption under Section 115F?
I. Equity shares of an Indian private limited company
II. Debentures of an Indian private limited company
III. Deposits with a public limited Indian company
IV. Units of an equity-oriented mutual fund
V. Securities of the Central Government
options: I, II, and III only
I, III, IV, and V only
I, III, and V only
III and V only
questions.explanation: Under Section 115F, the net consideration must be invested in any 'specified asset' as defined in Section 115C(f). Specified assets are: (i) shares in an Indian company (public or private); (ii) debentures issued by an Indian company which is not a private company (public company only); (iii) deposits with an Indian company which is not a private company (public company only); (iv) securities of the Central Government; and (v) other notified assets. Debentures of a private company (II) and units of mutual funds (IV) are NOT specified assets under Section 115C(f). Shares of an Indian private company (I), deposits with a public company (III), and Central Government securities (V) qualify. Thus, Option 2 (I, III, and V only) is correct.

questions.category: Capital Gains & Chapter XII-A for NRIs
questions.question:
Mr. Daniel, an NRI, had the following income streams in India during the previous year 2025-26:
- Dividend income from shares of an Indian public company acquired in convertible foreign exchange: ₹1,80,000 (TDS of 20% deducted u/s 196A/195).
- Long-Term Capital Gains from the transfer of specified assets: ₹2,20,000 (TDS of 12.5% deducted u/s 195).
- Interest credited on his NRO savings account: ₹12,000 (TDS of 30% deducted u/s 195).

Mr. Daniel contends that under Section 115G, he is completely exempt from the requirement of furnishing a return of income under Section 139(1) since appropriate TDS was deducted on all his Indian income. Is his contention correct?
options: Yes, because tax at source has been fully deducted on all items of his Indian income.

No, because the exemption from filing return under Section 115G is available only if total income consists SOLELY of investment income, long-term capital gains, or both; having NRO savings interest disqualifies him.
Yes, provided he files a declaration in Form 10F with the Assessing Officer before the due date.
No, because Section 115G was repealed by the Finance Act, 2020 following the abolition of Dividend Distribution Tax.
questions.explanation: Under Section 115G of the Income-tax Act, 1961, a Non-Resident Indian is not required to furnish a return of income under Section 139(1) ONLY IF both the following conditions are satisfied: (a) his total income consists ONLY of investment income or income by way of long-term capital gains, or both; AND (b) tax deductible at source has been deducted from such income. In Mr. Daniel's case, although tax was deducted at source on all items, his total income includes NRO savings bank interest (₹12,000), which is other income and not investment income from foreign exchange assets or LTCG. Because his total income does not consist solely of investment income/LTCG, Section 115G does not apply, and his contention is incorrect. Option 1 is correct.

questions.category: Capital Gains & Chapter XII-A for NRIs
questions.question:
Mr. Arvind, an NRI, held the following foreign exchange assets acquired with convertible foreign exchange:
(i) Equity shares in Indian companies;
(ii) Debentures of an Indian public company; and
(iii) Central Government securities.

On 15.06.2025, Mr. Arvind returned to India for permanent settlement and became a 'resident' for tax purposes for AY 2026-27 and subsequent years. He wishes to continue availing the concessional tax provisions of Chapter XII-A on his investment income from these assets.

Under Section 115H, can he continue to avail Chapter XII-A benefits, and if so, for which of the assets?
options: Yes, by furnishing a written declaration along with his return of income u/s 139, but ONLY in respect of the debentures and Central Government securities; equity shares are statutorily excluded.
Yes, in respect of all three assets (equity shares, debentures, and Government securities) upon furnishing a written declaration with his return of income u/s 139.
No, because Chapter XII-A automatically ceases to apply to an assessee for any year in which he becomes a resident in India.
Yes, but only in respect of equity shares; debentures and Government securities lose the benefit upon becoming a resident.
questions.explanation: Section 115H provides that where a person who is an NRI becomes assessable as a resident in any subsequent year, he may furnish a written declaration along with his return of income under Section 139 that the provisions of Chapter XII-A shall continue to apply to him. Crucially, Section 115H explicitly restricts this continuance to investment income derived from foreign exchange assets being debentures of an Indian public company, deposits with an Indian public company, Central Government securities, and other notified assets—SHARES IN AN INDIAN COMPANY ARE SPECIFICALLY EXCLUDED! Hence, Arvind can continue Chapter XII-A benefits only for the debentures and Central Government securities, not for equity shares. Option 0 is correct.

questions.category: Capital Gains & Chapter XII-A for NRIs
questions.question:
Consider the following Assertion (A) and Reason (R):

Assertion (A): A Non-Resident Indian who derives long-term capital gains from the sale of specified assets is not mandatorily required to be assessed under Chapter XII-A and may choose to be taxed under the general provisions of the Income-tax Act, 1961.
Reason (R): Section 115-I gives an explicit option to a Non-Resident Indian to elect out of Chapter XII-A for any particular assessment year by furnishing a declaration to that effect in his return of income filed under Section 139.

Evaluate the correctness of Assertion (A) and Reason (R) and select the correct option:
options: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A).
(A) is true, but (R) is false.
(A) is false, but (R) is true.
questions.explanation: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and Reason (R) correctly explains Assertion (A). Chapter XII-A is a beneficial, optional regime for Non-Resident Indians. Under Section 115-I, an NRI may elect that the provisions of Chapter XII-A shall not apply to him for any particular assessment year by furnishing his return of income under Section 139 declaring therein that Chapter XII-A shall not apply to him for that year. When such an option is exercised, his total income for that AY is assessed under the general provisions of the Act (e.g. allowing general deductions or basic exemption limit where applicable). Hence, Option 0 is correct.

questions.category: Capital Gains & Chapter XII-A for NRIs
questions.question: Which of the following statements is INCORRECT regarding the capital gains computation provisions for non-residents under the Income-tax Act, 1961?
options: Under the first proviso to Section 48, capital gains are computed in the original foreign currency and reconverted into Indian rupees, and the indexation benefit under the second proviso to Section 48 is not available.
Under Section 115D(2), an NRI computing long-term capital gains from foreign exchange assets is entitled to claim cost inflation indexation under the second proviso to Section 48.
Under Section 115E, long-term capital gains arising to an NRI from the transfer of specified assets are chargeable to income-tax at a concessional rate of 12.5%.

If an NRI opts out of Chapter XII-A under Section 115-I, he can compute capital gains from the transfer of shares in an Indian company acquired in foreign currency under the first proviso to Section 48.
questions.explanation: Statement 1 is INCORRECT (and thus the correct option to select) because Section 115D(2) explicitly provides that the second proviso to Section 48 (which provides for cost inflation indexation) shall NOT apply in computing long-term capital gains of a Non-Resident Indian from a foreign exchange asset. Statements 0, 2, and 3 are correct statements of law: under the first proviso to Section 48 indexation is unavailable; under Section 115E LTCG on specified assets is taxed @ 12.5%; and opting out under Section 115-I brings the assessee under general provisions, where the first proviso to Section 48 applies to shares of Indian companies acquired in foreign currency.

questions.category: Capital Gains & Chapter XII-A for NRIs
questions.question:
Mr. George, an NRI, transferred a foreign exchange asset on 15.04.2024 and realized long-term capital gains. He invested the entire net consideration in debentures of a public Indian company on 10.08.2024 (cost: ₹8,00,000) and claimed full exemption under Section 115F for AY 2025-26.

Examine the following independent subsequent events:
Event 1: On 10.12.2025, George pledged these debentures as collateral with a scheduled commercial bank to secure a business loan.
Event 2: On 20.01.2026, George gifted these debentures to his married daughter who resides in London.
Event 3: On 15.02.2027, the Indian company redeemed the debentures prematurely and repaid the principal in cash.

Which of the above events will trigger the withdrawal of the Section 115F exemption under Section 115F(2)?
options: Event 3 only
Events 1 and 2 only
Events 2 and 3 only
Events 1, 2, and 3
questions.explanation:
Under Section 115F(2), if the new asset is 'transferred or converted into money' within 3 years from the date of its acquisition, the capital gain exempted earlier is deemed to be long-term capital gain of the previous year in which such transfer or conversion occurs.
- Event 1: Pledging an asset as collateral creates a charge/hypothecation but does not constitute a transfer of title or conversion into money; thus Section 115F(2) is not triggered.
- Event 2: A gift constitutes a transfer (even though exempt u/s 47(iii) for general capital gains, Section 115F(2) specifically uses the phrase 'transferred or converted into money'), which triggers the withdrawal of exemption within the 3-year lock-in.
- Event 3: Premature redemption of debentures amounts to conversion into money within 3 years (August 2024 to February 2027 is under 3 years), triggering Section 115F(2).
Thus, Events 2 and 3 trigger the clawback. Option 2 is correct.

questions.category: Capital Gains & Chapter XII-A for NRIs
questions.question:
Mr. Richard, a Non-Resident Indian, has long-term capital gains of ₹4,00,000 arising from the transfer of unlisted shares of an Indian private company acquired in foreign currency during PY 2025-26. He has no other taxable income in India during the year. He evaluates whether to be taxed under Chapter XII-A (Section 115E) or to opt out under Section 115-I and be taxed under the general provisions (Section 112(1)(c)).

Can Mr. Richard claim the benefit of the unexhausted basic exemption limit (under the default new tax regime or old regime) against this LTCG under either of the two options?
options: Yes, under both options, because an NRI with no other income is entitled to adjust unexhausted basic exemption limit against LTCG.
Yes under Section 112(1)(c), but no under Section 115E.
Yes under Section 115E, but no under Section 112(1)(c).
No under either option, because the benefit of adjusting unexhausted basic exemption limit against LTCG is available only to a resident individual or HUF, not to a non-resident.
questions.explanation: Under the proviso to Section 112(1) as well as under Chapter XII-A (Section 115E), the benefit of setting off or adjusting the unexhausted basic exemption limit against long-term capital gains is available ONLY to a resident individual or a resident HUF. A non-resident individual is statutorily barred from adjusting the basic exemption limit against special rate capital gains (under Section 112, 112A, 111A, or 115E). Therefore, under both options, Mr. Richard cannot adjust his unexhausted basic exemption limit, and his entire LTCG of ₹4,00,000 is chargeable to tax at 12.5% plus applicable cess. Hence, Option 3 is correct.

questions.category: Special Tax Rates under Chapter XII & XII-BB
questions.question:
Apex Global Inc., a foreign company incorporated in the USA having no Permanent Establishment in India, earned the following income streams in India during the P.Y. 2025-26:
(i) Dividend received from an Indian company: ₹12,00,000
(ii) Dividend received from a business unit located in an IFSC qualifying under Section 80LA(1A): ₹8,00,000
(iii) Interest received from an Infrastructure Debt Fund referred to in Section 10(47): ₹15,00,000
(iv) Interest received from an Indian concern on foreign currency borrowings (not covered u/s 194LC or 194LD): ₹10,00,000
Apex Global Inc. incurred administrative expenses of ₹2,50,000 in India to earn these incomes. What is the total income-tax liability (exclusive of surcharge and health and education cess) of Apex Global Inc. under Section 115A for A.Y. 2026-27?
questions.explanation: Under Section 115A(1)(a), the gross receipts are taxed at special concessional rates without any deduction under Sections 28 to 44C, Section 57, or Chapter VI-A. General dividend of ₹12,00,000 is taxable @ 20% = ₹2,40,000; dividend from an IFSC unit referred to in Section 80LA(1A) of ₹8,00,000 is taxable @ 10% = ₹80,000; interest from an Infrastructure Debt Fund u/s 10(47) of ₹15,00,000 is taxable @ 5% = ₹75,000; and other foreign currency loan interest of ₹10,00,000 is taxable @ 20% = ₹2,00,000. Administrative expenses of ₹2,50,000 are strictly non-deductible as per Section 115A(2). Total tax payable = ₹2,40,000 + ₹80,000 + ₹75,000 + ₹2,00,000 = ₹5,95,000. Option 0 incorrectly applies a flat 20% to all incomes. Option 2 incorrectly deducts the administrative expenses before tax computation. Option 3 miscalculates the concessional rate for IDF interest as 10%.

questions.category: Special Tax Rates under Chapter XII & XII-BB
questions.question: A foreign institutional investor received interest during the P.Y. 2025-26 on long-term rupee-denominated bonds issued by an Indian company from borrowings raised outside India. What is the applicable special tax rate under Section 115A read with Section 194LC if the bonds are listed only on a recognised stock exchange located in an International Financial Services Centre (IFSC) and were issued on 15th September 2023?
options: 4% on gross interest
5% on gross interest
9% on gross interest
20% on gross interest
questions.explanation: Under Section 115A(1)(a)(iiac) read with Section 194LC(2)(i), long-term bonds or rupee-denominated bonds issued by an Indian company or business trust listed only on a recognised stock exchange located in an IFSC have differentiated tax rates based on the date of issue. Where such bonds were issued between 01.04.2020 and 30.06.2023, the concessional rate is 4%. However, for bonds issued on or after 01.07.2023 listed solely on an IFSC exchange, the special tax rate is 9%. General ECBs/rupee-denominated bonds issued on or before 30.06.2023 not listed on an IFSC exchange are taxed @ 5%. Since these bonds were issued on 15th September 2023 and listed exclusively in an IFSC, the applicable tax rate is 9% on gross interest.

questions.category: Special Tax Rates under Chapter XII & XII-BB
questions.question:
Consider the following statements regarding the computation of total income and tax liability of a non-resident under Section 115A of the Income-tax Act, 1961:
(i) No deduction in respect of any expenditure or allowance is permissible under Sections 28 to 44C and Section 57 in computing dividend, interest, royalty, or FTS.
(ii) No deduction under Chapter VI-A is allowed against dividend and interest income covered under Section 115A, without any exception.
(iii) A unit located in an International Financial Services Centre (IFSC) is permitted to claim deduction under Section 80LA against dividend and interest income referred to in Section 115A.
(iv) If the non-resident assessee has other income in India along with Section 115A income, the Chapter VI-A deductions can be claimed against such other income.
Which of the above statements are correct?
options: (i) and (ii) only
(ii), (iii) and (iv) only
(i), (ii) and (iv) only
(i), (iii) and (iv) only
questions.explanation: Statements (i), (iii), and (iv) are correct. Section 115A(2) explicitly prohibits deductions under Sections 28 to 44C and Section 57. Section 115A(3) denies deductions under Chapter VI-A against dividend and interest, but specifically carves out an exception stating that this restriction does not apply to a deduction allowed to a unit of an IFSC under Section 80LA; hence Statement (ii) is incorrect because it claims there is no exception. Statement (iv) is correct because deductions under Chapter VI-A remain available against other normal incomes included in the gross total income. Therefore, the correct combination is (i), (iii), and (iv) only.

questions.category: Special Tax Rates under Chapter XII & XII-BB
questions.question: Zenith Corp., a non-resident foreign company, earned royalty income of ₹50,00,000 from an Indian company under an agreement approved by the Central Government during the P.Y. 2025-26. It has no other income in India. Under the domestic provisions of Section 115A, royalty is taxable @ 20%. However, under the applicable Double Taxation Avoidance Agreement (DTAA), royalty is taxable @ 10%. The Indian payer deducted tax at source @ 10% in accordance with the DTAA. Is Zenith Corp. exempt from furnishing its return of income under Section 139(1) by virtue of Section 115A(5)?
options: No, because the rate of tax deducted at source (10%) is lower than the statutory rate of 20% specified in Section 115A(1)(b).
Yes, because Zenith Corp. has no other income in India and tax deductible under the governing DTAA has been fully deducted.
Yes, because Section 115A(5) provides an unconditional exemption from return filing for all non-resident companies earning solely royalty or FTS.
No, because foreign companies earning royalty from Indian concerns are never eligible for exemption from filing returns under Section 115A(5).
questions.explanation: Under Section 115A(5), a non-resident is exempt from filing a return of income under Section 139(1) only if two cumulative conditions are met: (a) total income consists solely of specified dividend, interest, royalty, or FTS; and (b) tax deductible at source has been deducted at a rate NOT LESS than the rate specified in Section 115A(1). For royalty, the rate specified in Section 115A(1)(b) is 20%. If tax has been deducted at a lower rate (here, 10%) by availing the beneficial provisions of the DTAA, condition (b) is violated. Hence, Zenith Corp. is not exempt and must file its return of income under Section 139(1).

questions.category: Special Tax Rates under Chapter XII & XII-BB
questions.question: TechnoSoft Ltd., a foreign corporate entity having no place of business or PE in India, received ₹40,00,000 as Fees for Technical Services (FTS) from an Indian concern pursuant to an agreement approved by the Central Government during P.Y. 2025-26. TechnoSoft Ltd. incurred ₹8,00,000 on technical engineers' salaries and software testing in providing such services. The tax treaty between India and the foreign company's home country provides a tax rate of 15% on gross FTS. What is the final Indian tax liability (including 4% health and education cess, assuming no surcharge is applicable) of TechnoSoft Ltd. for A.Y. 2026-27?
questions.explanation: Under Section 90(2), an assessee can opt for the provisions of the Income-tax Act or the DTAA, whichever is more beneficial. Under Section 115A, FTS is taxed @ 20% on gross basis without deduction of expenses (₹40,00,000 × 20% = ₹8,00,000 + 4% cess = ₹8,32,000). Under the DTAA, the rate is 15% on gross FTS, giving tax of ₹6,00,000. Adding health and education cess @ 4% yields ₹6,24,000 (note: cess applies to tax payable unless treaty specifically caps total tax). In both domestic law and treaty provisions, expenditure of ₹8,00,000 is not deductible as there is no PE under Section 44DA. Since ₹6,24,000 is more beneficial than ₹8,32,000, the final tax liability is ₹6,24,000. Option 0 incorrectly taxes net income (₹32L) at 20.8%. Option 1 reflects the higher domestic tax.

questions.category: Special Tax Rates under Chapter XII & XII-BB
questions.question: Nexus REIT, an Indian business trust, distributed ₹10,00,000 during the P.Y. 2025-26 to its non-resident unit holder, Mr. John (a resident of the UK). This distributed income represents interest income received by Nexus REIT from a Special Purpose Vehicle (SPV) in which the REIT holds 100% equity. At what rate is this interest income taxable in the hands of Mr. John under Section 115A, and is Nexus REIT required to deduct tax under Section 194LBA?
options: Taxable @ 20% under Section 115A; Nexus REIT must deduct tax @ 20% under Section 194LBA(1).
Taxable @ 5% under Section 115A; Nexus REIT must deduct tax @ 5% under Section 194LBA(2).
Taxable @ 10% under Section 115A; Nexus REIT must deduct tax @ 10% under Section 194LBA(2).
Exempt under Section 10(23FD) in the hands of the non-resident unit holder; no withholding tax applies.
questions.explanation: Under Section 115A(1)(a)(iiab), distributed income referred to in Section 194LBA(2), being interest income received by a business trust from an SPV and distributed to its non-resident unit holders, is chargeable to tax at a special concessional rate of 5%. Nexus REIT is required to deduct tax at source @ 5% under Section 194LBA(2). While dividend income from an SPV opting out of Section 115BAA is exempt u/s 10(23FD), interest income distributed by an SPV through a business trust is pass-through income taxable in the hands of unit holders and specifically charged @ 5% under Section 115A for non-residents.

questions.category: Special Tax Rates under Chapter XII & XII-BB
questions.question:
Pacific Horizon Fund is an Overseas Financial Organisation (Offshore Fund) established in Singapore and approved by SEBI. During the P.Y. 2025-26, it derived the following incomes in India:
(i) Income from units of a mutual fund specified u/s 10(23D) purchased in foreign currency: ₹25,00,000
(ii) Long-term capital gains on transfer of such mutual fund units (purchased in foreign currency): ₹40,00,000
(iii) Short-term capital gains on transfer of listed equity shares (STT paid): ₹15,00,000
Pacific Horizon Fund incurred management and advisory expenses of ₹3,00,000 attributable to earning the unit income. Which of the following statements correctly states the tax rates and allowable deductions under Section 115AB?
options: Income from units is taxed @ 20%; LTCG is taxed @ 10%; management expenses of ₹3,00,000 are deductible under Section 57.
Income from units is taxed @ 10%; LTCG is taxed @ 10%; indexation benefit is available under the second proviso to Section 48.
Income from units is taxed @ 15%; LTCG is taxed @ 12.5%; STCG is exempt under Section 10(38).
Income from units is taxed @ 10%; LTCG is taxed @ 12.5%; no deduction under Section 57 or Chapter VI-A is allowed against unit income and LTCG, and no indexation benefit is available.
questions.explanation: Under Section 115AB, income received by an Offshore Fund in respect of units purchased in foreign currency is taxable @ 10%, and long-term capital gains arising from the transfer of such units are taxable @ 12.5%. Under Section 115AB(2), no deduction is allowable under Sections 28 to 44C, Section 57(i)/(iii), or Chapter VI-A against such income or LTCG. Furthermore, the first and second provisos to Section 48 (foreign currency conversion and indexation) do not apply to the computation of LTCG under Section 115AB. STCG on equity-oriented shares where STT is paid is taxable @ 20% under Section 111A. Hence, Option 3 is completely accurate.

questions.category: Special Tax Rates under Chapter XII & XII-BB
questions.question: An approved Overseas Financial Organisation (Offshore Fund) transferred units of a domestic mutual fund during the P.Y. 2025-26 after holding them for 38 months. The mutual fund invests only 25% of its total proceeds in equity shares of domestic companies. What is the tax treatment and applicable rate for the capital gains arising on this transfer?
options: The capital gain is deemed to be a short-term capital gain under Section 50AA and is taxable at normal applicable rates, because not more than 35% of the fund's proceeds are invested in equity shares of domestic companies.
The capital gain is a long-term capital gain taxable @ 10% under Section 115AB, because the units were held for more than 36 months.
The capital gain is a long-term capital gain taxable @ 12.5% under Section 115AB with indexation benefit.
The capital gain is a short-term capital gain taxable @ 20% under Section 111A because the holding period is less than 48 months.
questions.explanation: Under Section 50AA, a 'specified mutual fund' is defined as a mutual fund where not more than 35% of its total proceeds is invested in the equity shares of domestic companies. Any capital gain arising from the transfer, redemption, or maturity of units of a specified mutual fund acquired on or after 01.04.2023 is statutorily deemed to be a short-term capital gain, irrespective of the period of holding. Consequently, Section 115AB's concessional LTCG rate of 12.5% does not apply; the gain is treated as STCG and taxed at the normal rates of tax applicable to the assessee. Section 111A does not apply because the fund is not an equity-oriented fund.

questions.category: Special Tax Rates under Chapter XII & XII-BB
questions.question:
Which of the following conditions must be satisfied for an entity to qualify as an 'Overseas Financial Organisation' under the Explanation to Section 115AB of the Income-tax Act, 1961?
1. It must be established under the laws of a country outside India.
2. It must have entered into an arrangement for investment in India with a public sector bank, public financial institution, or an approved mutual fund u/s 10(23D).
3. Such arrangement must be approved by the Reserve Bank of India.
4. Such arrangement must be approved by the Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI).
options: 1, 2, and 3 only
1 and 2 only
1, 2, and 4 only
questions.explanation: According to Explanation (a) to Section 115AB, 'Overseas Financial Organisation' means any fund, institution, association or body, whether incorporated or not, established under the laws of a country outside India, which has entered into an arrangement for investment in India with any public sector bank or public financial institution or a mutual fund specified under Section 10(23D), AND such arrangement must be approved by the Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI), not the RBI. Therefore, condition 3 is incorrect and condition 4 is correct, making 1, 2, and 4 the correct set of requirements.

questions.category: Special Tax Rates under Chapter XII & XII-BB
questions.question: Mr. Richard, a non-resident individual, holds Global Depository Receipts (GDRs) of an Indian listed company purchased in foreign currency through an approved intermediary under a Central Government notified scheme. During P.Y. 2025-26, he received dividend of ₹6,00,000 on these GDRs and realized a long-term capital gain of ₹14,00,000 upon transferring a portion of the GDRs outside India to another non-resident. Which of the following correctly reflects the taxability and applicable provisions under Section 115AC and Section 47(viia)?
options: Dividend is taxable @ 20% under Section 115A; LTCG is taxable @ 12.5% under Section 115AC.

Dividend is taxable @ 10% under Section 115AC; the transfer of GDRs outside India between two non-residents is not regarded as a transfer under Section 47(viia) and hence LTCG is exempt from Indian tax.
Dividend is taxable @ 10% under Section 115AC; LTCG is taxable @ 12.5% with foreign currency conversion under the first proviso to Section 48.
Both dividend and LTCG are fully exempt from tax in India by virtue of Section 10(34) and Section 10(38).
questions.explanation: Under Section 115AC(1)(b), dividend on GDRs purchased in foreign currency is taxable at a concessional rate of 10%. Under Section 47(viia), any transfer of a capital asset, being bonds or Global Depository Receipts referred to in Section 115AC(1), made outside India by a non-resident to another non-resident is not regarded as a transfer for capital gains purposes. Consequently, the long-term capital gain of ₹14,00,000 arising from the transfer between two non-residents outside India is exempt from tax in India. Therefore, Option 1 is correct. (Note: if transfer were taxable in India, Section 115AC(3) explicitly denies foreign currency conversion and indexation).

questions.category: Special Tax Rates under Chapter XII & XII-BB
questions.question:
Dr. Weber, a non-resident individual, has the following income in India for the previous year 2025-26:
- Interest on notified foreign currency bonds of an Indian public sector company covered u/s 115AC: ₹4,00,000
- Long-term capital gains on transfer of bonds covered u/s 115AC to an Indian resident: ₹5,00,000
Tax deductible at source has been properly deducted on the interest income by the payer. Dr. Weber did not file a return of income under Section 139(1), claiming that since his entire income is covered under Section 115AC, he is exempt under Section 115AC(4). Is his contention legally valid?
options: Yes, because Section 115AC(4) exempts any non-resident whose total income comprises solely of incomes specified under Section 115AC(1).
Yes, because long-term capital gains on notified bonds are taxed at a flat concessional rate of 12.5% and do not require return filing.
No, because exemption under Section 115AC(4) is available only to corporate non-residents and foreign companies, not to individuals.

No, because Section 115AC(4) exempts the non-resident from filing a return of income ONLY if the total income consists exclusively of interest or dividend referred to in clauses (a) and (b) of Section 115AC(1), and not capital gains.
questions.explanation: Under Section 115AC(4), a non-resident is relieved from the obligation to furnish a return of income under Section 139(1) only if his total income consists SOLELY of interest or dividend income referred to in Section 115AC(1)(a) and (b), and tax deductible at source has been fully deducted. The relief under Section 115AC(4) does NOT extend to cases where the total income includes capital gains (even though such capital gains are covered by Section 115AC(1)(c)). Because Dr. Weber has long-term capital gains of ₹5,00,000, his contention is invalid and he is legally bound to file a return of income under Section 139(1).

questions.category: Special Tax Rates under Chapter XII & XII-BB
questions.question:
Under Section 115AC(5), where an assessee acquires Global Depository Receipts (GDRs) or foreign currency bonds in an amalgamated company or a resulting company by virtue of holding GDRs or bonds in the amalgamating or demerged company:
What is the specific tax treatment accorded to such newly acquired GDRs or bonds?
options: The concessional tax treatment under Section 115AC(1) continues to apply to the GDRs or bonds held in the amalgamated or resulting company as if they were acquired in accordance with Section 115AC(1).
The concessional tax provisions lapse, and any future dividend or capital gains will be taxed at normal statutory rates applicable to foreign companies.
The exchange of GDRs in amalgamation is treated as a taxable transfer triggering immediate long-term capital gains tax @ 12.5%.
The new GDRs are exempt from all future taxes in India for a moratorium period of 5 years from the date of amalgamation.
questions.explanation: Section 115AC(5) specifically provides that where the assessee acquired GDRs or bonds in an amalgamated or resulting company by virtue of his holding GDRs or bonds in the amalgamating or demerged company in accordance with the provisions of Section 115AC(1), the concessional tax treatment (10% on interest/dividend and 12.5% on LTCG) would continue to apply to such GDRs or bonds. Furthermore, the transfer of GDRs or bonds in amalgamation or demerger is itself not regarded as a transfer under Section 47. Hence, Option 0 is correct.

questions.category: Special Tax Rates under Chapter XII & XII-BB
questions.question:
A Foreign Portfolio Investor (FII/FPI) registered with SEBI earned the following categories of income during the previous year 2025-26:
1. Dividend on listed equity shares: ₹20,00,000
2. Short-term capital gains on transfer of equity shares through a recognised stock exchange (STT paid): ₹35,00,000
3. Short-term capital gains on transfer of unlisted debt securities (no STT): ₹15,00,000
4. Long-term capital gains on transfer of listed equity shares (STT paid on acquisition and sale): ₹18,00,000
Which of the following correctly matches each income category with its statutory tax rate under Section 115AD?
options: 1 @ 20%; 2 @ 20%; 3 @ 15%; 4 @ 12.5% (gross without any basic exemption)
questions.explanation: Under Section 115AD(1): (a) Income received in respect of securities (other than units u/s 115AB) is taxed @ 20%; (b) Short-term capital gains u/s 111A (STT paid) are taxed @ 20% (as amended by Finance (No. 2) Act, 2024); (c) Short-term capital gains other than those u/s 111A are taxed @ 30%; and (d) Long-term capital gains u/s 112A exceeding ₹1.25 lakh are taxed @ 12.5%. Therefore, the rates are 20%, 20%, 30%, and 12.5% exceeding ₹1.25 lakh, matching Option 2.

questions.category: Special Tax Rates under Chapter XII & XII-BB
questions.question:
Alpha Investment Fund, an FII registered with SEBI, acquired listed equity shares of an Indian corporate on 10th June 2021 by remitting US Dollars. It sold these shares on 15th January 2026 through the Bombay Stock Exchange and realized capital gains. In computing the capital gains of Alpha Investment Fund:
Statement I: The benefit of computation of capital gains in foreign currency under the first proviso to Section 48 is not available.
Statement II: The benefit of indexation under the second proviso to Section 48 is not available.
Statement III: Alpha Investment Fund can claim deductions under Chapter VI-A against such capital gains.
Which of the above statements are correct?
options: Statements I, II and III are all correct
Statements I and II only are correct
Statements II and III only are correct
Statement I only is correct
questions.explanation: Under Section 115AD(3), the first and second provisos to Section 48 do not apply to the computation of capital gains arising from the transfer of securities by an FII/Specified Fund. This means neither foreign currency conversion protection (1st proviso) nor cost inflation indexation (2nd proviso) is permissible. Furthermore, under Section 115AD(2), no deduction under Chapter VI-A is allowable against short-term or long-term capital gains arising from the transfer of securities. Therefore, Statement I and Statement II are correct, while Statement III is incorrect.

questions.category: Special Tax Rates under Chapter XII & XII-BB
questions.question:
A Category III Alternative Investment Fund located in an International Financial Services Centre (IFSC) satisfies all criteria of a 'Specified Fund' under Section 115AD. During P.Y. 2025-26, it earned ₹2 crore as income from securities (other than 115AB units). Consider the following aspects of its taxation:
(i) The tax rate on such securities income is 10% under Section 115AD(1)(i).
(ii) Surcharge and health & education cess are not applicable to the specified fund on such securities income.
(iii) Alternate Minimum Tax (AMT) under Section 115JEE is applicable to the specified fund.
(iv) The specified fund must furnish an annual statement of income eligible for concessional taxation electronically on or before the due date specified under Section 139(1) to be eligible for these concessional rates.
Which of the above statements are correct?
options: (i), (ii) and (iii) only
(i) and (iv) only
(ii), (iii) and (iv) only
(i), (ii) and (iv) only
questions.explanation: Statements (i), (ii), and (iv) are correct. Under Section 115AD(1)(i), securities income (other than units u/s 115AB) in the hands of a Specified Fund is taxed @ 10% (as against 20% for FIIs). Surcharge and health and education cess are not applicable to a specified fund in respect of income received from securities referred to in Section 115AD(1)(a). As per Notification No. 64/2022, furnishing an annual statement of eligible income electronically under digital signature on or before the due date u/s 139(1) is a mandatory pre-condition to avail concessional tax rates. Statement (iii) is incorrect because the provisions of AMT under Section 115JEE specifically do not apply to a specified fund. Hence, (i), (ii), and (iv) only are correct.

questions.category: Special Tax Rates under Chapter XII & XII-BB
questions.question:
Mr. David, a non-resident individual who has opted out of the default tax regime (paying tax under normal provisions), has the following income components for P.Y. 2025-26:
- Dividend from Indian companies: ₹1,10,00,000
- Short-term capital gains on securities u/s 115AD(1)(b): ₹1,20,00,000
- Other Indian business income: ₹3,20,00,000
Total Income = ₹5,50,00,000.
What are the applicable surcharge rates on the income-tax computed on each of these components for A.Y. 2026-27?
options: Surcharge @ 15% on income-tax payable on dividend and capital gains u/s 115AD; surcharge @ 25% on income-tax computed on other business income.
Surcharge @ 15% on income-tax payable on dividend and capital gains u/s 115AD; surcharge @ 37% on income-tax computed on other business income.
Surcharge @ 37% on total income-tax across all components, because total income exceeds ₹5 crore.
Surcharge @ 15% across all components, because dividend and capital gains exceed ₹2 crore.
questions.explanation: Under the surcharge rules for individuals/AOPs having income under Section 115AD: Surcharge on the income-tax payable on dividend and capital gains under Section 115AD(1)(b) is capped at a maximum of 15%. For the other income, the total income excluding dividend and capital gains is ₹3,20,00,000. Since this other income exceeds ₹2 crore but does not exceed ₹5 crore, the surcharge rate on the income-tax computed on other income is 25% (it would be 37% only if other income alone exceeded ₹5 crore). Therefore, surcharge is 15% on tax on dividend and capital gains, and 25% on tax on other business income. Option 0 is correct.

questions.category: Special Tax Rates under Chapter XII & XII-BB
questions.question: An Association of Persons (AOP) consisting solely of corporate members is registered as an FII in India. During P.Y. 2025-26, its total income derived from transactions in Indian securities was ₹4,80,00,000. What is the applicable rate of surcharge on the income-tax payable by this AOP?
options: 25%, since the total income of the AOP exceeds ₹2 crore but does not exceed ₹5 crore.
37%, as per normal slabs for non-corporate entities under the regular tax regime.
15%, because the maximum surcharge on an AOP consisting solely of companies as its members is capped at 15% where total income exceeds ₹1 crore.
Nil, because foreign corporate AOPs are totally exempt from surcharge.
questions.explanation: As per the statutory provisions governing surcharge on an Association of Persons (AOP) where all the members are companies: the rate of surcharge is 10% where the total income exceeds ₹50 lakhs but does not exceed ₹1 crore, and 15% where the total income exceeds ₹1 crore. The higher surcharge rates of 25% and 37% do not apply to an AOP consisting entirely of corporate members. Since the total income here is ₹4.80 crore (which exceeds ₹1 crore), the applicable surcharge is capped at 15%.

questions.category: Special Tax Rates under Chapter XII & XII-BB
questions.question: Carlos, a world-class tennis player and a citizen of Spain, is a non-resident in India for tax purposes. During P.Y. 2025-26, he participated in a tennis championship in Mumbai and received ₹25,00,000 as prize money. He earned ₹3,00,000 for contributing analytical articles on the championship to an Indian sports magazine and ₹12,00,000 from an Indian athletic apparel company for appearing in a television commercial. Carlos incurred ₹6,00,000 on airfare and coaching in India. Assuming proper tax was deducted at source on all receipts, what is Carlos's final tax liability in India, and is he required to file an income-tax return under Section 139(1)?
options: Tax liability is ₹7,07,200 (20.8% of net income ₹34,00,000); return filing under Section 139(1) is mandatory.
Tax liability is ₹8,32,000 (20.8% of gross receipts ₹40,00,000); return filing under Section 139(1) is not required.
Tax liability is ₹8,00,000 (20% of gross receipts ₹40,00,000); return filing under Section 139(1) is mandatory because gross receipts exceed ₹10,00,000.
Tax liability is ₹8,32,000; return filing is required because advertisement income is treated as business income under Section 28.
questions.explanation: Under Section 115BBA(1)(a), income earned by a non-resident sportsman who is not a citizen of India by way of (i) participation in any game in India (₹25L), (ii) contribution of articles in newspapers/magazines (₹3L), and (iii) advertisement (₹12L) is taxable @ 20% plus 4% health & education cess = 20.8% on gross receipts. Under Section 115BBA(2), no deduction in respect of any expenditure or allowance is permissible (expenses of ₹6,00,000 are disallowed). Total tax = ₹40,00,000 × 20.8% = ₹8,32,000. Under Section 115BBA(3), since his total income consists only of Section 115BBA income and tax deductible at source has been fully deducted, he is NOT required to file a return of income under Section 139(1).

questions.category: Special Tax Rates under Chapter XII & XII-BB
questions.question: Rohan, an accomplished professional cricketer, holds Indian citizenship but has been residing in the UK for the past 6 years and is a non-resident for tax purposes in India for P.Y. 2025-26. During the year, he played in an exhibition cricket tournament in India and earned ₹18,00,000 as match fees, and incurred ₹4,00,000 towards coaching and sports kit. He contends that his income is taxable @ 20% on gross basis under Section 115BBA and he is exempt from filing an income-tax return. Is Rohan's contention correct?
options: Yes, because Section 115BBA applies uniformly to all non-resident sportsmen participating in games in India.
Yes, provided the Board of Control for Cricket in India (BCCI) certifies that he is a non-resident professional player.
No, because cricket is treated as a recreational game and is taxable @ 30% under Section 115BB.

No, because Section 115BBA specifically applies only to a sportsman who is NOT a citizen of India; since Rohan is an Indian citizen, Section 115BBA does not apply and his income is taxable at normal applicable slab rates with allowable business deductions.
questions.explanation: Section 115BBA(1)(a) explicitly restricts its application to 'a sportsman (including an athlete), who is not a citizen of India and is a non-resident'. If a sportsman is an Indian citizen, even though he is a non-resident for tax purposes, Section 115BBA does not apply to him. Rohan's income will be computed under the regular provisions of the Act (Profits and Gains of Business/Profession or Other Sources), allowing eligible business deductions under Section 37(1), and taxed at the normal progressive slab rates. He will also be required to file a return of income if his total income exceeds the basic exemption limit. Hence, Option 3 is correct.

questions.category: Special Tax Rates under Chapter XII & XII-BB
questions.question:
Adele, a renowned British singer and non-resident in India (not a citizen of India), visited India in November 2025. During her stay, she:
1. Performed at a live concert in Bengaluru, earning ₹80,00,000.
2. Participated in a high-stakes televised card game and won ₹10,00,000.
Which of the following correctly describes the tax treatment of these two receipts under the Income-tax Act, 1961?
options: Concert income of ₹80,00,000 is taxable @ 20% under Section 115BBA; card game winnings of ₹10,00,000 are taxable @ 30% under Section 115BB.
Both concert income and card game winnings are taxable @ 20% under Section 115BBA because both were earned during her performance tour in India.
Concert income is taxable @ 20% under Section 115BBA; card game winnings are completely exempt from tax in India for foreign citizens.
Both incomes are aggregated and taxed at the maximum marginal rate applicable to non-residents.
questions.explanation: Under Section 115BBA(1)(c), any income received or receivable by a non-resident entertainer (who is not a citizen of India) from their performance in India is taxable @ 20% on gross basis without any deduction of expenditure. However, games whose winnings are taxable under Section 115BB (such as card games, gambling, betting, horse races, or crossword puzzles) are expressly excluded from the scope of sports/entertainment concessions and are taxable @ 30% under Section 115BB. Therefore, the concert income of ₹80,00,000 is taxed @ 20% u/s 115BBA, whereas the card game winnings of ₹10,00,000 are taxed @ 30% u/s 115BB.

questions.category: Special Tax Rates under Chapter XII & XII-BB
questions.question: The Australian Rugby Board, a non-resident sports institution, received ₹1,50,00,000 as guarantee money from an Indian sports federation in relation to a rugby series played in India during P.Y. 2025-26. The Australian Rugby Board incurred ₹35,00,000 towards administrative and legal arrangements for the tour. Assuming the Indian federation deducted tax at source as required by Chapter XVII-B, what is the tax payable by the Australian Rugby Board and its return filing obligation?
options: Tax payable is ₹23,92,000 (20.8% of net income ₹1,15,00,000); return of income must be filed under Section 139(1).
Tax payable is ₹31,20,000 (20.8% of gross guarantee money); return of income must be filed under Section 139(1) because guarantee money exceeds ₹1 crore.
Tax payable is ₹31,20,000 (20% tax + 4% cess on gross ₹1,50,00,000); no deduction of expenses is allowed, and no return of income is required to be filed under Section 139(1).
Guarantee money paid to non-resident sports associations is exempt under Section 10(23) provided reciprocity exists.
questions.explanation: Under Section 115BBA(1)(b), any amount guaranteed to be paid or payable to a non-resident sports association or institution in relation to any game or sport played in India is taxable @ 20% (plus 4% cess = 20.8%). Under Section 115BBA(2), no deduction in respect of any expenditure (here ₹35,00,000) is allowable. The tax payable is 20.8% on ₹1,50,00,000 = ₹31,20,000. Under Section 115BBA(3), if the total income consists solely of such guarantee money and tax has been deducted at source under Chapter XVII-B (specifically under Section 194E), the association is NOT required to file a return of income under Section 139(1). Option 2 is correct.

questions.category: Special Tax Rates under Chapter XII & XII-BB
questions.question:
Under Section 115JG read with Notification No. 85/2018, which of the following conditions must be satisfied for capital gains arising from the conversion of an Indian branch of a foreign bank into an Indian subsidiary company to be exempt from tax?
(i) The conversion must be in accordance with the scheme framed by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI).
(ii) All assets and liabilities of the Indian branch immediately before conversion must become assets and liabilities of the Indian subsidiary at book values (ignoring revaluation).
(iii) The foreign bank or its nominee must hold 100% of the share capital of the Indian subsidiary from conversion until the last day of the previous year of conversion.
(iv) The foreign bank must continue to hold at least 51% of the voting power of the Indian subsidiary for a period of five years immediately succeeding the previous year of conversion.
(v) The foreign bank can receive cash consideration up to 10% of the net asset value in addition to allotment of shares.
options: (i), (ii), (iii) and (v) only
(i), (ii), (iii) and (iv) only
(i), (iii) and (iv) only
(ii), (iii), (iv) and (v) only
questions.explanation: Under Notification No. 85/2018 issued under Section 115JG(1), the conditions for capital gains exemption are: (a) amalgamation/conversion in accordance with RBI scheme; (b) all assets and liabilities transferred at book values appearing in the branch's books (revaluation ignored); (c) the foreign bank/nominee must hold the whole (100%) of the share capital during the period beginning from conversion date and ending on the last day of that previous year; (d) continue to hold not less than 51% of voting power for 5 years immediately succeeding that previous year; and (e) the foreign bank does NOT receive any consideration or benefit directly or indirectly other than allotment of shares in the Indian subsidiary. Statement (v) is incorrect because NO consideration other than shares is permitted. Thus, (i), (ii), (iii), and (iv) only are correct.

questions.category: Special Tax Rates under Chapter XII & XII-BB
questions.question: Global Bank Ltd., a foreign banking company, converted its Indian branch into an Indian subsidiary company, Global India Bank Ltd., on 1st November 2025 in accordance with an RBI scheme fulfilling all conditions under Section 115JG. During P.Y. 2025-26 (365 days), the branch operated for 214 days (1st April to 31st October 2025) and the subsidiary operated for 151 days (1st November 2025 to 31st March 2026). The total allowable depreciation on the block of assets for the entire year (as if no conversion occurred) is ₹36,50,000. Additionally, the Indian branch owned a cold chain facility asset whose cost was fully claimed as deduction under Section 35AD in an earlier year. How will the depreciation be apportioned, and what is the actual cost of the Section 35AD asset in the hands of the subsidiary?
options: Depreciation is allowed entirely (₹36,50,000) to the Indian subsidiary; actual cost of the 35AD asset is its fair market value on conversion date.
Depreciation is divided equally (₹18,25,000 each); actual cost of the 35AD asset is Nil.
Depreciation of ₹21,40,000 to the branch and ₹15,10,000 to the subsidiary; actual cost of the 35AD asset is the original cost to the foreign bank branch.
Depreciation of ₹21,40,000 to the branch and ₹15,10,000 to the subsidiary (in the ratio of days used: 214:151); actual cost of the Section 35AD asset to the subsidiary is Nil.
questions.explanation: Under Notification No. 85/2018 governing Section 115JG: (a) The aggregate deduction for depreciation under Section 32 allowable to the Indian branch and the Indian subsidiary shall not exceed the deduction calculated at prescribed rates as if the conversion had not taken place, apportioned in the ratio of the number of days for which the assets were used by them. Here, ratio is 214:151, giving ₹21,40,000 to the Indian branch and ₹15,10,000 to the Indian subsidiary. (b) The actual cost of any capital asset on which deduction has been allowed or is allowable under Section 35AD shall be treated as 'Nil' in the case of the Indian subsidiary company. Thus, Option 3 is correct.

questions.category: Special Tax Rates under Chapter XII & XII-BB
questions.question:
Foreign Bank AG converted its Indian branch into an Indian subsidiary on 1st December 2025 in full compliance with Section 115JG and Notification No. 85/2018. As on the date of conversion, the Indian branch had:
- Accumulated business loss under Section 72: ₹45,00,000 (accumulated over past 3 years)
- Unabsorbed depreciation under Section 32(2): ₹30,00,000
- Minimum Alternate Tax (MAT) credit under Section 115JAA: ₹15,00,000
What is the statutory treatment of these balances in the hands of the Indian subsidiary company?
options: The accumulated business loss and unabsorbed depreciation are deemed to be the loss and unabsorbed depreciation of the Indian subsidiary for the previous year of conversion, and MAT credit of ₹15,00,000 is deemed to be the tax credit of the Indian subsidiary.
The accumulated loss and unabsorbed depreciation can be carried forward only for the balance remaining period of 5 years out of the original 8-year limit; MAT credit lapses upon conversion.
Only unabsorbed depreciation carries over indefinitely; accumulated business loss and MAT credit lapse because the legal personality of the assessee has changed.
The accumulated loss and unabsorbed depreciation can be set off only against profits arising after 5 years of operation by the subsidiary.
questions.explanation: According to Notification No. 85/2018 issued under Section 115JG: (1) The accumulated loss (under PGBP, other than speculation loss) and unabsorbed depreciation of the Indian branch are deemed to be the loss or allowance for depreciation of the Indian subsidiary company for the previous year in which the conversion was effected, and provisions relating to set-off and carry forward apply accordingly (i.e. fresh 8-year carry forward begins for business loss, and unabsorbed depreciation carries forward indefinitely). (2) The tax credit of the Indian branch under Section 115JAA is deemed to be the tax credit of the Indian subsidiary company for the previous year in which conversion was effected. Thus, Option 0 correctly states the statutory position.

questions.category: Special Tax Rates under Chapter XII & XII-BB
questions.question: EuroBank Inc., a foreign bank, converted its Indian branch into an Indian subsidiary, Euro India Bank Ltd., in P.Y. 2022-23 and claimed capital gains exemption under Section 115JG. In June 2025 (during P.Y. 2025-26), EuroBank Inc. diluted its shareholding in Euro India Bank Ltd. to 40% voting power. What are the legal consequences of this action under Section 115JG(3), and within what time limit can the Assessing Officer rectify the original assessment?
options: No consequences arise because the mandatory 51% holding condition applies only for 2 years from the date of conversion.
The exemption is revoked for P.Y. 2025-26 only, and the capital gain is assessed as deemed income of the subsidiary company in P.Y. 2025-26.

The exemption or relief originally granted is deemed to have been wrongly allowed; the Assessing Officer is empowered to recompute the total income for P.Y. 2022-23 by passing a rectification order under Section 154 within 4 years from the end of P.Y. 2025-26.
The Assessing Officer must initiate reassessment under Section 148 within 3 years from the end of P.Y. 2022-23.
questions.explanation: Under Notification No. 85/2018, the foreign bank must continue to hold not less than 51% voting power in the Indian subsidiary for 5 years immediately succeeding the previous year of conversion. Under Section 115JG(3), if any condition is subsequently violated, the benefit/exemption originally granted is deemed to have been wrongly allowed. The Assessing Officer is empowered to recompute the total income of the assessee for the conversion year (P.Y. 2022-23) by amending the assessment order under Section 154. The statutory 4-year period for rectification under Section 154 is reckoned from the end of the previous year in which the failure took place (i.e., 4 years from 31st March 2026, meaning up to 31st March 2030). Thus, Option 2 is correct.

questions.question:
Mr. Arthur, a citizen of the United Kingdom and a non-resident in India, is employed with an Indian IT consulting firm. His services were rendered in India during the previous year 2025-26. Under his employment contract, his monthly salary is denominated in British Pounds (£5,000 per month). His salary for the month of October 2025 became due on 31st October 2025 and was disbursed to his UK bank account on 7th November 2025. The State Bank of India's Telegraphic Transfer (TT) buying and selling rates were as follows:
- 30th September 2025: TT Buying Rate = ₹105/£; TT Selling Rate = ₹107/£
- 31st October 2025: TT Buying Rate = ₹106/£; TT Selling Rate = ₹108/£
- 7th November 2025: TT Buying Rate = ₹108/£; TT Selling Rate = ₹110/£
- 30th November 2025: TT Buying Rate = ₹109/£; TT Selling Rate = ₹111/£

For the purpose of withholding tax under Section 192, at which exchange rate must the salary payable in foreign currency be converted into Indian Rupees?
options: TT Selling Rate of SBI as on 31st October 2025 (₹108/£)
TT Buying Rate of SBI as on 30th September 2025 (₹105/£)
TT Buying Rate of SBI as on 31st October 2025 (₹106/£)
TT Buying Rate of SBI as on 7th November 2025 (₹108/£)
questions.explanation: Under Section 192(6) read with Rule 26 of the Income-tax Rules, 1962, where salary is payable in foreign currency, the amount of tax deducted is to be calculated after converting the salary payable into Indian currency at the Telegraphic Transfer (TT) buying rate adopted by the State Bank of India on the last day of the month immediately preceding the month in which the salary is due, or is paid in advance or in arrears. For salary due for October 2025 (due on 31st October 2025), the immediately preceding month ended on 30th September 2025. Consequently, the TT buying rate of SBI as on 30th September 2025 (₹105/£) must be adopted. Converting at the date of accrual, payment date, or using the TT selling rate is legally incorrect under Rule 26.

questions.question: NovaNex Technologies Pvt. Ltd., an eligible start-up recognized under Section 80-IAC, allotted sweat equity shares to its non-resident Chief AI Architect, Dr. Lin, on 15th July 2025 (P.Y. 2025-26, A.Y. 2026-27) as perquisites taxable under Section 17(2)(vi). Dr. Lin resigned from the employment of NovaNex Technologies Pvt. Ltd. on 20th October 2027. Subsequently, Dr. Lin sold these sweat equity shares on 10th January 2029. By what date is NovaNex Technologies Pvt. Ltd. legally required to deduct or pay tax on the value of such perquisite under Section 192(1C)?
options: Within 14 days from 31st March 2031 (being 48 months from the end of A.Y. 2026-27), i.e., by 14th April 2031
Within 14 days from 10th January 2029 (date of sale of shares), i.e., by 24th January 2029
Within 14 days from 20th October 2027 (date of cessation of employment), i.e., by 3rd November 2027
On the 7th day of the month following the month of allotment, i.e., by 7th August 2025
questions.explanation: Under Section 192(1C), an eligible start-up referred to in Section 80-IAC responsible for paying any income by way of perquisite being specified security or sweat equity shares allotted to an employee must deduct or pay tax on the value of such perquisite within 14 days from the earliest of the following three dates: (a) after the expiry of 48 months from the end of the relevant assessment year (i.e., 48 months from 31.03.2027 = 31.03.2031); (b) from the date of the sale of such shares (10.01.2029); or (c) from the date of the assessee ceasing to be an employee (20.10.2027). The earliest of these events is the cessation of employment on 20th October 2027. Therefore, tax must be deducted or paid within 14 days thereof, i.e., by 3rd November 2027.

questions.question:
David Warner, a foreign national and an Australian professional cricketer (non-resident in India), visited India during the previous year 2025-26. During his stay in India, he earned the following receipts:
1. Match participation fees from Indian Premier League matches: ₹8,00,000
2. Remuneration for featuring in a television commercial for an Indian sports brand: ₹2,00,000
3. Contribution of articles analyzing cricket strategies published in an Indian national daily newspaper: ₹50,000
4. Prize winnings from a horse race at the Royal Western India Turf Club, Mumbai: ₹50,000

What is the total amount of tax required to be withheld at source under the relevant provisions of the Income-tax Act, 1961 (including health and education cess @ 4%)?
options: ₹2,18,400 u/s 194E and ₹15,600 u/s 194BB, aggregating to ₹2,34,000
₹2,10,000 u/s 194E and ₹15,000 u/s 194BB, aggregating to ₹2,25,000
₹2,28,800 u/s 194E with Nil TDS on horse race winnings, aggregating to ₹2,28,800
₹2,39,200 under Section 195 at the rates in force
questions.explanation: Income covered under Section 115BBA includes match participation fees (₹8,00,000), advertisement remuneration (₹2,00,000), and contribution of sports articles in newspapers (₹50,00,000 is typo; ₹50,000), totaling ₹10,50,000. Under Section 194E, tax is deductible @ 20% plus 4% cess = 20.8% on payments made to a non-resident sportsman. TDS u/s 194E = ₹10,50,000 × 20.8% = ₹2,18,400. Income from horse races (₹50,000) is governed by Section 115BB and subject to TDS u/s 194BB @ 30% plus 4% cess = 31.2% (since the payee is a non-resident). TDS u/s 194BB = ₹50,000 × 31.2% = ₹15,600. Total TDS = ₹2,18,400 + ₹15,600 = ₹2,34,000. Winnings from horse races are specifically excluded from Section 115BBA / 194E.

questions.question:
David Warner, a foreign national and an Australian professional cricketer (non-resident in India), visited India during the previous year 2025-26. During his stay in India, he earned the following receipts:
1. Match participation fees from Indian Premier League matches: ₹8,00,000
2. Remuneration for featuring in a television commercial for an Indian sports brand: ₹2,00,000
3. Contribution of articles analyzing cricket strategies published in an Indian national daily newspaper: ₹50,000
4. Prize winnings from a horse race at the Royal Western India Turf Club, Mumbai: ₹50,000

Tax has been fully deducted at source on all receipts at the prescribed rates. In this context, is David Warner exempt from the requirement of furnishing a return of income under Section 139(1) for Assessment Year 2026-27?
options: Yes, because under Section 115BBA(2), any non-resident sportsman whose entire tax liability is fully deducted at source is unconditionally exempt from filing a return of income.
Yes, provided his total income does not exceed the maximum amount not chargeable to tax under the regular provisions.
No, because non-resident individuals are never eligible for any exemption from filing returns of income in India regardless of the source of income.

No, because the statutory exemption under Section 115BBA(2) is available only if the non-resident's total income comprises solely of income specified in Section 115BBA; having horse race winnings disentitles him from this exemption.
questions.explanation: Section 115BBA(2) provides relief from filing a return of income under Section 139(1) to a non-resident sportsman/entertainer only if two cumulative conditions are fulfilled: (i) his total income consists ONLY of income referred to in Section 115BBA; and (ii) tax deductible at source under Section 194E has been fully deducted. In this case, David Warner earned winnings from horse races (₹50,000) taxable under Section 115BB. Because his total income includes income other than that specified in Section 115BBA, the exemption under Section 115BBA(2) is not available, making the filing of a return of income mandatory under Section 139(1).

questions.question: During an international cricket tournament hosted in India, the organizing committee paid ₹12,00,000 each to Mr. Billy Bowden (a non-resident umpire from New Zealand) and Mr. Ranjan Madugalle (a non-resident ICC match referee from Sri Lanka). The organizing committee deducted tax at source @ 20.8% under Section 194E, treating them as non-resident sportsmen. The deductees disputed the applicability of Section 194E. Applying the judicial precedent laid down by the Calcutta High Court in Indcom v. CIT (TDS) (2011) 335 ITR 485, what is the correct withholding tax treatment?
options: Section 194E applies correctly because match referees and umpires are integral participants in sports matches played in India and thus qualify as sportsmen.

Section 194E is not applicable because umpires and match referees are technical professionals rendering services and not 'sportsmen'; however, since income accrued in India, TDS is deductible under Section 195 at the rates in force.
Neither Section 194E nor Section 195 applies because international match officials are exempt from Indian taxation under Vienna Convention diplomatic immunities.
Section 194J applies at the domestic rate of 10% for professional technical fees, irrespective of the residential status of the payee.
questions.explanation: The Calcutta High Court in Indcom v. CIT (TDS) (2011) 335 ITR 485 held that umpires and match referees are technical persons/professionals who render professional services in connection with games. They cannot be termed as 'sportsmen (including an athlete)' or 'sports associations' within the meaning of Section 115BBA. Consequently, Section 194E is not attracted. However, since the income accrued and arose in India by virtue of services rendered in India, it constitutes taxable income in India, and tax is deductible under the general non-resident withholding provision of Section 195 at the rates in force.

questions.question: The Pak-Indo-Lanka Joint Management Committee (PILCOM) was formed to conduct a World Cup cricket tournament in India, Pakistan, and Sri Lanka. PILCOM disbursed guarantee money of £8,85,000 from its London bank accounts directly to the cricket boards of Australia, England, New Zealand, Sri Lanka, and Kenya in relation to matches played in India. PILCOM contended that no tax was deductible under Section 194E because: (i) payments were made outside India from a bank account in London; (ii) payments represented fixed guarantee money irrespective of match results; and (iii) payees were eligible for treaty benefits under respective DTAAs. Applying the Supreme Court ruling in PILCOM v. CIT (2020) 425 ITR 312 (SC), evaluate PILCOM's contentions.
options: PILCOM's contentions are valid; payments made by a non-resident entity from foreign bank accounts are outside the extraterritorial jurisdiction of Section 194E.
PILCOM is not liable to deduct tax because guarantee money paid to foreign cricket boards represents business profits in the absence of a Permanent Establishment under the respective DTAAs.

PILCOM is liable to deduct tax under Section 194E because guarantee money is inextricably connected to games played in India, establishing an Indian source of income; the liability under Section 194E is absolute and does not depend on DTAA benefits at the withholding stage.
PILCOM is liable to deduct tax only under Section 195 after obtaining an order from the Assessing Officer determining the appropriate proportion under Section 195(2).
questions.explanation: In PILCOM v. CIT (2020) 425 ITR 312 (SC), the Supreme Court held that the phrase 'in relation to any game or sport played in India' in Section 115BBA(1)(b) establishes a direct nexus between the guarantee money and the matches played in India. The source of the income was in India. Even though payments were made from bank accounts in London, income accrued or arose in India to the non-resident sports associations. Furthermore, the Supreme Court ruled that the statutory obligation under Section 194E is specific and absolute; the deductor cannot unilaterally plead DTAA provisions to avoid withholding tax under Section 194E, though the payee may claim treaty benefits in their assessment. Hence, PILCOM was liable to deduct tax under Section 194E.

questions.question:
Pragati Infrastructure Debt Fund (a notified IDF conforming to prescribed guidelines) credited interest during previous year 2025-26 to its non-resident investors as follows:
- To BlueBay Capital Inc. (a foreign corporate entity registered in Delaware, USA): ₹50,00,000
- To Mr. Roberto, an individual non-resident residing in Italy: ₹12,00,000
Neither investor has total income exceeding ₹50 lakhs. What is the applicable withholding tax liability under Section 194LB of the Income-tax Act, 1961?
options: 20.8% on BlueBay Capital Inc. (₹10,40,000) and 20.8% on Mr. Roberto (₹2,49,600) under general interest withholding provisions
5% flat on both investors without health and education cess, amounting to ₹2,50,000 and ₹60,000 respectively
Nil TDS because interest payable by notified infrastructure debt funds is entirely exempt from tax under Section 10(47)
5.2% (5% plus 4% health and education cess) on both investors, amounting to ₹2,60,000 for BlueBay Capital Inc. and ₹62,400 for Mr. Roberto
questions.explanation: Under Section 194LB, where any income by way of interest is payable by a notified Infrastructure Debt Fund (referred to in Section 10(47)) to a non-corporate non-resident or a foreign company, tax is deductible at the concessional rate of 5% on the gross amount of interest. Since the payment is made to non-residents, health and education cess @ 4% is added to the base rate of 5%, resulting in an effective withholding rate of 5.2% (no surcharge is applicable as income does not exceed the surcharge threshold of ₹50 lakhs). TDS on BlueBay Capital Inc. = ₹50,00,000 × 5.2% = ₹2,60,000. TDS on Mr. Roberto = ₹12,00,000 × 5.2% = ₹62,400.

questions.question:
InfraCorp Ltd., an Indian infrastructure company, makes interest payments during P.Y. 2025-26 to various non-resident lenders in respect of foreign borrowings:
1. Interest on foreign currency loan borrowed under an agreement entered into on 15.03.2021 as approved by the Central Government.
2. Interest on Rupee Denominated Bonds (Masala Bonds) issued outside India on 15.11.2018.
3. Interest on long-term bonds issued on 10.05.2022, which are listed exclusively on a recognized stock exchange located in GIFT-IFSC.
4. Interest on long-term bonds issued on 12.08.2023, which are listed exclusively on a recognized stock exchange located in GIFT-IFSC.

What are the respective base rates of tax deduction at source under Section 194LC (before surcharge and cess) for items (1), (2), (3), and (4)?
questions.explanation: Under Section 194LC: (1) Interest on foreign currency loan borrowed under an agreement between 01.07.2012 and 30.06.2023 is subject to TDS @ 5%. (2) Rupee Denominated Bonds issued outside India between 17.09.2018 and 31.03.2019 are exempt from tax under Section 10(4C), hence TDS is Nil. (3) Long-term bonds / RDBs issued between 01.04.2020 and 30.06.2023 listed exclusively on an IFSC recognized stock exchange attract a concessional rate of 4%. (4) Long-term bonds / RDBs issued on or after 01.07.2023 listed exclusively on an IFSC stock exchange attract a concessional rate of 9%. Therefore, the respective base rates are 5%, Nil, 4%, and 9%.

questions.question: Stuttgart Machinery AG, a German manufacturing corporation not having a Permanent Establishment or PAN in India, entered into a contract to receive royalties of ₹40,00,000 from an Indian company during P.Y. 2025-26. Under the India-Germany DTAA, the agreed withholding tax rate on royalties is 10%. Stuttgart Machinery AG furnished to the payer its legal name, official email address, contact details, address in Germany, a valid Tax Residency Certificate (TRC) issued by the German tax authorities, and its German Tax Identification Number (TIN). The Indian payer contends that since Stuttgart Machinery AG does not hold an Indian PAN, tax must be withheld @ 20% under Section 206AA. Evaluate the legal validity of the Indian payer's contention.
options: The payer is correct because Section 206AA contains a non-obstante clause overriding all other provisions including DTAAs, making PAN mandatory for non-residents.

The payer is incorrect because Rule 37BC provides specific relaxation from Section 206AA to non-residents receiving royalties if specified details, including TRC and TIN, are furnished; tax is deductible at the treaty rate of 10%.
The payer is incorrect, but tax must still be deducted at the domestic rate of 20% u/s 115A plus cess, because DTAA benefits cannot be claimed without an Indian PAN under any circumstances.
The payer is correct because Rule 37BC applies exclusively to interest on long-term bonds under Section 194LC and does not cover royalty or FTS payments.
questions.explanation: Section 206AA mandates TDS at a higher rate (higher of prescribed rate, rates in force, or 20%) if the deductee fails to furnish PAN. However, Rule 37BC provides an express exception for non-corporate non-residents and foreign companies not having PAN in respect of payments by way of interest, royalty, fees for technical services (FTS), dividends, and capital gains on transfer of capital assets. Under Rule 37BC, higher TDS u/s 206AA is not attracted if the deductee furnishes: (a) name, email, contact number; (b) address in home country; (c) Tax Residency Certificate (TRC); and (d) Tax Identification Number (TIN) or unique identification number. Since Stuttgart Machinery AG satisfied all conditions of Rule 37BC, Section 206AA cannot be invoked, and tax must be deducted at the beneficial DTAA rate of 10%.

questions.question:
Rule 37BC of the Income-tax Rules, 1962 provides relaxation from the punitive higher rate of TDS under Section 206AA to non-corporate non-residents and foreign companies who do not hold a Permanent Account Number (PAN) in India, subject to furnishing prescribed documentation. Which of the following streams of payments are covered within the protective scope of Rule 37BC?
1. Interest payments
2. Royalty payments
3. Fees for Technical Services (FTS)
4. Dividend distributions
5. Consideration on transfer of any capital asset
6. Commission on sales or business profits chargeable under Section 28
options: 1, 2, 3, and 4 only
1, 2, and 3 only
1, 2, 3, 4, and 5 only
questions.explanation: Rule 37BC(1) explicitly enumerates five specified categories of payments in respect of which Section 206AA shall not apply to a non-resident deductee not having a PAN, provided prescribed information (name, email, address, TRC, TIN) is furnished. These specified payments are: (i) interest, (ii) royalty, (iii) fees for technical services, (iv) dividends, and (v) payments on transfer of any capital asset. Other income categories, such as business commissions, ordinary commercial receipts, or other business profits not covered under these five categories, are not sheltered under Rule 37BC, and failing to furnish PAN for such payments would trigger Section 206AA. Thus, items 1, 2, 3, 4, and 5 only are covered.

questions.question:
Consider the following two statements regarding withholding tax obligations under Section 195(1):
Assertion (A): A person responsible for making a remittance to a non-resident is under no statutory obligation to deduct tax at source under Section 195(1) if the payment does not contain any element of income chargeable to tax under the provisions of the Income-tax Act, 1961.
Reason (R): In GE India Technology Centre P. Ltd. v. CIT (2010) 327 ITR 456, the Supreme Court held that the expression 'chargeable under the provisions of the Act' in Section 195(1) qualifies the remittance; withholding tax applies only to sums that bear the character of chargeable income, and not on pure offshore commercial reimbursements or non-taxable receipts.

Choose the correct option:
options: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
(A) is true, but (R) is false.
(A) is false, because Section 195(1) mandates tax deduction on all gross outward remittances irrespective of income chargeability.
questions.explanation: In GE India Technology Centre P. Ltd. v. CIT (2010) 327 ITR 456, the landmark Supreme Court ruling clarified that the obligation to deduct tax at source under Section 195(1) arises only when the remittance contains an element of income chargeable to tax in India under the provisions of the Act. If the payment is not chargeable to tax in India (such as payments for offshore procurement of goods without business connection or PE), the payer is under no statutory liability to deduct tax under Section 195(1).
