The expression 'any other sum chargeable under the provisions of the Act' is the governing jurisdictional test. Thus, both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) correctly explains (A).

questions.question: Apex Holdings LLC (a US-based private equity firm with no physical presence, office, or permanent establishment in India) purchased all the shares of an Indian manufacturing entity, Bharat Precision Ltd., from Pioneer Global Corp (another Delaware-incorporated company). The transaction took place in New York, and funds were wired from Apex Holdings' US bank account to Pioneer Global's US bank account. Capital gains arising to Pioneer Global are deemed to accrue or arise in India under Section 9(1)(i). Apex Holdings LLC contends that as a non-resident entity with no branch or presence in India, it is outside the territorial reach of Section 195 and is not liable to deduct Indian withholding tax. How should Apex Holdings' contention be evaluated in light of Explanation 2 to Section 195(1)?
options: Valid, because Indian domestic withholding laws cannot impose extraterritorial compliance obligations on foreign payers with no Indian nexus.
Valid, because Section 195 applies strictly to resident payers; payments between two non-residents executed outside India are outside the scope of Chapter XVII-B.
Invalid, but Apex Holdings is required to deduct tax only if Pioneer Global fails to pay advance tax under Section 209.

Invalid, because Explanation 2 to Section 195(1) explicitly clarifies that the obligation to deduct tax applies and has always applied to all persons, resident or non-resident, whether or not the non-resident has a residence, place of business, business connection, or any other presence in India.
questions.explanation: Explanation 2 to Section 195(1) (inserted retrospectively post the Supreme Court's Vodafone ruling) clarifies that the obligation to comply with Section 195(1) and make deduction thereunder applies and shall be deemed to have always applied and extends to all persons, resident or non-resident, whether or not the non-resident payer has: (a) a residence or place of business or business connection in India; or (b) any other presence in any manner whatsoever in India. Because the capital gains accrued in India under Section 9(1)(i), the sum is chargeable to tax under the Act. Hence, Apex Holdings LLC was legally required to deduct tax under Section 195(1), regardless of being a foreign company operating entirely outside India.

questions.question:
Analyze the following statements concerning the 'Time of Deduction' of withholding tax under Section 195 of the Income-tax Act, 1961:
I. Tax is deductible at the time of credit of such income to the account of the payee (including 'Interest payable account' or 'Suspense account') or at the time of payment in cash, cheque, draft, or any other mode, whichever is earlier.
II. Where interest is payable to a non-resident by the Government, tax is deductible only at the time of actual payment thereof.
III. Where interest is payable to a non-resident by a public sector bank or a public financial institution, tax is deductible only at the time of actual payment thereof.

Which of the above statements are correct?
options: I and II only
I and III only
I, II, and III
I only
questions.explanation: Under Section 195(1), the general rule is that tax must be deducted at the time of credit of the sum to the account of the payee (including suspense or payable accounts) or payment, whichever is earlier (Statement I is correct). However, the second proviso to Section 195(1) carves out a specific exception: in the case of interest payable by the Government (Statement II) or a public sector bank within the meaning of Section 10(23D) or a public financial institution within the meaning of Section 10(23D) (Statement III), tax deduction is required to be made ONLY at the time of payment thereof in cash or by issue of cheque/draft or other mode. Therefore, statements I, II, and III are all correct.

questions.question: An Indian telecommunications company enters into a turnkey offshore engineering contract with a Japanese contractor, Tokyo Systems Corp. The total contract value is ₹20 crores, which comprises offshore equipment design, software supply, and onshore testing. The Indian payer considers that only 20% of the contract value represents income chargeable to tax in India, while the remaining 80% represents non-taxable offshore supply. The payer intends to apply to the Assessing Officer for determination of the appropriate proportion of sum chargeable to tax. Which of the following statements regarding the procedure under Section 195(2) and Rule 29BA is INCORRECT?
options: The application for determination of appropriate proportion must be made by the payer electronically in Form 15E under digital signature or electronic verification code.
An application for a fresh certificate can only be made 6 months after the expiry of the earlier certificate, and under no circumstances can it be made prior to its expiry.
The Assessing Officer, while determining the appropriate proportion, must examine the taxability under the provisions of the Act read with the relevant DTAA.

While examining the application, the Assessing Officer is required to consider the tax payable on estimated income of the previous year, tax payable of the preceding 4 previous years, and existing tax liabilities of the recipient.
questions.explanation: Under Rule 29BA(6), an application for a fresh certificate may be made, if the assessee so desires, either after the expiry of the period of validity of the earlier certificate OR within three months before the expiry thereof. Therefore, the statement claiming that an application for a fresh certificate can only be made 6 months after expiry and never prior to expiry is completely INCORRECT. All other statements accurately reflect Rule 29BA: application is in Form 15E electronically, the AO evaluates taxability under the Act and DTAA, and the AO considers estimated current year taxes, past 4 years' tax performance, and existing direct tax liabilities.

questions.question: Compare the statutory provisions of Section 195(2) and Section 195(3) of the Income-tax Act, 1961. Which of the following correctly captures the core distinction between these two sub-sections?
options: Section 195(2) enables the PAYER to apply to the AO for determining the appropriate proportion of sum chargeable to tax, whereas Section 195(3) enables the NON-RESIDENT PAYEE to apply to the AO for a certificate authorizing receipt of sum without deduction of tax.
Section 195(2) enables the non-resident payee to apply for lower deduction, whereas Section 195(3) empowers the payer to obtain a nil deduction certificate.
Section 195(2) is an appeal provision against order of AO under Section 201, whereas Section 195(3) provides for mandatory withholding in notified cases.
Section 195(2) applies only to royalties and FTS, whereas Section 195(3) applies exclusively to interest and salaries.
questions.explanation: Section 195(2) provides a mechanism for the person responsible for paying (the payer) who considers that the whole of the sum would not be income chargeable in the hands of the recipient, to apply to the Assessing Officer to determine the appropriate proportion of sum chargeable to tax. In contrast, Section 195(3) empowers the recipient/payee (the non-resident entitled to receive interest or other sum) to apply in the prescribed form (Form 15C/15D under Rule 29B) to the AO for grant of a certificate authorizing him to receive such sum without deduction of tax. Option A correctly captures this fundamental distinction.

questions.question: Under a cross-border cloud software hosting agreement entered into on 1st April 2025, Bharat Cloud Services Ltd. agreed to pay $50,000 monthly to CloudNet Inc. (a US entity), with a contract clause stipulating that all Indian taxes deductible under Section 195 shall be borne by Bharat Cloud Services Ltd. On 5th August 2025, Bharat Cloud Services Ltd. paid the withholding tax of ₹8,32,000 to the credit of the Central Government. Following a subsequent ruling of the Supreme Court settling the law that such cloud hosting services do not constitute royalty or FTS, Bharat Cloud Services Ltd. claims that no tax was required to be deducted and seeks a refund of the tax borne by it. What is the statutory remedy, prescribed form, and limitation period under Section 239A?
options: File a revision petition under Section 264 within 1 year from the date of payment of tax.
File a rectification application under Section 154 within 4 years from the end of the financial year in which tax was paid.

File an application before the Assessing Officer in Form 29D within 30 days from the date of payment of such tax; the AO must pass an order within 6 months from the end of the month in which the application is received.
File an appeal before the CIT(Appeals) under Section 248 within 30 days from the end of the relevant assessment year.
questions.explanation: Section 239A provides that where under an agreement or other arrangement in writing, the tax deductible on any income (other than interest) under Section 195 is to be borne by the person by whom the income is payable, and such person having paid such tax to the credit of the Central Government claims that no tax was required to be deducted on such income, he may file an application before the Assessing Officer for refund of such tax in Form 29D. The application must be filed within 30 days from the date of payment of such tax. The AO, after giving an opportunity of being heard, must pass an order in writing allowing or rejecting the application within 6 months from the end of the month in which the application is received.

questions.question: A resident deductor deducted tax under Section 195 and deposited the same into the Central Government account in respect of a contract for technical consulting with a foreign vendor. The contract was subsequently cancelled due to force majeure, and no remittance was ever made to the foreign vendor. The resident deductor applies for a refund of the deposited TDS pursuant to CBDT Circular No. 07/2007 (as modified by Circular No. 07/2011 and Circular No. 11/2016). Which of the following conditions is NOT required or is contrary to the prescribed guidelines for granting such refund?
options: The deductor must submit an undertaking that no TDS certificate under Section 203 (Form 16A) has been issued to the non-resident, or indemnify the Department against any duplicate refund claim.
The refund can only be granted if the non-resident deductee has not filed an Indian return of income and the time limit for filing the return of income has expired.
The resident deductor is entitled to interest on the refunded amount under Section 244A from the date of payment of such tax.
The refund shall be granted to the deductor even if the deductee non-resident has already claimed credit for the tax in its Indian return of income, provided the deductor furnishes a bank guarantee.
questions.explanation: Under CBDT Circular No. 07/2007 read with Circular No. 07/2011 and Circular No. 11/2016, a refund of tax deposited under Section 195 can be granted to the deductor only if the non-resident deductee has NOT filed a return of income and the time for filing the return has expired. If the non-resident has already filed a return and claimed credit for the TDS, no refund can be granted to the deductor, even with a bank guarantee (as the Department cannot grant double credit/refund). The circular also mandates: (i) an undertaking/indemnity regarding Form 16A; (ii) disallowance of corresponding expense in the deductor's assessment; and (iii) grant of interest under Section 244A from the date of payment. Hence, Option D states a contrary and invalid proposition.

questions.question: Pinnacle Mutual Fund (a mutual fund registered with SEBI and specified under Section 10(23D)) is distributing income of ₹10,00,000 on its units to Vanguard Equity LP, a non-corporate entity resident in the United Kingdom, during P.Y. 2025-26. Under the domestic provisions of Section 196A, tax is deductible @ 20% (plus 4% cess = 20.8%). Vanguard Equity LP furnishes a valid Tax Residency Certificate (TRC) issued by HMRC and Form 10F. Under Article 12 of the India-UK DTAA, the withholding tax rate on such income is capped at 15%. What is the rate and amount of tax to be deducted at source by Pinnacle Mutual Fund?
options: 20.8% under Section 196A amounting to ₹2,08,000, because statutory withholding rates in Chapter XVII-B cannot be overridden by DTAA provisions
15% under the India-UK DTAA amounting to ₹1,50,000, because the proviso to Section 196A mandates deduction at 20% or the treaty rate, whichever is lower, upon furnishing of a TRC
15.6% (15% treaty rate plus 4% health and education cess) amounting to ₹1,56,000
10.4% under the concessional rate for foreign portfolio funds
questions.explanation: Under Section 196A, tax is deductible @ 20% plus cess from income in respect of units of a mutual fund paid to a non-resident. However, the proviso to Section 196A provides that where a DTAA applies to the payee and the payee has furnished a valid Tax Residency Certificate (TRC) under Section 90(4)/90A(4), tax shall be deducted at 20% or at the rate provided in such agreement, whichever is lower. The India-UK DTAA prescribes a lower rate of 15%. Since treaty rates are inclusive of surcharge and cess (settled law), tax must be deducted at 15% flat, amounting to ₹1,50,000 (₹10,00,000 × 15%).

questions.question: Mr. Vikram, a citizen of India residing in Dubai (qualifying as a Non-Resident Indian), acquired units of the Unit Trust of India (UTI) in 2022 out of funds in his Non-Resident (External) [NRE] Account maintained with SBI in Mumbai in strict compliance with FEMA regulations. In June 2025, UTI distributed dividend income of ₹3,00,000 in respect of these units to Mr. Vikram. UTI's compliance officer deducted tax at source @ 20.8% under Section 196A. Examine the correctness of the compliance officer's action.
options: The compliance officer is incorrect; Section 196A(2) explicitly provides that no tax deduction shall be made from income payable in respect of UTI units to an NRI or NR HUF where the units were acquired out of funds in an NRE Account or foreign currency remittance under FEMA.
The compliance officer is correct; all distributions by mutual funds or UTI to non-residents are subject to mandatory 20.8% TDS under Section 196A without any exception.
The compliance officer is incorrect; tax was deductible under Section 194K at the domestic rate of 10% instead of Section 196A.
The compliance officer is correct, but tax should have been deducted at the concessional rate of 10.4% under Section 115E.
questions.explanation: Section 196A(2) provides an explicit statutory exception: no deduction of tax shall be made from any income payable in respect of units of the Unit Trust of India to a non-resident Indian (an individual citizen of India or person of Indian origin) or a non-resident Hindu Undivided Family, where the units have been acquired from UTI out of funds in a Non-Resident (External) Account maintained with any bank in India or by remittance of funds in foreign currency in accordance with FEMA regulations. Since Mr. Vikram is an NRI who acquired UTI units out of his NRE Account, the distribution is entirely exempt from withholding tax under Section 196A.

questions.question:
Atlantis Global Offshore Fund, an offshore fund referred to in Section 115AB(1)(a), earned the following income during previous year 2025-26 from units purchased in foreign currency:
1. Dividend distribution on mutual fund units referred to in Section 10(23D): ₹25,00,000
2. Long-term capital gains on transfer of such mutual fund units: ₹60,00,000

What are the applicable base rates of withholding tax under Section 196B of the Income-tax Act, 1961 (before surcharge and cess) on the unit dividend and the long-term capital gains, respectively?
options: 20% on unit dividend and 10% on long-term capital gains
10% on unit dividend and 10% on long-term capital gains
10% on unit dividend and 12.5% on long-term capital gains
20% on unit dividend and 12.5% on long-term capital gains
questions.explanation: Under Section 196B, the person responsible for making payments to an Offshore Fund must deduct tax at source at the following rates: (i) @ 10% in respect of income from units referred to in Section 115AB(1)(i) (i.e., income received in respect of units of mutual funds or UTI purchased in foreign currency); and (ii) @ 12.5% in respect of long-term capital gains arising from the transfer of such units referred to in Section 115AB. (The rate on long-term capital gains was revised to 12.5% by the Finance (No. 2) Act, 2024, aligning with Section 115AB). Therefore, the respective base rates are 10% on unit income and 12.5% on long-term capital gains.

questions.question:
Hermes Capital Ltd., a non-resident corporate entity incorporated in Singapore, held Global Depository Receipts (GDRs) issued by an Indian listed company under an approved scheme referred to in Section 115AC. During P.Y. 2025-26, Hermes Capital Ltd. recorded the following transactions:
- Dividend received on GDRs: ₹10,00,000
- Transfer of GDRs outside India to Orion Asset Management Inc. (another non-resident corporate entity) yielding long-term capital gains of ₹25,00,000
- Transfer of foreign currency convertible bonds of an Indian company in India yielding long-term capital gains of ₹16,00,000

What is the total withholding tax liability under Section 196C (base rate without surcharge/cess)?
options: ₹1,00,000 on dividend, ₹3,12,500 on offshore GDR transfer, and ₹2,00,000 on onshore bond transfer, totaling ₹6,12,500
₹2,00,000 on dividend and ₹2,00,000 on bond transfer, totaling ₹4,00,000
₹1,00,000 on dividend only, as all capital gains on 115AC instruments are exempt from TDS

₹1,00,000 on dividend (10%) and ₹2,00,000 on onshore bond transfer (12.5%), totaling ₹3,00,000; the offshore transfer of GDRs between two non-residents is exempt from tax under Section 47(viia) and attracts Nil TDS
questions.explanation: Under Section 196C: (1) Dividend on GDRs is subject to TDS @ 10% = ₹1,00,000. (2) Transfer of GDRs made outside India by one non-resident to another non-resident is specifically exempt from capital gains tax under Section 47(viia); since the transaction is not chargeable to tax in India, no tax is deductible under Section 196C or Section 195 (GE India principle). (3) Long-term capital gains on transfer of foreign currency bonds in India attract TDS u/s 196C @ 12.5% = ₹2,00,000 (₹16,00,000 × 12.5%). Total TDS = ₹1,00,000 + ₹2,00,000 = ₹3,00,000.

questions.question:
Consider the following statements regarding withholding tax provisions under Section 196D on payments made to Foreign Institutional Investors (FIIs) and Specified Funds:
1. Tax is deductible @ 20% on income in respect of securities referred to in Section 115AD(1)(a) payable to an FII.
2. No tax deduction at source is to be made under Section 196D from capital gains arising to an FII from the transfer of securities referred to in Section 115AD.
3. The enhanced rates of surcharge (@ 25% and 37%) are not applicable in case of tax deductible under Section 196D on dividend income paid to an FII.
4. Where a DTAA applies to an FII and a valid Tax Residency Certificate (TRC) is furnished, tax shall be deducted at 20% or the treaty rate, whichever is lower.

Which of the above statements are correct?
options: 1, 2, and 4 only
1 and 2 only
2, 3, and 4 only
questions.explanation: All four statements are correct: (1) Section 196D(1) prescribes 20% TDS on income from securities referred to in Section 115AD(1)(a) payable to an FII. (2) Section 196D(2) explicitly provides that no deduction of tax shall be made from any income by way of capital gains arising from the transfer of securities referred to in Section 115AD payable to an FII. (3) The proviso to Section 196D(1) restricts the maximum rate of surcharge on dividend income to 15%, meaning enhanced surcharge of 25% and 37% does not apply. (4) Section 196D(1A) allows the benefit of lower DTAA rates if the FII furnishes a valid Tax Residency Certificate (TRC) under Section 90(4)/90A(4).

questions.question: Compare the withholding tax framework under Section 196D for payments of securities income made to a Foreign Institutional Investor (FII) versus a 'Specified Fund' referred to in Section 10(4D) located in an International Financial Services Centre (IFSC). Which of the following statements accurately highlights the statutory distinctions?
options: Both FIIs and Specified Funds are subject to identical TDS @ 20% plus applicable surcharge and 4% cess.

Tax is deductible @ 20% (plus applicable surcharge and cess, subject to DTAA) on payments to an FII, whereas tax is deductible @ 10% on payments to a Specified Fund, with NO surcharge and NO health & education cess being leviable on such payments to the Specified Fund.
Payments to Specified Funds are subject to 5% TDS with full surcharge, whereas FIIs are exempt from TDS on dividend income.
Tax is deductible @ 10% for both entities, but an FII can claim treaty benefits while a Specified Fund cannot.
questions.explanation: Under Section 196D: (i) In the case of an FII, tax is deductible @ 20% (or lower treaty rate if TRC is furnished) plus applicable surcharge (capped at 15% on dividends) and 4% health & education cess. (ii) In the case of a Specified Fund referred to in Section 10(4D), tax is deductible @ 10% on income from securities [not being exempt u/s 10(4D)]. Crucially, the statutory notes to Section 196D provide that surcharge and health & education cess would NOT be applicable to a specified fund in respect of income received from securities referred to in Section 115AD(1)(a). Option B correctly reflects this critical difference.

questions.question:
Nexus REIT, an Indian Real Estate Investment Trust registered with SEBI, makes distributions during P.Y. 2025-26 to Mr. Hans, a non-resident individual unit holder residing in Germany. The distribution comprises three distinct streams:
1. Interest income received from a Special Purpose Vehicle (SPV) in which Nexus REIT holds 100% equity.
2. Dividend income received from an SPV which has exercised the option to pay concessional corporate tax under Section 115BAA.
3. Rental income from commercial real estate assets directly owned and leased out by Nexus REIT.

What are the respective rates of tax deduction at source under Section 194LBA?
options: Interest: 20%; Dividend: 20%; Rental income: 30% (all plus cess)
Interest: Nil; Dividend: Nil; Rental income: Nil (as business trust distributions are pass-through)
Interest: 5% u/s 194LBA(2); Dividend from 115BAA SPV: 5% u/s 194LBA(2); Rental income from directly owned asset: at the rates in force u/s 194LBA(3) (all increased by applicable cess/surcharge)
Interest: 5%; Dividend from 115BAA SPV: 10%; Rental income: 10%
questions.explanation: Under Section 194LBA: (1) Under Section 194LBA(2), any interest distributed by a business trust received from an SPV to a non-resident unit holder is subject to TDS @ 5% (plus cess). (2) Under Section 194LBA(2), dividend received from an SPV that has exercised the concessional tax regime under Section 115BAA and distributed to a non-resident unit holder is subject to TDS @ 5% (plus cess). (Note: if the SPV did not opt for 115BAA, dividend is exempt in unit holder's hands and no TDS is made). (3) Under Section 194LBA(3), distribution of rental income received from real estate assets directly owned by the REIT to a non-resident unit holder is subject to TDS at the 'rates in force' (i.e., 30% plus cess for non-resident non-corporate). Hence, Option C is correct.

questions.question: An Indian manufacturing company intends to make an offshore remittance of ₹45,00,000 to an engineering firm in France for technical installation services. The payment is chargeable to tax under the Income-tax Act, 1961 read with the India-France DTAA. The payer has not made any application to the Assessing Officer under Section 195(2) or Section 197. In accordance with Section 195(6) and Rule 37BB of the Income-tax Rules, 1962, which part of Form 15CA and what accompanying certification must be submitted prior to executing the remittance through an authorized dealer bank?
options: Form 15CA Part A only, without any Chartered Accountant certificate, since the remittance is under ₹50 lakhs.
Form 15CA Part B, along with a self-declaration from the non-resident payee.
Form 15CA Part D only, because installation charges are covered under the negative list of 33 exempt remittances.
Form 15CA Part C electronically, accompanied by an accountant's certificate in Form 15CB after obtaining the certificate from a Chartered Accountant in practice.
questions.explanation: Under Rule 37BB, the scheme of Form 15CA is divided as follows: (i) Part A is used if remittance or its aggregate does not exceed ₹5,00,000 during the financial year; (ii) Part B is used where remittance exceeds ₹5,00,000 and an order/certificate under Section 195(2), 195(3), or 197 has been obtained from the AO; (iii) Part C is used where remittance exceeds ₹5,00,000, the sum is chargeable to tax, and a certificate from an accountant (Chartered Accountant) in Form 15CB has been obtained; and (iv) Part D is used where the remittance is not chargeable to tax (other than the 33 specified exempt categories where neither 15CA nor 15CB is needed). Because this remittance exceeds ₹5,00,000, is chargeable to tax, and no AO certificate exists, Form 15CA Part C accompanied by Form 15CB is required.

questions.question: Under Section 173 of the Income-tax Act, 1961, which of the following statements correctly describes the statutory mechanism for the recovery of tax due from a non-resident assessee?
options: Tax arrears of a non-resident can only be recovered by attaching bank accounts situated in India, and cannot extend to assets that enter India subsequent to the assessment year.

Tax payable by a non-resident, whether assessed directly or through a representative assessee, may be recovered by deduction under Chapter XVII-B and any arrears may be recovered from any assets of the non-resident which are, or may at any time come, within India.
Recovery from assets within India can only be initiated if the representative assessee has been convicted of willful tax evasion under Section 276C.
The Assessing Officer must obtain prior approval of the Settlement Commission before proceeding to recover tax from assets of the non-resident that come into India after the relevant previous year.
questions.explanation: As per Section 173 of the Income-tax Act, 1961, in the case of a non-resident entitled to income arising from any business connection, property, asset/source of income, or transfer of a capital asset in India, tax chargeable thereon (whether in his own name or in the name of his agent liable as a representative assessee) may be recovered by deduction under Chapter XVII-B. Furthermore, any arrears of tax may also be recovered in accordance with the provisions of the Act from any assets of the non-resident which are, or may at any time come, within India. These provisions operate without prejudice to the general rights and liabilities under Section 161(1) or Section 167. Therefore, Option B is correct, while Options A, C, and D misstate the statutory conditions.

questions.question: The Tax Recovery Officer (TRO) has drawn up a certificate under Section 222 in respect of tax arrears of ₹85 lakhs due from Mr. Henderson, who is an assessee in default. Mr. Henderson is a resident of Country Y (a country with which India has an agreement under Section 90 for reciprocal recovery of tax) and possesses real estate in Country Y. What is the prescribed procedure under Section 228A for enforcing recovery against such foreign property?
options: The TRO must directly file an execution petition before the High Court of Country Y without involving the Central Government.
The TRO must issue a garnishee order directly to the foreign revenue collector under Section 226(3) demanding remittance within 30 days.
The TRO forwards the certificate drawn up under Section 222 to the CBDT, which may then take appropriate action having regard to the terms of the agreement with Country Y.
The TRO must first arrest Mr. Henderson under Section 222(1)(c) before any foreign certificate can be forwarded to the CBDT.
questions.explanation: Section 228A(1) provides that where an assessee is in default or is deemed to be in default in making a payment of tax, the Tax Recovery Officer may, if the assessee is a resident of a country with which India has an agreement for reciprocal recovery of tax, or has any property in that country, forward to the CBDT a certificate drawn up by him under Section 222. The CBDT may thereafter take such action thereon as it may deem appropriate having regard to the terms of the agreement with such foreign country. Correspondingly, under Section 228A(2), certificates received from foreign authorities can be forwarded by CBDT to the jurisdictional TRO in India for attachment, arrest, or appointment of a receiver. Hence, Option C correctly outlines the statutory channel, while Options A, B, and D are legally baseless.

questions.question: A foreign enterprise, Nordic Marine AS, established a Liaison Office (LO) in Mumbai with the requisite approval of the Reserve Bank of India under FEMA. In respect of the reporting obligations under Section 285 of the Income-tax Act, 1961, which of the following statements is legally accurate?
options: Nordic Marine AS must furnish an annual statement in Form No. 49C to the jurisdictional Assessing Officer within eight months from the end of the financial year, verified by a Chartered Accountant or an authorized signatory.
Nordic Marine AS is exempt from submitting any annual statement to the Assessing Officer since a liaison office is prohibited from generating commercial revenue in India.
The liaison office must file Form No. 49D electronically within 30 days from the close of each calendar quarter, verified exclusively by an Indian advocate.
The statement in Form No. 49C is required to be submitted only once every five years upon renewal of the RBI permission under FEMA.
questions.explanation: Under Section 285 read with Rule 114DA of the Income-tax Rules, every non-resident person having a liaison office in India set up in accordance with the guidelines issued by the Reserve Bank of India under the Foreign Exchange Management Act, 1999 (FEMA) is required to file a statement in the prescribed form (Form No. 49C) to the Assessing Officer having jurisdiction. This statement must be submitted within eight months from the end of such financial year (i.e., on or before 30th November) providing details of activities carried out by the liaison office during the financial year. The statement must be verified by a Chartered Accountant or by the authorized signatory of the non-resident. Failure to comply can also attract penalties. Thus, Option A is the correct legal position.

questions.question: Zeta Global Holdings Ltd., a company incorporated in the Cayman Islands, holds 100% shares of an Indian operating company, Beta Tech Ltd. On 15th October 2025, Zeta Global Holdings Ltd. entered into a share purchase agreement whereby all its shares were acquired by Omega LLC, USA. This offshore share transfer derived its value substantially from assets located in India within the meaning of Explanation 5 to Section 9(1)(i) and had the effect of transferring the management and control of Beta Tech Ltd. By what date must Beta Tech Ltd. furnish information in Form No. 49D under Section 285A, and what is the penalty under Section 271GA in case of failure?
options: Within 90 days from the end of the financial year (by 29th June 2026); penalty is a flat sum of ₹1,00,000.
Within 60 days of the transaction (by 14th December 2025); penalty is 1% of the total turnover of Beta Tech Ltd.
Within 30 days from the end of the financial year (by 30th April 2026); penalty is ₹5,00,000.
Within 90 days of the transaction (by 13th January 2026); penalty is 2% of the value of the transaction.
questions.explanation: Under Section 285A read with Rule 114DB, an Indian concern through or in which Indian assets are held must electronically furnish Form No. 49D. Normally, Form No. 49D must be filed within 90 days from the end of the financial year in which the transfer takes place. However, if the transaction has the effect of directly or indirectly transferring the rights of management or control in relation to the Indian concern, the information must be furnished within 90 days of the transaction itself. For a transaction occurring on 15th October 2025, the 90-day window expires on 13th January 2026. Furthermore, under Section 271GA, failure to furnish such information attracts a penalty equal to 2% of the value of the transaction where management or control is transferred (and ₹5,00,000 in any other case). Therefore, Option D is correct.

questions.question: Under Section 163(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961, the Assessing Officer may treat certain persons as the statutory agent of a non-resident. Which of the following correctly identifies the statutory scope and territorial nexus required for such treatment?
options: All categories of persons specified under Section 163(1), including purchasers of Indian capital assets, must strictly be resident individuals physically residing in India.

While persons employed by/on behalf of the NR, having a business connection, or through whom the NR receives income must be in India, a person who has acquired a capital asset in India by transfer from the NR may be treated as an agent whether resident or non-resident.
An agent can only be appointed during the lifetime of the non-resident and cannot be appointed after the expiry of the relevant previous year.
A person who has a business connection can only be treated as an agent if he holds an active power of attorney executed before an Indian consular officer abroad.
questions.explanation: Section 163(1) specifies five categories who may be treated as an agent of a non-resident: (i) employed by or on behalf of the NR; (ii) having any business connection with the NR; (iii) from or through whom the NR receives income; (iv) trustee of the NR; and (v) any other person who (whether resident or non-resident) has acquired by transfer a capital asset in India. In the first four cases, the person must be in India, whereas in the fifth case, even a non-resident person can be treated as the agent of another non-resident. Furthermore, the appointment of an agent may be made before or after the expiry of the previous year, and even if the non-resident is no longer alive at the date of appointment. Thus, Option B is correct.

questions.question: Mr. Vikram, a registered stockbroker on the Bombay Stock Exchange, executed bonafide hedging transactions in commodity derivatives on behalf of a London broker, Apex Commodities UK. Apex Commodities UK was acting in the ordinary course of its brokerage business for an undisclosed foreign corporate client. The Assessing Officer seeks to treat Vikram as the statutory agent of the foreign corporate client under Section 163 without issuing any prior show-cause notice. Is the Assessing Officer's action tenable in law?
options: Yes, because any broker in India executing transactions for an undisclosed principal is strictly and automatically deemed to be the statutory agent under Section 163(1)(ii).
Yes, because Section 163 does not require any opportunity of being heard prior to passing an order treating a person as an agent.

No, because the proviso to Section 163 protects an Indian broker dealing in the ordinary course through a foreign broker who also acts as a broker and not as a principal; furthermore, Section 163(2) mandates a reasonable opportunity of being heard.
No, solely because hedging transactions in commodities are completely exempt from direct taxes under Chapter IV-D of the Income-tax Act.
questions.explanation: According to the proviso to Section 163(1), where transactions are carried on in the ordinary course of business through a broker in India and the broker does not deal directly with or on behalf of the non-resident principal, but deals with or through a non-resident broker who also carries on such transactions in the ordinary course of his business and not as a principal, the broker in India cannot be treated as a statutory agent in respect of income arising to the non-resident. Thus, bonafide hedging transactions executed through an Indian broker and a foreign broker for an undisclosed principal are protected. Moreover, Section 163(2) expressly mandates that before a person can be treated as an agent of a non-resident, he must be given a reasonable opportunity of being heard by the Assessing Officer. Therefore, the AO's action is untenable on both substantive and procedural grounds, making Option C correct.

questions.question: When a person is treated as an agent of a non-resident under Section 163, he becomes a representative assessee under Section 160(1)(i). Which of the following statements correctly states the legal rights, liabilities, and protections available to such representative assessee under Sections 161 and 162?
options: He is subject to the same duties and liabilities as the non-resident, but he is entitled to retain out of money in his hands a sum equal to the tax estimated, and has a statutory right to recover any tax paid from the non-resident or be indemnified.
His liability is absolute and personal, meaning his personal assets in India can be auctioned even if he has never received or possessed any funds or property of the non-resident.
He cannot retain any money of the non-resident unless he obtains an attachment decree from a Civil Court under the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908.
The tax assessment on the representative assessee bars the Department from ever recovering any residual arrears directly from the non-resident under Section 173.
questions.explanation: Under Section 161, a representative assessee is subject to the same duties, responsibilities, and liabilities as if the income were received by him beneficially, and tax is levied upon and recoverable from him in like manner and to the same extent as it would be from the person represented. However, under Section 162, any representative assessee who pays any sum under the Act on behalf of another is entitled to recover the sum so paid from the person on whose behalf it is paid, or to retain an equivalent amount out of any moneys in his hands belonging to such person. He also has the right to secure an estimate of the tax from the AO to retain sufficient funds, and is indemnified for all payments made. Section 173 explicitly preserves the right to recover arrears from the non-resident's assets without prejudice to Section 161. Hence, Option A is fully accurate.

options: Resident and Ordinarily Resident (ROR); Total Income is ₹4,63,500.
Resident but Not Ordinarily Resident (RNOR); Total Income is ₹3,38,500.
Non-Resident (NR); Total Income is ₹40,000.
Resident but Not Ordinarily Resident (RNOR); Total Income is ₹18,500.
questions.explanation:
1. Residential Status: Stay in India during P.Y. 2025-26 = 293 days (≥ 182 days) => Resident. Having stayed in the UK for 20 years, he was a non-resident in 9 out of 10 preceding years and his stay in India in the 7 preceding years was < 730 days. Hence, his status is Resident but Not Ordinarily Resident (RNOR).
2. Scope of Total Income u/s 5(1): An RNOR is taxable only on income received/accrued in India, or income derived from a business controlled in or profession set up in India.
- Rental income in London (₹1,80,000) and German company dividends (₹1,20,000) accrued and were received outside India => Not taxable.
- Son B is a major (19 years) => His income is not clubbed.
- Son A is a minor (12 years): As per Section 64(1A), income accruing to a minor child is clubbed in the hands of the parent. However, the minor's foreign income (₹75,000) accrued and received abroad is not taxable in an RNOR parent's hands. The minor's Indian income of ₹20,000 is includible, subject to exemption of ₹1,500 under Section 10(32) [as old regime was opted]. Taxable clubbed income = ₹20,000 - ₹1,500 = ₹18,500.
- Repatriation of past foreign capital gains (₹50,000) is remittance of past savings, not income of P.Y. 2025-26 => Not taxable.
Total Income = ₹18,500. Option D is correct.

questions.question: Peeyush, who returned to India on 12th June 2025 permanently after 20 years in the UK (status: Resident but Not Ordinarily Resident for A.Y. 2026-27), claims that the repatriation of ₹50,000 of past capital gains earned in the UK during P.Y. 2024-25 cannot be taxed upon remittance in P.Y. 2025-26. Furthermore, he contends that dividend income from German companies deposited in a London bank account cannot be taxed in India. Which of the following legal propositions validates Peeyush's claims?
options: All foreign remittances are deemed to accrue in India under Section 9(1)(i) unless an exemption certificate is obtained from the CBDT.

Remittance or repatriation of income already accrued and received abroad in an earlier year does not constitute receipt of income in India in the year of remittance; moreover, an RNOR is exempt from foreign-source income unless derived from a business controlled in or profession set up in India.
Dividends from foreign companies are always taxable in India under Section 115A regardless of residential status or place of accrual.
An RNOR is treated on par with a resident and ordinarily resident in respect of all capital gains repatriated through authorized dealer banking channels.
questions.explanation: Under the Indian Income-tax Act, income is charged at the point of first receipt or accrual. Remittance or repatriation of money from a foreign bank account to India does not amount to 'receipt of income' in India; it is merely a transfer of accumulated funds/capital. Since the capital gains arose and were received abroad in P.Y. 2024-25 when Peeyush was a non-resident, subsequent remittance in P.Y. 2025-26 is not taxable. Additionally, under Section 5(1), a Resident but Not Ordinarily Resident (RNOR) is not chargeable on foreign-source income (such as German company dividends collected in London) unless it is derived from a business controlled in or a profession set up in India. Thus, Option B accurately encapsulates the legal rationale.

options: ₹14,50,000 (Global income is taxable as he is a Government of India employee)
₹10,50,000 (Salary, Foreign Allowance, and Bank Interest are taxable)
₹1,00,000 (Only Bank Interest is taxable since services were rendered in Canada)
questions.explanation:
1. Residential Status: Having spent 0 days in India during P.Y. 2025-26, Mr. David is a Non-Resident.
2. Scope of Total Income u/s 5(2) and Section 9:
- Salary: Under Section 9(1)(iii), income chargeable under the head 'Salaries' payable by the Government to a citizen of India for service outside India is deemed to accrue or arise in India. Therefore, salary of ₹5,00,000 is taxable in India.
- Foreign Allowance: Under Section 10(7), allowances or perquisites paid or allowed as such outside India by the Government to a citizen of India for rendering service outside India are wholly exempt. Thus, foreign allowance of ₹4,00,000 is exempt.
- Interest on fixed deposits in India: Accrues in India under Section 9(1)(v) => ₹1,00,000 is taxable.
- Agricultural income and rental income in Country X: Accrue and received outside India; hence not taxable in the hands of a non-resident.
Gross Total Income = ₹5,00,000 + ₹1,00,000 = ₹6,00,000. Option C is correct.

questions.question:
Regarding the taxability of salary and allowances paid to individuals serving abroad, evaluate the correctness of the following propositions:
Statement I: Salary payable by the Government of India to a foreign citizen for services rendered outside India is deemed to accrue or arise in India under Section 9(1)(iii).
Statement II: Foreign allowances paid by an Indian commercial public sector undertaking (PSU) or private multinational company to an Indian citizen deployed abroad are exempt under Section 10(7).
Statement III: The exemption under Section 10(7) is exclusively available to Indian citizens who receive allowances or perquisites from the Government of India for rendering services outside India.
options: Only Statement III is correct.
Statements I and II are correct, but Statement III is incorrect.
Statements II and III are correct, but Statement I is incorrect.
All statements are correct.
questions.explanation:
Statement I is incorrect: Section 9(1)(iii) deems salary to accrue or arise in India only if it is payable by the Government to a 'citizen of India' for service outside India; salary paid by the Government to a non-citizen for services outside India does not accrue in India.
Statement II is incorrect: Section 10(7) applies strictly to allowances or perquisites paid by the 'Government' to a citizen of India for services rendered outside India. Employees of PSUs, corporations, or private companies cannot claim exemption under Section 10(7).
Statement III is correct: The plain language of Section 10(7) restricts the benefit exclusively to citizens of India receiving allowances/perquisites from the Government for service outside India. Hence, only Statement III is correct (Option A).

questions.question: Mr. A, a citizen of India, left India for the USA for employment purposes on 01.05.2025 and did not visit India thereafter during P.Y. 2025-26. His friend, Mr. B, also an Indian citizen, had left India for employment in the USA on 24.04.2025 and remained outside India. In New York, Mr. A borrowed ₹10,00,000 from Mr. B at 10% interest per annum. Mr. A utilized the entire borrowed sum to purchase equity shares of X Ltd., an Indian company. The interest of ₹1,00,000 was paid by Mr. A to Mr. B directly in New York. Is the interest of ₹1,00,000 chargeable to income tax in India in the hands of Mr. B under Section 9(1)(v)?
options: Yes, because the borrowed funds were invested in the shares of an Indian domestic company, creating an Indian economic nexus.
Yes, because both Mr. A and Mr. B are citizens of India and Section 9(1)(v) taxes all global interest between Indian citizens.
Yes, because interest paid by any person to buy shares of an Indian company is deemed to accrue or arise in India regardless of who pays it.

No, because interest payable by a non-resident is deemed to accrue or arise in India only if borrowed and used for a business or profession carried on in India; borrowing to invest in shares is not for a business/profession carried on by A in India.
questions.explanation:
1. Residential Status: Both Mr. A (stay 31 days) and Mr. B (stay 24 days) are Indian citizens leaving India for employment abroad during the previous year; their threshold for residency is 182 days. Since neither satisfies this, both are non-residents for P.Y. 2025-26.
2. Deemed Accrual u/s 9(1)(v)(c): Interest payable by a non-resident is deemed to accrue or arise in India only if the debt is incurred or moneys borrowed and used 'for the purposes of a business or profession carried on by such person in India'. Where moneys are borrowed by a non-resident for any other purpose—such as earning dividend income or capital gains from shares—it is not deemed to accrue or arise in India.
Because Mr. A utilized the funds to buy shares (not for a business or profession carried on by him in India), the interest of ₹1,00,000 paid to Mr. B in New York is NOT deemed to accrue or arise in India. Therefore, it is not taxable in India in B's hands. Option D is correct.

questions.question: JJ Limited, a company incorporated in Australia, entered into a contract with KK Limited, an Indian company, to render technical services for designing and setting up a mega fertilizer plant in Odisha. Under the contract, JJ Limited rendered offshore engineering services from its Sydney design studio for a fee of ₹1.0 crore and onshore installation/testing services in Odisha for a fee of ₹1.5 crore. JJ Limited contends that the fee of ₹1.0 crore for offshore services is not liable to tax in India because the services were rendered entirely outside India. Is JJ Limited's contention valid under the Income-tax Act, 1961?
options: Valid, because the territorial nexus doctrine dictates that fees for technical services can only be taxed in India if the personnel physically perform the services within Indian territory.

Invalid, because under the Explanation below Section 9(2), fees for technical services are deemed to accrue or arise in India where the services are utilized in India, irrespective of whether the services were rendered in India or the non-resident has a place of business in India.
Valid, provided JJ Limited submits a Tax Residency Certificate (TRC) certifying that its Sydney office has no branch office or agency in India.
Invalid, but only if the payment of ₹1.0 crore is converted into Australian Dollars through an authorized dealer in India.
questions.explanation: Under Section 9(1)(vii), income by way of fees for technical services (FTS) payable by a resident is deemed to accrue or arise in India, except where payable in respect of services utilized in a business or profession carried on outside India or for making income from any source outside India. Here, the services were utilized for setting up a fertilizer plant in Odisha (in India). Furthermore, the Explanation below Section 9(2) explicitly clarifies that income by way of FTS is deemed to accrue or arise in India to a non-resident and be included in his total income, whether or not the non-resident has a residence or place of business or business connection in India, and whether or not the non-resident has rendered services in India. Therefore, the entire fee of ₹2.5 crores (both onshore ₹1.5 cr and offshore ₹1.0 cr) is deemed to accrue or arise in India. JJ Limited's contention is invalid, making Option B correct.

options: All four transactions (I, II, III, and IV) attract income tax in India.
Only transactions I and III attract tax; II and IV are exempt business profits.
Only transaction III attracts tax because payments by the Government are uniquely covered under Section 9(1)(vi).
Only transactions I, III, and IV attract tax; legal services before the Supreme Court are exempt from business connection.
questions.explanation:
All four transactions attract income tax in India under Section 9:
(I) Drawings and designs ('engineering fees') are fees for technical services (FTS) under Section 9(1)(vii) and are taxable in India as they are utilized for electrical work in India, irrespective of PE (Aeg Aktiengesellschaft v. CIT).
(II) A professional connection exists between the Mumbai firm and the UK barrister. As held by the Supreme Court in Barendra Prasad Roy v. ITO, the term 'business' in Section 9(1)(i) includes 'profession'; thus a professional connection amounts to a business connection, making the £5,000 deemed to accrue in India.
(III) Royalty payable by the Government of India for the use of a patent is deemed to accrue or arise in India under Section 9(1)(vi).
(IV) Debentures worth ₹20 lakhs issued for technical know-how represent FTS in kind under Section 9(1)(vii), and subsequent 8% interest payable by the Indian company on such debentures is deemed to accrue in India under Section 9(1)(v).
Hence, Option A is the correct answer.

questions.question: In the landmark judgment of Barendra Prasad Roy v. ITO (1981) 129 ITR 295, the Supreme Court of India interpreted the term 'business connection' under Section 9(1)(i) in the context of professional retainers paid to foreign professionals. What was the central ratio decidendi established by the Court?
options: A business connection can only arise if a foreign professional stays in India for at least 90 days in the relevant previous year.
The expression 'business' is narrower than 'profession', and therefore retainers paid to foreign advocates are purely personal gifts outside the scope of Section 9.

The expression 'business' is of wide import and includes within its scope 'profession'; consequently, a close, continuous professional connection between an Indian solicitors' firm and a foreign barrister constitutes a 'business connection' under Section 9(1)(i).
A foreign barrister arguing before the Supreme Court is an officer of the Court and is granted sovereign diplomatic immunity from Indian taxation.
questions.explanation: In Barendra Prasad Roy v. ITO (1981) 129 ITR 295, the Supreme Court held that the expression 'business' in Section 9(1)(i) includes within its scope 'profession' as well. An engagement of a UK barrister by a Calcutta/Mumbai solicitors' firm to represent a client before Indian courts involves an intimate, real, and continuous professional connection. Because 'profession' is subsumed within 'business' for the purpose of the charging provisions of Section 9(1)(i), such an association amounts to a 'business connection' in India, and fees paid under such professional engagement are deemed to accrue or arise in India. Therefore, Option C correctly articulates the ratio of the Supreme Court.

questions.question:
Mr. Z, an American tourist, came to India for the first time in his life on 17th June 2025 and left India on 29th September 2025. He had never visited India in any preceding financial year. Consider two independent scenarios:
Scenario A: Mr. Z is a foreign citizen with no Indian origin.
Scenario B: Mr. Z is a person of Indian origin (his grandparents were born in undivided India) and his total income from Indian sources for A.Y. 2026-27 is ₹16,00,000.
Determine Mr. Z's residential status for Assessment Year 2026-27 under Scenario A and Scenario B.
options: Scenario A: Resident; Scenario B: Resident but Not Ordinarily Resident.
Scenario A: Non-Resident; Scenario B: Non-Resident.
Scenario A: Non-Resident; Scenario B: Resident and Ordinarily Resident.
Scenario A: Resident but Not Ordinarily Resident; Scenario B: Non-Resident.
questions.explanation:
1. Stay in India during P.Y. 2025-26: June (14 days: 17th to 30th) + July (31 days) + August (31 days) + September (29 days) = 105 days.
Preceding 4 previous years' stay = Nil (first time visit).
2. Scenario A (American tourist): Under Section 6(1), an individual is resident if in India for ≥ 182 days, or ≥ 60 days in PY plus ≥ 365 days in 4 preceding years. Here, stay is 105 days (< 182 days) and preceding 4 years is 0 days (< 365 days). Thus, he is Non-Resident.
3. Scenario B (Person of Indian origin with Indian income > ₹15 lakhs): Under Explanation 1(c) to Section 6(1), for a person of Indian origin visiting India whose total income (other than foreign sources) exceeds ₹15 lakhs, the 60 days threshold is substituted with 120 days. To become resident (specifically RNOR), he must stay in India for ≥ 120 days in the PY AND ≥ 365 days in the 4 preceding years. Here, his stay in P.Y. 2025-26 is only 105 days (< 120 days), and his stay in the 4 preceding years is Nil. Thus, he fails both conditions and remains a Non-Resident.
Hence, under both scenarios, he is a Non-Resident. Option B is correct.

questions.question:
M/s. Global Airlines, a company incorporated in the USA and not having any bilateral tax treaty relief, operates passenger and cargo flights between New York and Mumbai. During Previous Year 2025-26, it collected the following revenues:
(i) ₹60,00,000 for carriage of passengers and cargo booked from Mumbai to New York (out of which ₹35,00,000 was received in Mumbai and ₹25,00,000 in New York);
(ii) ₹65,00,000 for carriage of passengers booked from New York to Mumbai, where the entire fare was received in New York in US Dollars.
Total operating expenses incurred by the airline during the year were ₹95,00,000. What is the income chargeable to tax in India for M/s. Global Airlines under Section 44BBA?
options: Nil (since operating expenses of ₹95 lakhs exceed total gross profit)
questions.explanation:
Under Section 44BBA, a non-resident engaged in the business of operation of aircraft is subject to presumptive taxation where 5% of the aggregate of specified amounts is deemed to be business profits:
1. Amount paid or payable (whether in or out of India) for carriage of passengers, cargo, etc., from ANY place in India: Here, carriage from Mumbai to New York is ₹60,00,000. Deemed income = 5% of ₹60,00,000 = ₹3,00,000 (place of receipt is immaterial for flights originating in India).
2. Amount received or deemed to be received IN INDIA for carriage from any place outside India: For flights from New York to Mumbai (₹65,00,000), the money was received in New York, NOT in India. Hence, deemed income is Nil.
3. Presumptive scheme overrides Sections 28 to 43A; therefore, actual operating expenses of ₹95,00,000 cannot be deducted.
Total income chargeable to tax = ₹3,00,000. Option A is correct.

questions.question:
Assume that in the case of M/s. Global Airlines (a foreign airline operating between New York and Mumbai under Section 44BBA), the collections for P.Y. 2025-26 are as follows:
- Passenger fare for journey originating in Mumbai to New York: ₹60,00,000 (₹40,00,000 received in India and ₹20,00,000 received in the USA);
- Passenger fare for journey originating in New York to Mumbai: ₹70,00,000 (₹30,00,000 received in India and ₹40,00,000 received in the USA).
What is the total income chargeable to tax in India under Section 44BBA?
questions.explanation:
Under Section 44BBA, deemed income equals 5% of the qualifying base:
1. Carriage from any place in India (Mumbai to New York): The entire ₹60,00,000 is included regardless of whether received in or out of India. 5% of ₹60,00,000 = ₹3,00,000.
2. Carriage from outside India into India (New York to Mumbai): ONLY the amount received or deemed to be received IN INDIA is included. Here, ₹30,00,000 was received in India (the ₹40,00,000 received in the USA is excluded). 5% of ₹30,00,000 = ₹1,50,000.
Total deemed profit chargeable to tax = ₹3,00,000 + ₹1,50,000 = ₹4,50,000.
Therefore, Option C is the correct answer.

questions.question: Atlant Italy, a company incorporated in France, supplies hardware alongside integrated operating software to cellular operators in India for GSM Cellular Radio Telephone Systems. The software is pre-loaded and embedded in the hardware and has no independent functional existence or commercial utility apart from operating the specific telecommunication hardware. The Assessing Officer asserts that consideration attributable to the embedded software constitutes 'royalty' under Section 9(1)(vi). Applying the jurisprudence laid down by the Delhi High Court in CIT v. Alcatel Lucent Canada (2015) 372 ITR 476, is the Assessing Officer's contention sustainable?
options: Yes, because Explanation 4 to Section 9(1)(vi) covers all software transfers regardless of medium or bundling with hardware.
Yes, because cellular operators in India acquire an intellectual property license to exploit telecommunication spectrum.
No, but only if the payment is routed through a French sovereign export credit agency.

No, because where software is embedded in hardware, forms an integral part of the telecom equipment, and has no independent existence, the transaction is for supply of goods/hardware and consideration cannot be taxed as 'royalty' under Section 9(1)(vi).
questions.explanation: In CIT v. Alcatel Lucent Canada (2015) 372 ITR 476 (and Ericsson A.B.), the Delhi High Court held that where software is embedded in the hardware and forms an integral, inseverable part of the equipment without any independent functional existence, the purchaser merely acquires the hardware system. In such cases, there is no transfer of copyright or right to use a computer program per se; rather, the software is merely the operating medium for the physical machinery. Therefore, consideration paid for equipment containing embedded software cannot be bifurcated or characterized as 'royalty' under Section 9(1)(vi). The AO's contention is not sustainable. Option D is correct.

questions.question:
Singtel Ltd. is a foreign company incorporated in Singapore, where 55% of its equity shares are held by Godavari (P) Ltd., an Indian company. For Previous Year 2025-26, the financial metrics of Singtel Ltd. are as follows:
- Trading Operations Income: India ₹25 crores; Singapore ₹50 crores (Total ₹75 crores).
  * Note: In India, ₹5 crores arose where BOTH purchases and sales were from/to associated enterprises (AEs); ₹2 crores AE purchase & 3rd party sale; ₹3 crores 3rd party purchase & AE sale.
  * In Singapore, ₹10 crores arose where BOTH purchases and sales were from/to AEs; ₹4 crores AE purchase & 3rd party sale; ₹5 crores 3rd party purchase & AE sale.
- Interest and dividend from investments: India ₹20 crores; Singapore ₹15 crores (Total ₹35 crores).
Compute the percentage of passive income to total income and evaluate Condition 1 of the Active Business Outside India (ABOI) test for POEM guidelines.
options: Passive income is ₹35 crores (31.82% of total income); Condition 1 is satisfied.
Passive income is ₹50 crores (45.45% of total income); since it does not exceed 50%, Condition 1 is satisfied.
Passive income is ₹69 crores (62.73% of total income); Condition 1 is violated.
Passive income is ₹15 crores (13.64% of total income); Condition 1 is satisfied.
questions.explanation:
Under the POEM guidelines for determining Active Business Outside India (ABOI):
1. Total Income = Trading income (₹25 cr + ₹50 cr) + Investment income (₹20 cr + ₹15 cr) = ₹110 crores.
2. Passive Income is defined as the aggregate of:
   (a) Income from transactions where BOTH purchase and sale of goods are from/to associated enterprises: India ₹5 crores + Singapore ₹10 crores = ₹15 crores. (Transactions where only one side is an AE are active business income!)
   (b) Income by way of royalty, dividend, capital gains, interest, or rental income: ₹20 crores + ₹15 crores = ₹35 crores.
   Total Passive Income = ₹15 crores + ₹35 crores = ₹50 crores.
3. Percentage of Passive Income to Total Income = (50 / 110) * 100 = 45.45%.
Since passive income (45.45%) is not more than 50% of total income, Condition 1 of the ABOI test is satisfied. Option B is correct.

options: Resident in India, because more than 50% of its equity share capital is owned by an Indian company, Godavari (P) Ltd.
Resident in India, because 3 board meetings were conducted in India, establishing significant operational presence.
Non-Resident in India, because it satisfies all four cumulative tests of ABOI (Active Business Outside India) and the majority of its board meetings (5 out of 8) were held outside India.
Resident but Not Ordinarily Resident, as ABOI status allows foreign companies concessional dual residency status.
questions.explanation:
To determine POEM for Singtel Ltd.:
1. ABOI Criteria (all 4 conditions must be cumulatively satisfied):
   - Passive Income: 45.45% (≤ 50%) => Satisfied.
   - Indian Assets: ₹210 cr / ₹610 cr = 34.43% (< 50%) => Satisfied.
   - Indian Employees: 70 / 160 = 43.75% (< 50%) => Satisfied.
   - Indian Payroll: ₹8 cr / ₹20 cr = 40.00% (< 50%) => Satisfied.
Since all four conditions are met, Singtel Ltd. is engaged in Active Business Outside India (ABOI).
2. POEM Determination: For a company engaged in ABOI, the POEM shall be presumed to be outside India if the majority of board meetings are held outside India. During P.Y. 2025-26, 5 out of 8 board meetings were held in Singapore (outside India).
Consequently, the POEM of Singtel Ltd. is outside India. Therefore, Singtel Ltd. is a Non-Resident for A.Y. 2026-27. Option C is correct.

options: ₹47,80,000 (Expenses of ₹26,000 and indexation benefit are disallowable under Section 115AD)
₹43,54,000 (After allowing indexation benefit on J Ltd. bonds and deduction of expenses)
₹47,54,000 (After allowing interest expenses of ₹26,000 but disallowing indexation)
₹38,86,000 (After excluding dividend income and applying indexation on bonds)
questions.explanation:
Computation of Total Income under Section 115AD for STYLE Inc.:
1. Dividend income: ₹6,20,000.
2. Interest on securities: ₹17,32,000. Under Section 115AD(2), no deduction is allowable under Sections 28 to 44C or Section 57. Thus, expenses of ₹26,000 cannot be deducted.
3. Long-term capital gains on bonds of J Ltd.: Sale consideration (₹47,00,000) - Cost of acquisition (₹32,00,000) = ₹15,00,000. Under Section 115AD(3), the 1st and 2nd provisos to Section 48 (foreign exchange conversion and indexation) do not apply to FIIs.
4. Short-term capital gains on listed shares of E Ltd. (STT paid): ₹12,40,000 - ₹7,80,000 = ₹4,60,000.
5. Short-term capital gains on unlisted shares of M Ltd.: ₹8,40,000 - ₹3,72,000 = ₹4,68,000.
Total Income = ₹6,20,000 + ₹17,32,000 + ₹15,00,000 + ₹4,60,000 + ₹4,68,000 = ₹47,80,000. Option A is correct.

Computation of Tax Liability under Section 115AD:
1. Tax @ 20% on dividend and interest on securities: 20% of ₹23,52,000 = ₹4,70,400.
2. Tax @ 12.5% on LTCG on bonds: Under Section 115AD(1)(b) as amended by Finance (No. 2) Act, 2024, LTCG is taxable @ 12.5%: 12.5% of ₹15,00,000 = ₹1,87,500.
3. Tax @ 20% on STCG u/s 111A (STT-paid listed equity shares): Under Section 111A as amended by Finance (No. 2) Act, 2024, rate is 20%: 20% of ₹4,60,000 = ₹92,000.
4. Tax @ 30% on other STCG (unlisted equity shares): 30% of ₹4,68,000 = ₹1,40,400.
Total tax before cess = ₹4,70,400 + ₹1,87,500 + ₹92,000 + ₹1,40,400 = ₹8,90,300.
Add: Health and Education Cess @ 4% = 4% of ₹8,90,300 = ₹35,612.
Total tax liability = ₹8,90,300 + ₹35,612 = ₹9,25,912.
Rounding off under Section 288B = ₹9,25,910. Option D is correct.

questions.question: Under Section 115JG of the Income-tax Act, 1961, special provisions apply to the conversion of an Indian branch of a foreign bank into an Indian subsidiary company in accordance with the scheme framed by the Reserve Bank of India. Which of the following conditions and consequences is INCORRECT in respect of such conversion?
options: Capital gains arising from the transfer of any capital asset or intangible asset by the foreign bank to the newly formed Indian subsidiary shall not be regarded as a transfer under Section 47.
The accumulated business losses and unabsorbed depreciation of the Indian branch can be carried forward and set off by the Indian subsidiary company.
The Indian subsidiary company must pay a mandatory one-time branch exit tax equal to 15% of the book value of net assets transferred.
The cost of acquisition of the assets transferred to the Indian subsidiary company shall be deemed to be the cost for which the foreign bank acquired them, increased by cost of improvement.
questions.explanation:
Section 115JG facilitates the seamless conversion of an Indian branch of a foreign bank into an Indian subsidiary in accordance with RBI framework:
1. The transfer of assets/liabilities by the foreign bank to the Indian subsidiary is exempt from capital gains tax (Section 47 / 115JG).
2. Accumulated loss and unabsorbed depreciation of the branch are allowed to be carried forward and set off in the hands of the Indian subsidiary.
3. The cost of acquisition and written down value (WDV) carry over from the foreign bank to the Indian subsidiary without step-up.
4. There is NO 'branch exit tax' of 15% prescribed under the Act for such RBI-approved conversion.
Therefore, Option C is incorrect (and hence the correct answer).

questions.explanation:
Under Section 115BBA, income of a non-resident non-citizen sportsman from (i) participation in any game/sport in India (₹15L), (ii) advertisements (₹10L), and (iii) contribution of articles in journals/magazines (₹2L) is taxable at a flat rate of 20% (plus surcharge, if any, and HEC @ 4%).
1. Total Income: Under Section 115BBA(2), NO deduction in respect of any expenditure or allowance is allowed under any provision of the Act. Thus, training/travel expenses of ₹4,00,000 cannot be deducted. Total income = ₹15L + ₹2L + ₹10L = ₹27,00,000.
2. Tax Deduction: Tax is deductible at source @ 20% (plus cess) under Section 194E.
3. Return of Income: Under Section 115BBA(3), an assessee is not required to furnish a return of income under Section 139(1) if his total income consists only of income referred to in Section 115BBA and tax deductible at source has been fully deducted.
Hence, Option B is correct.
